meetings.headline: Assessors will recommend a single (not split) tax rate and rejecting all three optional exemptions for FY2026
meetings.summary: The Board of Assessors reviewed FY2026 valuation and growth figures, worked through mapping and MUNIS data delays, and discussed hiring a third party to redo property neighborhoods after a citizen work group flagged inconsistent boundaries. The board leaned toward hiring an outside firm, rather than the citizen work group, to redo property-neighborhood boundaries after inconsistencies were flagged.

meetings.headline: Commission says school department is illegally withholding scholarship trust records; records request due Sept 26
meetings.summary: The Trust Fund Commission (two members present) spent most of the meeting on its ongoing dispute with the school department over scholarship and charitable gift funds, saying the district lacks authority to distribute money without producing the underlying trust declarations and citing a public records request due back September 26. It also discussed advertising and eligibility for the Nathaniel Day Poor Fund and the American Legion Fund, a warrant article for the November special town meeting on the board's authority to act without a full commission, outreach plans, and a standing vacancy for a third commissioner. No substantive votes were taken; the meeting adjourned after a motion.

budget_items.what_was_said: The town's trust funds are pooled with the Conservation Commission and Cemetery Commission and the treasurer reports quarterly on interest performance. The chair said he would not go over the treasury and finance director reports line by line.

The commission needs to correct and ratify the fund's filing before it can be advertised, then send it through town counsel to the Attorney General's office for approval of how the fund may be used. That review was described as taking several weeks.

budget_items.topic: Nathaniel Day Poor Fund - example distribution
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair used a hypothetical example of a named recipient receiving a public distribution from the Nathaniel Day Poor Fund to illustrate that awards from public trusts must be publicly disclosed.
The chair cited a federal/state poverty income threshold as an example of who would qualify for aid such as Medicare and food stamps, and by extension the trust funds.

The chair described a hypothetical trust fund for mental health support, using an example distribution amount to illustrate that awards are public even when the underlying need is a sensitive medical condition.

budget_items.topic: Historical Susan Howard poor fund example
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair described having seen old receipts showing a historical medical expense that a poor fund once helped cover, noting there is no longer a Susan Howard poor fund.
A member said the commission has a modest total balance in trust, only part of which is available to distribute this year, and that unused annual amounts do not roll over.

The chair used hypothetical gift amounts to distinguish a direct donor-to-recipient payment (not a trust) from money that is actually held in a school trust fund and thus subject to the commission's oversight.

budget_items.topic: Public records request to school department
budget_items.what_was_said: The commission's public records request to the school department, town manager, select board chair, town council and treasurer for scholarship fund amounts and declarations was sent September 5th and the response window was said to close September 26th.

The chair argued that state statute gives the school department unfettered discretion to move appropriated money between lines once town meeting approves a total, using an exaggerated example of buying scratch tickets to make the point.

decisions.decision: The Nathaniel Day Poor Fund application will stay offline for about another week and a half while the chair reviews wording concerns with legal counsel before advertising.
The commission will not vote on or finalize the Declarations of the American Legion Poor Fund, Howard Sidewalk Fund, and Gazebo Fund tonight, choosing to handle all of them together at once.

The chair will give the select board only same-day notice of the warrant-article presentation rather than advance materials, so debate happens live rather than being pre-scripted with the board's attorney.
The commission will hold off engaging the bylaw review committee until a new chair/appointment to that committee is in place.

The commission will not advertise or publicize the available trust funds until the school department produces the requested scholarship fund information, though outreach planning will proceed in parallel.

The commission also discussed Hollis Road residence budget items, a storm water utility warrant article, and a resolved no-trespass situation at the Pleasant Street Conservation Area.

what_happened.line: The commission approved the Lake Shirley boat ramp rebuild at Shady Point, granting waivers to work inside the normal 30-foot no-disturb and 50-foot no-build wetland buffers.
Four other wetland hearings, including a new house and driveway at 404 Page Street, were continued to October 7 rather than decided.
The commission approved three routine RDAs with standard conditions: a DPW cemetery expansion, a septic force main repair, and a shed/sand permit.
A non-binding warrant article was finalized asking whether storm water funding should move out of the operating budget into a dedicated storm water utility.
A vote on replacing flooring at the town-owned Hollis Road residence was deferred pending clarification of a vendor's deposit request.

why_it_matters: The boat ramp decision sets a precedent for allowing construction inside protected wetland buffers along Lake Shirley when a project shows a public benefit.

The storm water warrant article, if it reaches town meeting, would ask voters to decide whether storm water work gets its own dedicated funding stream instead of competing inside the general operating budget.
Residents near 404 Page Street, 108 Sunny Hill Road, the Violet irrigation pond, and 141 Pleasant Street will have another chance to be heard before any of those projects are decided.

meetings.headline: Select Board advanced the Food Pantry's temporary move to 30 School Street, waiving fees and OK'ing a license.
meetings.summary: The board presented three staff Merit Awards, publicly introduced new town manager Jessica "Jack" Miller, and voted to authorize a license agreement and waive building fees advancing the Lunenburg Food Pantry's temporary relocation to 30 School Street, amid public-comment dispute over whether that structure is "permanent" or "temporary." The board also referred zoning cleanup and stormwater-fee articles to the planning board for the November special town meeting, accepted a donated boulder for town hall, discussed but declined for now a MassWorks grant to study senior housing at the former TCP school, and debated (and largely declined) moving to a biweekly meeting schedule.

minutes.headline: Town meeting approved the school department's full state-aid request over a select-board bid to cut it
minutes.summary: This special town meeting was called by citizen petition mainly to decide how to allocate unanticipated state education aid and to restore cut middle-school sports. After an extended dispute over which vote threshold applies to different kinds of money articles and a lengthy sound-system delay, the meeting rejected a select-board amendment to reduce the school department's requested state-aid appropriation and approved the full amount for staffing, literacy and athletics needs. what_happened.line: Town meeting voted down a select-board amendment to cut the school department's requested state-aid appropriation, then approved the full amount.
The approved funds are earmarked for school staffing, K-12 literacy programming, and high school athletics transportation.
A second article was passed over after its goals were folded into the other two articles that passed.

The moderator ruled, on town counsel's advice, that raise-and-appropriate articles need a two-thirds vote while fund transfers need only a majority, settling a procedural dispute that opened the meeting.

why_it_matters: This decides how new, unanticipated state education aid gets spent -- toward school staffing, literacy programs and athletics -- rather than sitting unallocated in town free cash.
The vote-threshold ruling (two-thirds for raise-and-appropriate articles, majority for fund transfers) sets the procedure future money articles at town meeting will be judged against.
The WRAP fund transfer restores middle school sports and busing that had been cut from the school budget.

meetings.headline: Task force will draft a non-binding article asking town meeting to choose stormwater utility vs. operating budget funding
meetings.summary: The Stormwater Task Force reviewed impervious-surface billing data reconciled against the assessor's roll, settled on an ERU-based flat-fee approach rather than tiers, and discussed an abatement/credit program for commercial properties. Most of the meeting planned the path to the November 17 special town meeting: a non-binding straw poll on utility vs. operating-budget funding, a warrant article due September 17, a schedule of FinCom, Select Board and public information sessions in October/November, and a two-meeting process (around September 8 and 14) to draft, share and vote on the article language before sending it to town counsel Adam.

minutes.headline: Task force will draft a non-binding article asking town meeting to choose stormwater utility vs. operating budget funding
minutes.summary: The Stormwater Task Force reviewed impervious-surface billing data reconciled against the assessor's roll, settled on an ERU-based flat-fee approach rather than tiers, and discussed an abatement/credit program for commercial properties. Most of the meeting planned the path to the November 17 special town meeting: a non-binding straw poll on utility vs. operating-budget funding, a warrant article due September 17, a schedule of FinCom, Select Board and public information sessions in October/November, and a two-meeting process (around September 8 and 14) to draft, share and vote on the article language before sending it to town counsel Adam.

budget_items.what_was_said: After reconciling impervious-surface data with the assessor's roll, the consultant said the final flat per-household number came out around this figure and the task force preferred a flat fee over calculating perable area per residence.
The task force said there were questions on four properties and that they had gotten answers, citing this figure in the discussion of one parcel.
Two properties approaching a million square feet were cited as an example of how high a utility fee could get for very large non-residential parcels.
A comparison town's abatement system was described as capping relief at this level, described as a powerful incentive for commercial property owners to improve stormwater management.

The finance committee's objection to the utility approach centered on overhead described as around this share of the budget; a member argued the same share of overhead would exist under an operating-budget approach too.

budget_items.topic: Override amount for stormwater engineer position
budget_items.what_was_said: The task force recalled the failed override figure proposed to fund a junior engineer position, unsure whether it would need to change for the next attempt.
Because the junior engineer position would also do other DPW project-manager work, the task force suggested only about half the position's cost should be attributed to the stormwater comparison.

decisions.decision: Task force agreed to bill using an ERU (equivalent residential unit) approach based on actual impervious surface area rather than a tiered fee structure.
Agreed the warrant article should include enough financial/rate substance for voters to understand the choice, but should not include a draft bylaw.
Agreed stormwater fees will be billed separately from the property tax bill, with an option for residents to pay quarterly via a tear-off coupon.
Agreed municipal parcels will not be billed, but nonprofits and churches will be billed like any other property.
Agreed the task force needs to vote on the article language itself before it can be submitted, and that members cannot deliberate over email/BCC due to open meeting rules.
Set a schedule of two meetings (around September 8 and September 14) to draft, review, and vote on the article before sending it to town counsel Adam ahead of the September 17 warrant deadline.

Planned FinCom presentation for October 8, Select Board presentation for October 20, and a public information session in the first week of November (around November 3), spaced roughly two weeks apart ahead of the November 17 town meeting.

meetings.headline: The committee voted to restore a second-grade teacher and literacy funding over an audit or a second BCBA.
meetings.summary: The School Committee heard extended public comment on district turnover, reading scores, and school funding, then reviewed three alternative spending scenarios (financial audit, second-grade class-size reduction, or a second BCBA) for $418,000 in additional state aid to be requested at a special town meeting, alongside restoring athletic transportation. Staff presented a spreadsheet calculating the total connection fee owed for the condo units tying into an existing line, based on the original betterment amount and a half-betterment privilege fee charged per additional unit. meetings.headline: Committee decided any new town building houses only town offices — no school departments — after prior project's scope crept
meetings.summary: The Building Design Committee reviewed the TC Pacios walkthrough (records storage volume, roof condition) and worked through detailed space-needs planning for a town hall annex — conference rooms, counter space, storage and records-retention rules — using an AI-generated planning guide and employee questionnaire results. minutes.headline: Board agrees to temporarily blend wells to address manganese/PFAS violations pending DEP's long-term plan
minutes.summary: The Water Commissioners reviewed payroll warrants, edited minutes wording, and debated at length a commissioner's new manganese/PFAS data-tracking spreadsheet, with another commissioner questioning whether the board was overstepping into the superintendent's operational role. meetings.headline: Planning Board revised draft zoning bylaws for cluster, senior, and inclusionary housing for the 2027 town meeting
meetings.summary: The Planning Board held a working session reviewing the second draft of proposed zoning bylaw amendments -- cluster housing, senior housing, inclusionary housing, and a new minor site-plan-review provision -- aimed at the May 2027 annual town meeting. Members refined tree-species language, discussed submission standards, debated payment-in-lieu and affordable-unit percentages for the inclusionary bylaw, and set a plan to consult town counsel, brief other boards, and hold a public forum in the fall. No substantive votes were taken; the only vote was the procedural motion to adjourn.

budget_items.what_was_said: As an alternative to payment in lieu, the board discussed requiring a rising percentage of units be affordable as development size increases.
Using an assumed sale price and the draft 2% payment-in-lieu rate, a member calculated what a nine-unit development would pay the town, and compared it to what it costs to build a house.
The board re-ran the payment-in-lieu math at a higher percentage to see if it came closer to the value of a home, and considered doubling the draft rate.

budget_items.topic: Revised payment-in-lieu tiers by development size
budget_items.what_was_said: A member proposed new escalating payment-in-lieu percentages by number of units, meant to get the town closer to whole without erasing a developer's profit margin.

budget_items.topic: Finance Committee review of the bylaw package
budget_items.what_was_said: The board noted the Finance Committee usually finds no financial impact from zoning bylaws but agreed to brief them anyway since the warrant goes through them.

budget_items.topic: Inclusionary bylaw applicability to Parmiter Road development
budget_items.what_was_said: The board asked the building inspector for an opinion on whether the existing inclusionary bylaw applies to the Parmiter Road development, since it appears to exceed the unit threshold.

decisions.decision: Add language specifying shade trees must be of native species in both the cluster and senior housing bylaw sections.

Address extra submission standards for cluster and senior cluster developments in the site plan rules and regulations rather than in the bylaw itself, to be done when regs are updated for minor site plan review.
Clarify in the senior housing bylaw that the no-floodlighting provision applies specifically to multi-family buildings, not single-family garages.
Run the payment-in-lieu numbers at 5% (8-16 units), 7.5% (17-24 units), and 10% (25+ units) for the next draft.
Incorporate the member's suggested off-site-unit and existing-unit-conversion language (based on another town's bylaw) into the inclusionary draft.
Hold the common-driveway/dwelling-unit-count bylaw change until after the state legislature acts on a possible statewide duplex-by-right mandate, then add it to the May 2027 town meeting warrant.
Tim will take the lead presenting the draft changes to the Open Space group; the chair will sit in remotely.
Meet individually with each relevant board (Selectmen, Zoning Board, Open Space, Board of Health, Finance Committee) rather than holding one joint meeting.
Favor the library community room or the senior center over the high school as the public forum venue.
Try to get the town's topographic model of Lunenburg on display at the public forum.
Ask the building inspector for an opinion on whether the existing inclusionary bylaw applies to the Parmiter Road development.

meetings.headline: Assessors heard a stormwater task force pitch a new utility fee shifting costs onto big paved lots
meetings.summary: The Board of Assessors approved minutes from six earlier meetings and heard a lengthy presentation from a resident representing the town's stormwater task force on a proposed stormwater utility fee meant to close a DPW budget gap and meet EPA mandates, which would shift more cost onto large paved commercial/industrial properties. The board also reviewed the neighborhood-reclassification project's timeline (deferred to spring), got an update that the new principal assessor has been ratified and starts August 18th, and discussed raising the veterans' property tax exemption for a possible November town meeting warrant article rather than September. No substantive item beyond the minutes and adjournment was decided by a formal, counted vote.

meetings.headline: Personnel Committee, unsure of its own authority, parsed the town attorney's new reading of its bylaws
meetings.summary: The Personnel Committee (a three-member board, not yet fully seated) spent nearly the whole meeting working through correspondence from town counsel Mark Terry interpreting the committee's bylaws — its role in job descriptions, wage/salary equity reviews, reclassifications, new-hire pay above minimum step, and department budget pay-adjustment sections — and repeatedly found the bylaw language unclear on where its authority actually begins and ends. No formal votes were taken on substance; the committee agreed to seek outside opinions on the bylaws, meet with the attorney, request personnel data from HR, and possibly amend the bylaws with a plainer mission statement at a future town meeting.

budget_items.what_was_said: The committee discussed a bylaw requirement to periodically review wage and salary schedules for equity, and debated whether an outside entity, HR, or the committee itself should conduct it. No such review appeared to have been done recently; the committee proposed doing it at least every three years and getting historical data on when it was last done.

The chair raised whether funds would need to be allocated, possibly via a special town meeting article, to pay an outside consultant to conduct the wage and salary review. No dollar figures were discussed; the group planned to ask the town attorney about timing and process.

The bylaw requires each department head to include a pay adjustment section in its annual budget request, with expenditures from it needing personnel board approval. The committee was unsure whether its role is to approve or merely review these sections and planned to seek clarification from the town attorney.

The bylaw requires the personnel committee to determine that a position reclassification is consistent with the salary administration plan before it proceeds, with the request ultimately needing a town meeting vote to fund. The committee discussed that a department head and HR bring the request forward, not the employee directly.

budget_items.topic: New hire pay above minimum step
budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager must consult the committee chair before authorizing a new hire's pay above the minimum step of a grade range, and the full committee must vote if the hire is above step four. Discussion suggested such a vote could occur in executive session for privacy.

decisions.decision: The committee will discuss the attorney's bylaw letter section by section rather than reading it into the record.
The committee will compile a list of documents (job descriptions, employment contracts, current steps/grades) it wants access to on the shared drive, to raise with the town attorney and HR.
The chair will maintain a SharePoint folder for each SAP position containing its job description and related grade/salary information.
The next meeting (August 17) will focus on the chair's follow-up conversation with Attorney Mark Terry, who is expected to attend.

The committee will send HR Director Julie Belliveau a written request for a spreadsheet of all SAP-covered employees with grade/step, current job descriptions, anticipated new hires under the SAP, current collective bargaining agreements, and individual employment contracts, and will invite her to attend meetings.
The committee will keep meeting at the current lower Ritter conference room venue through the end of the year, revisiting accessible winter locations (library, town hall, DPW) later.

meetings.headline: The school committee voted to submit its own warrant article demanding the full extra state aid for the September 3rd special town meeting.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg School Committee reviewed FY26 end-of-year line item transfers and several donations (LEAF grants, band boosters, football boosters), heard the superintendent's summer report on hiring and grants, approved a 300th-anniversary fireworks display, and — the meeting's central business — amended and voted to submit its own warrant article requesting the full additional FY27 state education aid figure for a September 3rd special ("extra special") town meeting triggered by a citizen petition. The committee also ratified a new custodians' union contract, tabled a further FY26 budget update, and heard public comment urging both an MSBA application for Turkey Hill Elementary and full use of the additional state aid for schools rather than other town needs.

Argues the additional state education aid is not 'extra' money but taxpayers' own money returned for education and must be spent as such; describes her own child's larger class sizes and inability to fit a PE class into her schedule.

public_comment.stated_role: select board member, speaking as a resident
public_comment.topic: Praises the transparency of the custodians' contract summary, presents her own review of 10 years of cherry sheet data arguing state aid has never decreased year-over-year, and praises Mandy Gilman's citizen-petition process while urging the select board not to obstruct the special town meeting.

Asks whether the new part-time athletic director will also serve as a part-time assistant principal, as the prior athletic director had; told no, and that a full-time assistant principal would need town meeting appropriation.

what_happened.line: The Sewer Commission rejected both bids for the stalled 100 Laurel Lane sewer connection -- one for missing paperwork, one as too high -- leaving the ADU project without a contractor.

meetings.summary: A joint Select Board / Lunenburg Municipal Building Design Committee meeting opened with a presentation on Mass Save energy-summit incentives for building electrification, then shifted to a long workshop on the deteriorating TC Pacios (TCP) building — its failing systems, a history of a double-appropriated roof-repair fund later corrected at town meeting, and whether to repair or demolish it. No formal vote was taken on TCP or the Brooks House, but the group leaned toward not investing further in TCP, tasked the Facilities Director with cost estimates, and agreed the committee will bring formal recommendations on both buildings to a future meeting, with its next meeting set for August 3rd.

meetings.headline: Commission clarifies Legion Post 283 veterans fund's eligibility rules, avoiding a costly court filing
meetings.summary: The Trust Fund Commission appointed Richard Howard as vice chairman and then heard testimony from Ernie Sund, a founding devisee of the American Legion Post 283 trust fund, who clarified that eligibility is limited to Legion-eligible veterans (service during conflict years) who are three-year Lunenburg residents, not any veteran. The commission voted to accept a written clarification of donor intent based on that testimony, which the chair said avoids a probate cy pres court filing for the under-$75,000, under-20-year-old fund. Other agenda items, including treasurer/finance reports and a discussion of restricting appointees who ran contested elections, were deferred to the next meeting, set for August 27, 2026.

meetings.headline: Planning Board drafted zoning changes for minor site plan review, cluster housing, and senior/affordable housing.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Planning Board held an off-cycle working session to draft language for four zoning bylaw changes: minor site plan review, inclusionary housing, cluster housing, and a new senior housing bylaw. The board worked through a consultant's draft site plan amendment, discussed how an inclusionary housing bylaw with a payment-in-lieu and affordable housing trust could work alongside a proposed senior housing bylaw, and revised numerous cluster-housing standards (acreage threshold, open space percentage, density, buffers, performance guarantees). No formal votes were taken on the bylaw language itself; the board reached working consensus on several specific provisions and set its next working session for August 10th before adjourning with no public comment offered.

budget_items.topic: ARPA funds toward senior housing land
budget_items.what_was_said: A speaker recalled the town's own contribution to a past senior housing project as land plus ARPA funds. The exact dollar figure is garbled in the captions.

budget_items.topic: Inclusionary housing payment-in-lieu, tiered by units
budget_items.what_was_said: Discussion proposed a ramped payment-in-lieu into an affordable housing trust as unit thresholds rise, with a full unit required or its cash equivalent above the top threshold.

budget_items.topic: Housing trust's own home purchase, as a market comparison
budget_items.what_was_said: A board member cited a recent purchase by a housing trust as an example of how tight the local housing market has become.

budget_items.topic: Local housing market costs, cited during inclusionary bylaw discussion
budget_items.what_was_said: A board member described teardown and new-construction costs in town as context for why affordable inclusionary units are hard to produce without incentives.

budget_items.topic: State grant funding for a past affordable senior housing project
budget_items.what_was_said: A presenter described a prior town in which the state eventually funded affordable senior housing units on town-donated land after a multi-year process.

budget_items.topic: Grant to update the town's housing production plan
budget_items.what_was_said: The board discussed pursuing a state one-stop growth grant, since MRPC's regular funding program could not cover a housing production plan update.

decisions.decision: Drop the proposed C2 provision requiring full site plan review for minor changes near residential abutters, in favor of relying on the more easily amended site plan regulations.
Keep the inclusionary housing bylaw applicable to ANR lots for now, revisiting if a pattern of small estate-lot subdivisions emerges.
Reinstate a payment-in-lieu option and an offsite-unit option for developers triggering inclusionary housing requirements, with amounts to ramp up with the number of units.
Raise the single-family density cap in the cluster bylaw from two to four units per acre.
Keep the cluster housing minimum parcel size at 10 acres rather than lowering it to 5.
Add explicit language requiring the percolation test be completed before site plan review for cluster developments.
Reframe the cluster buffer as a non-disturbed area rather than a cleared buffer, with the planning board able to require landscaping if the area is already bare/grass.
Allow the required buffer area to count toward the cluster open-space percentage.
Remove letters of credit as an allowed performance guarantee for cluster developments, limiting security to cash, a AAA-rated bond, or a covenant.
Treat cluster developments as a single parcel with an exclusive-use area rather than individual lots, removing the need for a frontage standard.
Do not include an under-18 occupancy exclusion in the senior housing bylaw, so the bylaw remains eligible to carry inclusionary housing requirements.
Require native tree species in the landscaping/shade tree requirements.
Count only conditionable/livable space (not inaccessible attics) toward the senior housing maximum dwelling size cap.
Use a different parking standard than 1.5 spaces per unit for assisted-living-type senior housing, to be developed separately.
Hold the next working session on August 10th from 6:00 to 7:00 PM before the regular hearing agenda.

It also acted on several money and process items — adopting the IRS mileage rate, taking an eminent-domain easement for the Flatill Road bridge, designating the Cable Advisory Committee as special municipal employees, choosing police over a constable for three upcoming elections, and approving minutes including newly released executive-session employment agreements — while tabling the DPW union contract, the special election warrant, and the trust fund appointment, and deferring a decision on a special town meeting for additional state education funding.

The planning director described the cost of a full site plan review, including an engineering plan, for a business making only minor changes, calling the current requirement not business-friendly and part of the reason for a proposed minor site plan provision.

The planning director is working through about 70 outstanding 53G developer review-fee accounts dating back years and refunding unused balances; project review fees typically run in the low thousands depending on scope.
The planning director noted Lunenburg's tax revenue share from commercial and industrial development is below the threshold that keeps a town from being classified a bedroom community.

meetings.headline: Reactivated Personnel Committee elects officers, begins line-by-line review of the town's salary bylaws
meetings.summary: This was the first meeting of Lunenburg's Personnel Committee since it was reactivated after being inactive since 2024; the three appointed members elected officers and then read through the town's salary administration plan bylaw section by section, flagging language they want clarified by town counsel and the HR director. No formal policy changes were voted; the committee set a recurring meeting schedule and agreed to bring a list of questions to its next meeting on the 20th.

attendees.name_as_heard: Tanya Doll (also heard as Tanya Willard Doll)

budget_items.topic: Review of wage and salary schedules
budget_items.what_was_said: The bylaw requires the committee to review wage and salary schedules of all positions at a set interval and recommend action to the select board; members said comparable-town wage data has historically been hard to get accurately.

budget_items.topic: New hire starting pay / step approval
budget_items.what_was_said: New employees are to be hired at the minimum of the job's pay range unless the town manager, after consulting the chair, authorizes a higher step; the committee must formally vote to approve any new-hire pay above a stated step.

figures_as_heard: up to five days of vacation leave
budget_items.what_was_said: The plan lets the town manager offer recruitment incentives such as deposited vacation time or a sign-on bonus when hard-to-fill critical positions can't attract qualified applicants; the committee was unsure whether the town manager needs select board sign-off to use this.

Department heads must include a pay-adjustment section in their annual budget request, and any planned increase within the salary plan needs personnel committee approval before it goes into the budget; a member questioned whether step increases are actually automatic rather than discretionary.
Non-exempt employees get overtime at a stated multiplier of their regular rate for hours worked beyond a 40-hour week, counting paid leave time toward the 40 hours.

budget_items.topic: Compensatory time in lieu of overtime
budget_items.what_was_said: Employees may take compensatory time at the overtime rate instead of cash, but it must be used within a stated number of days.

Full-time employees accrue sick leave monthly up to a stated annual amount, cumulative up to a stated maximum, and it can be donated through a sick leave bank whose current status the committee was unsure of.

Employees who retire in good standing and were hired before a stated cutoff date get a percentage of accumulated unused sick leave paid out, rising with years of service; a member noted this only applies to employees hired before a certain date and few may still qualify.

budget_items.topic: Parental leave use of sick leave
budget_items.what_was_said: New parents may draw on a prorated cap of sick leave hours for parental leave.
Employees receive an annual longevity bonus as a percentage of salary starting after a stated years-of-service threshold, increasing at further milestones, paid each year on the anniversary date.

budget_items.topic: Pay upon transfer to a lower-graded job
budget_items.what_was_said: The committee discussed that an employee transferred to a lower-paying job could actually lose pay under the plan's placement formula, and planned to raise questions about it with counsel.

decisions.decision: Invite town counsel Attorney Terry and the HR director to the committee's next meeting (the 20th) to review bylaw language and roles.
Chair will ask the town's IT/facilities contact (Mason) about a portable meeting device (the 'owl') so meetings could move to other rooms.
Chair will compile a written list of the committee's questions for Attorney Terry and HR, to be sent ahead of the next meeting.
Committee will request copies of the recently finalized union contracts once available.
Committee will ask HR/town manager about the current status of the sick leave bank.
Committee will meet on the first and third Monday of each month going forward, and the chair will look into using the senior center or library as a more accessible meeting space.
Members will send any questions for Attorney Terry and HR to the chair by Monday the 13th so they can be answered in advance.

meetings.headline: Assessors reviewed a lakefront property revaluation plan and weighed raising the veterans' tax exemption.
meetings.summary: The Board of Assessors received a detailed update on a neighborhood-by-neighborhood review of waterfront and lake-adjacent property valuations, aimed at correcting mislabeled parcels while avoiding sudden value drops before recoding takes effect on future tax bills. The board also discussed the principal assessor search (two candidates in a second interview round), planned a senior means-tested exemption presentation for early August, and opened discussion on possibly raising the veterans exemption for a future town meeting article. No formal votes were taken; the meeting ended with informal agreement on next steps and September meeting dates.

budget_items.what_was_said: The presenter said that without adjusting factors, waterfront parcels inside site index one would have dropped in value by roughly this much per parcel.
The waterfront site index one factor was kept the same to avoid dropping values that have held for three years.
Sales reviewed showed little difference across the seven neighborhoods, so the factor was adjusted only slightly rather than left as before.
A small unbuildable waterfront parcel was found valued far higher than a neighboring home's lake-view land, which the board called unreasonable and possibly a data error.
Treating a property as lake-back rather than a standard neighborhood raised its value by this amount in the presenter's test.
A tentative sub-neighborhood factor was applied for properties near but not on the water, pending confirming sales.
The board target for the assessment ratio is 95%, and current values are at or near that target.
The current veterans exemption is reimbursed by the state at this amount, and it has not been increased while other exemptions were.

budget_items.topic: Veterans exemption comparison / state reimbursement formula
budget_items.what_was_said: Other communities have adopted a higher veterans exemption add-on, funded by the town rather than the state, and the state's own reimbursement formula was cited without certainty.
The office is currently being run by one staff member working a limited weekly schedule while covering the whole department.

budget_items.topic: Senior means-tested exemption utilization, prior year
budget_items.what_was_said: The board recalled a low number of applicants used the senior means-tested exemption in its second year, fewer than they had expected.

budget_items.topic: Combined circuit breaker and exemption benefit
budget_items.what_was_said: Combining the circuit breaker credit with the senior exemption was described as putting a substantial amount back into an eligible senior's spending money, though the specific figures given were garbled.

If the senior means-tested exemption amount is raised, the added cost is supposed to be redistributed across all other tax bills via a tax shift rather than paid from the overlay, and the mechanics still need to be worked out.
The exemption cost is currently being covered through an inflated overlay amount because the town lacks a proper overlay figure, which the assessor said needs to be corrected going forward.

decisions.decision: Keep the waterfront site index one factor and the seven-neighborhoods factor essentially unchanged so parcel values do not drop, rather than following the raw sales-derived factors.
Hold off recoding waterfront parcels' site index/land use codes until around August, after the second round of preliminary tax bills goes out, so the new values first appear on the actual tax bill.
Hold the senior means-tested exemption public presentation the week of August 10th at the senior center.
The assessing office resolved its PDF/Adobe software need directly with vendor staff, so the town does not need to purchase a license.
Tentatively set the board's next two meetings for September 9th and September 23rd.
Discuss increasing the veterans exemption further at a future meeting before deciding whether the board will sponsor it for the November special town meeting.
The assessor will research how a larger senior exemption amount could be redistributed across all tax bills via a tax shift instead of being funded through the overlay.

meetings.headline: Committee debates hiring an architect and pushes to fold TC Pacios into its town-hall design charge
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Municipal Building Design Committee reviewed a space-needs spreadsheet comparing today's town hall/Ritter building footprint to 2016 and 2020 proposals, and leaned toward an open 'bullpen' layout with shared counters for departments like assessors, treasurer/collector and town clerk. Members debated whether to spend committee funds on hiring an architect for preliminary concept drawings versus attempting a first layout themselves, and a member argued strongly that TC Pacios (its storage, voting function, and community activities like the food pantry and teen center) must be folded into the committee's charge before any town hall/Ritter plan can succeed. The chair set the next meeting for July 20th and plans to press the select board to formally include TC Pacios in the committee's scope at its July 14th meeting.

budget_items.topic: Office square footage across past proposals
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair compared today's office footprint to 2016 and 2020 proposals and said the total, with meeting rooms, bathrooms and elevators added, still looks close to a similar overall building size.

The chair said record storage was the biggest driver of added square footage in past proposals, citing examples like Board of Health's file cabinets and one department's request to roughly double its existing space.
A member said town employees had been reasonable, citing this per-person figure as the basis for building the space footprint.

budget_items.what_was_said: A member counted roughly this many total town employees, including IT and facilities staff, to size a single larger meeting room.

budget_items.what_was_said: Dave suggested using the number of assessor's office employees multiplied by the per-person standard as a starting point since the department had not responded with its own request.

budget_items.topic: Cost to hire an architect/consultant for concept drawings
budget_items.what_was_said: A member proposed a statement of work of roughly 40 hours of consulting time at this hourly rate to produce preliminary concept drawings, estimating the total cost.

budget_items.topic: Burns and Taylor's prior design cost
budget_items.what_was_said: A member said Burns and Taylor spent this amount on a prior design without ever talking to town employees about their needs, calling it a wasted expense.

budget_items.what_was_said: Dave said the teen center board is pricing a geodesic dome over part of the parking lot to replace gym space, estimating this rough cost, which another member called a lot of money.

decisions.decision: General agreement to pursue a 'bullpen' shared-space layout rather than fully separate department offices, keeping the town clerk as its own distinct area.

Use each department's current employee count times the per-person square-footage standard as the placeholder figure for the assessor's office, since assessors/accounting had not returned their space request.
Committee leans toward attempting a first-pass layout themselves before deciding whether to pay for an outside architect/consultant.
Hold off contacting architect Damon Mcuade about consulting, since he has filed to run for select board and it would be inappropriate given the pending special election.
Add a future agenda item to formally review the TC Pacios building together with the facilities manager, including a report from him.

Chair will not speak during the select board's next meeting (no public comment scheduled) but will raise the case for including TC Pacios in the committee's charge at the select board's July 14th meeting, which is set to discuss town buildings.
Set the committee's next meeting for July 20th, skipping the usual first-Monday date because of the holiday weekend.

meetings.headline: The committee voted unanimously to ask the select board for a special town meeting to redirect state aid into the school budget.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg School Committee heard extensive public comment on middle school athletics funding, booster fundraising, and academic performance following the failed override, then reviewed routine business (minutes, a donation, four line-item transfers, warrants, and encumbrances). The superintendent reported on transportation vans, a facilities earmark, staffing changes, and Title IX/booster-donation guidance; the committee also approved an adult meal price increase, relocated the T-ball program to accommodate the food pantry, accepted a curriculum report describing the loss of all reading interventionists and larger class sizes, accepted a strong FY26 quarterly budget report, accepted a personnel report with numerous departures attributed to budget uncertainty, and voted unanimously to ask the select board to convene a special town meeting to direct additional state chapter 70 and other cherry sheet funds into the school budget.

public_comment.topic: Argues the override failed due to lost public confidence, not messaging; cites accreditation risk and reading proficiency, urges review of support programs, academic prioritization, IEP audit, and accountability.

public_comment.topic: Presented a by-sport athletics cost/revenue analysis built from FY24 actuals, arguing middle school sports were revenue-positive and questioning the decision to cut them for budget reasons.
Spoke on behalf of the community about restoring middle school athletics, requesting a detailed cost/revenue breakdown by sport and guidance on applying community-raised funds, by mid-July.

Requested permission to purchase five football helmets and to fund one-way transportation to away games using booster funds, and pushed back on the characterization of football boosters as "wealthier" than other programs.

public_comment.topic: Raised the fundraising policy's two-fundraiser limit, asked for guidance on donating funds for color guard/marching band uniforms and transportation, requested restoring fifth grade band and sixth grade jazz, and raised concerns about scheduling forcing students to choose between electives and academics.

meetings.headline: Commissioners rescinded their prior vote and will proceed with the new billing/accounting software vendor.
meetings.summary: The Water District Commissioners reversed a prior vote to cancel a new billing/accounting software switch, approved several purchases (pipe, materials, hydrants) for a PVC water main replacement on Metal Lane, and discussed ongoing PFAS treatment planning that remains stalled pending state guidance. They also tabled a legal/easement dispute over kayaks stored near the Hickory Hills wellfield, discussed the revenue benefits of selling water to commercial buyers, and set a revised July meeting schedule.

public_comment.topic: Asked whether the easement/deed restricting structures at the Hickory Hills pumping station is a recorded legal document, and whether Hickory Hills residents had sent any letter committing to remove kayaks/canoes stored there.

votes.motion: Approve the minutes of June 10th
Rescind the prior (June 10th) vote that had cancelled/changed the plan to switch billing software, and continue moving forward with the vendor (referred to as the 'beta' company)
Approve the pipe quote from EJP (EJ Prescott) for the Metal Lane water main replacement project
Approve purchase of $14,557.89 of materials (excluding hydrants) from Ferguson for the Metal Lane water main replacement project, funded from the equipment and main account
Approve $7,300 for the purchase of two hydrants for the Metal Lane main from the hydrant vendor (heard as 'FW')
Adjourn the meeting

budget_items.what_was_said: After an additional meeting with the vendor, the board decided to proceed with switching accounting systems effective July 1 to align with the new fiscal year, while the actual resident-billing switch may slip to October 1st or January 1st depending on testing.
Ductile iron pipe pricing was compared to the lowest PVC bid; PVC was chosen as a test run for the Metal Lane project, with the pipe quote awarded to EJP.
Ferguson won the materials quote; removing the hydrants from that quote brought the material cost down, to be paid from the equipment and main account.
Two hydrants were purchased separately from the materials quote to match the M&H brand already used on the rest of the project.

Using PVC instead of ductile iron was said to save enough per street that two streets could be done for the cost of one; a prior project (Rolling Acres) was said to have saved roughly half a million dollars by doing the work in-house.

budget_items.topic: Hydrant maintenance reimbursement from the town
budget_items.what_was_said: The district receives a flat annual reimbursement from the town's fire department budget for hydrant maintenance, unchanged by the number of hydrants; a commissioner raised whether hydrant testing/flushing costs are fully covered and asked it be revisited.

budget_items.topic: Cost and revenue from bulk/commercial water sales
budget_items.what_was_said: The district calculated its cost to pump/treat water per million gallons versus what it charges bulk buyers (mainly one large commercial hauler), estimating roughly the stated annual revenue since sales began, which offsets what would otherwise be charged to the roughly 2,500 users.

budget_items.topic: PFAS/PAS water treatment and SRF funding
budget_items.what_was_said: Voters denied SRF funding for treatment, but the board discussed continuing baseline engineering/survey work for a Keyes-to-Lancaster transmission main, comparing costs to other towns' treatment plants.
Revenue from bulk water sales is folded into the roughly stated operating budget; any surplus beyond covering the budget is used for capital items like equipment purchases.

budget_items.topic: New display TV for AMI meter monitoring
budget_items.what_was_said: The district purchased a large TV, described as inexpensive, to display real-time meter/leak data for staff and the public.

transfers.description: Materials purchase for Metal Lane water main project paid from the equipment and main account

decisions.decision: Proceed with switching accounting/billing software to the new vendor effective July 1st for accounting, with the resident billing switch possibly delayed to October or January depending on readiness.
Run the new billing system in parallel (dry run) alongside the existing NDS system before fully switching over, to check accuracy before sending bills.
Superintendent Fran will speak with a newspaper reporter (from the Ledger) about the sale of water to commercial buyers.
Hold off on any action regarding the zone one easement/kayak issue until the next meeting, pending the chair's input and a possible different approach than sending another letter to legal.
Test each of the four wells feeding the Lancaster source individually for PFAS to determine if a weaker well could be shut off while blending the others.
Cancel the July 8th and July 22nd commissioners' meetings and hold a single meeting on July 15th at 4:00, with a public notice of the schedule change.

Clerk will respond to a resident's inquiry by naming the district's attorney (KP Law, Brian Riley) but direct him to route further questions through the water district rather than contacting counsel directly, and will notify the attorney to confirm with the board before engaging.

meetings.headline: Task force keeps refining property-by-property stormwater fee data and leans toward a utility, not the operating budget
meetings.summary: The Stormwater Task Force spent nearly the entire meeting working line-by-line through a combined assessor/Weston & Sampson spreadsheet, assigning ERUs and fixing missing use codes, missing impervious-area data, and how condo/rental/HOA complexes should be billed. It also compared funding the program through the operating budget versus a stand-alone utility fee, leaning toward the utility option, and set next steps (checking an old CI spreadsheet, sending gaps to the consultant, finishing a bylaw draft) before a possible fall Town Meeting article.

attendees.role: task force member (built the property/ERU spreadsheet and MATLAB data processing)
DPW / task force member (holds assessor data, coordinates with assessor's office)

budget_items.topic: Sum of proposed stormwater fees across all properties
budget_items.what_was_said: The consolidated spreadsheet's fee column was summed across all properties to see what the ERU-based fee schedule would raise in total.
The per-ERU fee used in the spreadsheet was described as changeable depending on the final budget target for the program.
It was suggested the per-ERU fee could come down significantly in a future iteration if the budget requirement is reduced, making it more palatable to residents.
A task force member noted their own household's estimated annual fee under the current model.

budget_items.topic: 1295 Massachusetts Ave storage facility bay sale
budget_items.what_was_said: A member noted one storage bay unit in the facility recently sold, illustrating the property is actively subdivided and sold by unit.

budget_items.topic: Property tax calculator - operating budget scenario
budget_items.what_was_said: A member ran the town's property tax calculator assuming the stormwater program were funded through the operating budget with a given increase, to see the effect on the average single-family tax bill versus shifting cost to commercial/industrial.
Based on the calculator, a member said the average home's increase would be somewhat higher than an earlier estimate.

budget_items.topic: Estimated fee jump for one large gravel/industrial property
budget_items.what_was_said: A member estimated the storm water fee for one large industrial/gravel operation would rise sharply from its current near-zero assessment once properly classified.

budget_items.topic: Lunenburg Crossing tax bill and assessment
budget_items.what_was_said: Members looked up the shopping center's current tax bill and assessed value, noting the assessment had fallen from the prior figure, to gauge how a stormwater utility fee would compare to its existing tax burden.

budget_items.topic: Per-acre tax comparison, Lunenburg Crossing vs. typical home
budget_items.what_was_said: Members compared per-acre tax payments between a large commercial property and a typical one-acre single-family home to argue commercial parcels pay less per acre.
A member gave their own per-acre tax figure to illustrate the gap between residential and commercial per-acre taxation.
Members discussed that administrative overhead for billing (integrating into MUNIS, similar to the sewer billing process) had originally been high and was negotiated down.

decisions.decision: For 400 Lemon(ster) Shirley Road (Mary Coburn/Edal property), the use code will be corrected/forced to code 4101 rather than left blank.
Woodlands condominiums and Stone Farm Estates will keep individual per-unit assessment rather than being billed as one global fee, since prior treatment made sense.
1295 Massachusetts Ave storage facility bays: the fee will be assigned to the overall property owner/manager rather than split among individual bay renters.
Tri-Town Apartments (use code 9960) will be billed as one combined fee to the owning entity rather than split by individual building/unit.
The Emerald Place property's impervious area will be combined with the adjacent Arrive property and billed as a single combined fee to the ownership entity.
Future task force meetings will be held on Microsoft Teams instead of Zoom, since the group already has Teams licensing and had recording trouble on Zoom.

Before asking Weston & Sampson for additional survey data, the task force will first check the town's older CI (commercial/industrial) spreadsheet to see if it already has the missing impervious-area figures.
A member will compile the list of properties needing reassessment/additional impervious-area data and send the questions to Weston & Sampson (via the consultant referred to as "J"/"Jice").

The task force leaned toward pursuing a stand-alone stormwater utility rather than funding the program through the operating budget, given the larger tax-bill impact and lost commercial cost-shifting under the operating-budget option.
Combining the sewer commission and a stormwater commission would require action by the state legislature, so this is not being pursued as a near-term option.
The list of properties lacking impervious-area data will simply be sent on to the consultant rather than reviewed line-by-line by the full task force first.
Next two task force meetings set for Monday, July 13th and Thursday, July 30th.

A fall Town Meeting article would ask voters to act on the funding mechanism and any bylaw the task force drafts.

meetings.headline: The board voted to press the state legislature to preserve the Foundation Budget Review Commission and boost school aid in the FY27 budget.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Select Board ratified two seasonal appointments, adopted an updated environmentally preferable purchasing policy, and voted to support a legislative letter urging retention of the Foundation Budget Review Commission and higher school aid levels in the FY27 state budget. The town manager reported progress on a temporary food pantry site at the former School Street school, the awarded Flat Hill Road Bridge contract, and a dangerous/nuisance dog complaint headed to a standalone hearing; the board also scheduled a July 14 goals workshop, approved several sets of prior minutes, heard numerous committee reports, and voted to enter executive session on non-union personnel matters.

meetings.headline: Space-needs survey shows town departments need far less room than the committee's earlier 14,000-sq-ft plan
meetings.summary: The Building Design Committee spent the meeting reviewing department-by-department responses to its staff space-needs survey (town clerk, treasurer, HR, town manager, conservation, planning, facilities, building department, board of health, recreation), flagging where storage and interaction questions needed to be re-asked in clearer terms (e.g., "file cabinets" instead of square footage). No formal building or budget decision was made; the committee agreed to keep assessing needs independent of current buildings, standardize how storage is measured, and reconvene June 29th, while several members stressed the town currently has little appetite or capital funding for new construction.

budget_items.topic: Cost of new building storage space
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair noted that 500 square feet of storage in a new building translates into a large dollar figure, cautioning the committee that small square-footage numbers become much bigger costs when discussing new construction.

budget_items.topic: Prior building proposal vs. current survey estimate
budget_items.what_was_said: A member noted the space needs identified in the new staff survey come in well below his earlier per-person calculation, and well below the committee's previous proposal that was rejected by the town.
The town clerk's office was estimated at roughly 600 square feet for three staff, with the main gaps being vault space, counter space, and a private area for voting-related business.

The treasurer's office was reported at about 128 square feet for three employees, described as tight, with a need for more storage, a secure area for cash handling, and vault space; a member asked for actual square-footage or filing-cabinet estimates rather than vague terms.
HR's current space was reported at about 129 square feet for one employee, which the committee felt was adequate; a small amount of additional storage was requested.

The town manager's office and storage were estimated at roughly 450 square feet of office plus 120 square feet of storage, described as close to adequate, with a request for a private meeting room for up to six people.
Conservation's office and storage were estimated at about 187 square feet for one employee, with a request for a service counter and space to spread out plans with visitors.

The planning department reported about 750 square feet including a conference room, described as an inefficient layout; digitization was said to be reducing storage needs significantly and older records could move offsite.
Facilities reported about 160 square feet of office space at the Ritter building, with the main unmet need being dedicated shop/storage space, currently borrowed from DPW.

The building department reported about 350 square feet of office and counter space, with storage described in cubic feet rather than square feet, which the committee found hard to compare across departments.

budget_items.topic: Board of Health office and storage
budget_items.what_was_said: The Board of Health and a shared part-time staffer occupy about 179 square feet including fourteen filing cabinets, with digitization identified as a way to reduce future storage needs.

decisions.decision: Laura agreed to draft additional survey questions about how often staff interact with other departments/offices, to be sent through the town manager.

Committee agreed (per Chris's suggestion) to assess each department's space needs independent of whether Town Hall or the Ritter building currently houses them, rather than designing around existing buildings first.
Committee agreed to standardize future storage questions around number of filing cabinets (or filing method) and frequency of access, rather than square footage alone.
Next committee meeting set for June 29th.

meetings.headline: Board voted to send the Hickory Hills kayak-rack zone-one violation dispute to legal counsel, KP Law

Criticized a commissioner's ties to a Hickory Hills resident group over the kayak dispute, urged the district to spend whatever it takes on legal action, and suggested the district simply remove the kayak racks itself.

meetings.headline: Assessors overhauling flawed waterfront property valuations while approving FY2027 preliminary tax bills
meetings.summary: The Board of Assessors reorganized with a new member, elected officers, and paid tribute to the outgoing principal assessor for stabilizing the office, fixing chapter-land liens, and recovering missed new growth. Most of the meeting covered signing FY2027 preliminary tax warrants and commitments, ongoing GIS/mapping vendor troubles, and a consultant's report on overhauling the town's inconsistent waterfront property valuation neighborhoods, which the board agreed to continue revising. No members of the public were present or commented, and the board set its next three meeting dates before adjourning.

budget_items.what_was_said: The board noted these supplemental bills were already signed/approved the prior month, with no new supplemental bills added this cycle.

budget_items.what_was_said: Releasing a chapter-land tax lien when a property leaves agricultural (61A) classification requires paying back taxes and a fee to record the release at the Registry of Deeds.

budget_items.topic: Vision vendor quote to update property record cards
budget_items.what_was_said: The board discussed paying an outside vendor to update yearly property record cards after in-house software/PC issues made the process cumbersome, calling the cost well worth it.

The consultant's report proposed applying a combined waterfront valuation factor derived from recent lake-area sales, split into a base factor plus a per-lake sub-neighborhood adjustment, replacing outdated 'good/average/below average' waterfront ratings.
The board discussed Clause 18, a discretionary one-time tax relief tool for taxpayers in dire financial straits, noting the town has no applicants and has not yet finalized criteria for granting it.

budget_items.topic: Senior means-tested tax exemption / circuit breaker
budget_items.what_was_said: The board discussed Lunenburg's locally adopted senior means-tested exemption, which requires filing a federal tax return and qualifying for the state circuit breaker credit, described as a substantial tax break for eligible seniors.

decisions.decision: Board endorsed dedicating a separate server at town hall for GIS map updates so the principal assessor's laptop is no longer tied up for days during updates.
Board agreed to restore both property record card views on the website, with the more frequently updated one clearly labeled 'in process' to avoid confusing residents.
Board agreed to eliminate the 'average' and 'below average' waterfront quality ratings entirely and instead apply valuation factors based on actual property quality.
Board indicated the town intends to acquire the chapter-land property at issue, pending a letter from the Select Board.
Board set July 1, August 5, and September 2 as tentative dates for its next meetings, planning to meet only monthly over the summer.

meetings.headline: Failed town override cuts town concert funding and a town staff position, pushing website work onto PACC volunteers
meetings.summary: The Public Access Cable Committee handled routine business: minutes, a volunteer-applicant referral from the select board, the manager's monthly report, and a discussion clarifying that the failed town override (not the base FY2027 budget) is what cost the town its concerts and a town website/social-media staff position. The bulk of the meeting covered a consolidated policy/bylaw binder Steve compiled for review and eventual posting, an update on staffing the new cable advisory committee, and scheduling the July 6th meeting as an organizational meeting to fill two open PACC seats.

attendees.role: chair (conducted roll call, name not stated)

budget_items.what_was_said: The manager reported there are no town concerts because the override did not pass, so there is no funding for them.

A member clarified the override was meant to add extra funds on top of the base budget, not replace it; the base budget passed at town meeting regardless of the override's failure. Anyone counting on override money will not have it, though department heads may seek other adjustments.
It was noted that ordinary micro-adjustments happen within any budget (a role costs more or less, staff turnover) and these are called adjustments, distinct from the override question.
Line item transfers within the town budget are approved by the town manager; department heads can request them but need the town manager's sign-off, unlike in the past.

budget_items.topic: elimination of a town website/social media position
budget_items.what_was_said: Because the override failed, the town is eliminating a position handling website updates, social media and IT liaison work; PACC will informally take over doing the town website updates as a result.

January-through-March investment and interest was posted to the committee's account; the manager discovered the reported total interest actually combines two different bank sources (Main Street Bank and a second bank/entity) and will separate them going forward in Munis.
The committee had to buy a new eight-input ATEM switcher after the previous one burned out from hot-swapping, plus a new wireless transmitter and receiver after one failed.
The manager reported the purchase order for the Castus system was received; installation is not yet scheduled.
This report was not sent to the chair for the meeting because it was covered at the prior meeting.

Agreed that Steve (PACC) will take over doing the town website updates for the committee's own page, since the town position that did this is being eliminated.

what_happened.line: The Parks Commission voted to fund the part-time recreation director's FY27 salary entirely from the department's revolving account, as a one-year trial toward a self-sustaining position.
The commission elected Chris Sullivan as chair and Dan Burns as vice chair as longtime chair Karen Bernard prepares to step down.

what_happened.line: After the override failed, the committee leaned toward implementing a balanced budget built on cuts to class sizes, interventionists, middle school sports and transportation, and high school world language, rather than returning to voters right away.
The committee elected Laura as chair and Tony as vice chair for 2026-2027, with Mandy Gilman named secretary pending her acceptance.
The fifth-grade bus-release procedure was tabled so the superintendent can gather community feedback before any change.
The committee adopted revised policies on cash handling, student data privacy, medication administration, and advertising in schools.
The committee accepted a composite evaluation of the superintendent's first year.

why_it_matters: The override's failure is now translating into specific reductions -- class sizes, interventionist staffing, middle school sports and transportation, and a high school language program -- while the committee weighs a community task force before deciding whether to ask voters again.
The new cash-handling policy sets a cap on cash accepted per school transaction, which came up directly in connection with how prom tickets can be sold going forward.

Families with fourth- and fifth-graders should watch for the superintendent's community feedback process on bus release, since it is being handled as an administrative procedure rather than a committee policy vote.

meetings.summary: The Select Board acknowledged the resignations of the vice chair (citing health, amid the aftermath of the failed override) and two town staff members, then reorganized its own leadership, electing a new chair, vice chair and clerk. It also voted on an ambulance-billing write-off, a nuisance dog investigation, waivers for a town event and a right of first refusal, discussed possibly calling a special town meeting on the budget while deferring to the School and Finance Committees, and heard a town manager's report on bridge and flooring project bids and a culvert grant.

The RFP for 925 Mass Ave will be issued next week with responses due back in July.

meetings.headline: Task force is assigning stormwater ERU fees property-by-property, leaning toward per-ERU billing over flat tiers
meetings.summary: The Stormwater Task Force reviewed John's detailed matching of the assessor's full property list against Weston & Samson's impervious-area survey, working through Massachusetts use codes one by one to assign a baseline ERU (equivalent residential unit) and resulting fee to every property in town, including tricky cases like garage-only lots, duplexes, condo complexes, and the Housing Authority. No formal vote was taken on the methodology; the group reached working consensus on several categories, assigned homework to review the rest before the next meeting, and discussed presenting both an operating-budget and a stand-alone-utility funding option to voters at the fall special town meeting.

budget_items.what_was_said: John said his baseline model, based on the proposed budget divided across all assessed ERUs, produces a flat annual fee per ERU. He noted this comes down further once the missing ~1,000 residential parcels found by Weston & Samson are added in.

budget_items.topic: Revenue difference: charging by ERU vs. by tier
budget_items.what_was_said: John said charging every property for its actual number of ERUs, instead of truncating each property to the bottom of its tier, raises more revenue overall.
A member referenced the overall budget figure driving the per-ERU fee calculation.

budget_items.topic: Fee for the highest-ERU property (largest impervious area)
budget_items.what_was_said: John calculated what the town's largest single ERU property (believed to be Walmart) would owe at the per-ERU rate, and flagged that his chart's scale may have cut off the true top ERU value.

budget_items.topic: Carousel Lane / Emerald Place combined ERU total
budget_items.what_was_said: Members worked out that Weston & Samson's total impervious area for the whole Carousel Lane complex, divided by the standard ERU size, comes close to the per-unit estimate the group had built up building by building, and used that to size a single combined bill for the property's roughly 155 line items.

budget_items.what_was_said: A member read off the Weston & Samson impervious-area figure and resulting ERU count for another large development, and questioned whether it seemed low for its size.

budget_items.topic: Cost of hiring outside help ('a guy') to review all properties
budget_items.what_was_said: A member speculated that if the task force had funding to hire additional help, the overall program budget and the resulting per-resident assessment would both come down.

budget_items.topic: Operating budget vs. stand-alone utility funding structure
budget_items.what_was_said: The group discussed that if the stormwater fee were folded into the operating budget it would rise each year under the town's annual levy increase, unlike a stand-alone utility fee, and agreed both options need to be presented to voters at the fall special town meeting.

decisions.decision: Use code 106 (accessory lot with an improvement, e.g. a detached garage on a split-off lot) will be assigned one ERU.
A property with multiple houses/units but only one line item and one tax bill in the assessor's spreadsheet will be charged one ERU, matched to the tax bill rather than the number of dwellings.

The Carousel Lane / Emerald Place condominium complex, owned by a single LLC, will be billed as one combined property using Weston & Samson's total-property ERU estimate rather than per individual unit.
The Lunenburg Housing Authority property on White Street is flagged as a likely exception (a government entity that would effectively be taxing itself), pending further review.
Members will each review the mass use code document and John's assigned ERU-per-use-code list, and send back any disagreements before the next meeting so John can revise the model.
Next meeting tentatively set for June 24 (a Wednesday), with June 29 as a fallback if that date does not work for everyone, pending confirmation with Tim and Mark.

The task force agreed it should revisit its own officer and liaison assignments (chair, vice chair, board representatives) now that town elections have occurred, though this was deferred rather than acted on.

minutes.headline: Task force is assigning stormwater ERU fees property-by-property, leaning toward per-ERU billing over flat tiers
minutes.summary: The Stormwater Task Force reviewed John's detailed matching of the assessor's full property list against Weston & Samson's impervious-area survey, working through Massachusetts use codes one by one to assign a baseline ERU (equivalent residential unit) and resulting fee to every property in town, including tricky cases like garage-only lots, duplexes, condo complexes, and the Housing Authority. No formal vote was taken on the methodology; the group reached working consensus on several categories, assigned homework to review the rest before the next meeting, and discussed presenting both an operating-budget and a stand-alone-utility funding option to voters at the fall special town meeting.

what_happened.line: The task force decided to bill the Carousel Lane/Emerald Place condo complex as one combined property rather than unit by unit.
The Lunenburg Housing Authority's White Street property was flagged as a likely exception, since billing it would mean the town taxing itself.

Members discussed presenting voters two funding options at the fall special town meeting: folding the fee into the operating budget, where it would rise with the annual levy, or a stand-alone utility fee.
Working consensus was reached on ERU assignments for several property categories, including accessory lots and multi-unit parcels billed on one tax bill.

Voters will be asked at the fall special town meeting to choose how the stormwater program is funded, a choice that affects whether the fee rises automatically with the town's annual tax levy.
Owners of shared or multi-unit properties should watch how their property is classified, since billing decisions are being made property-by-property rather than unit-by-unit.

meetings.headline: Assessors rewrite the principal assessor job posting and move to bring inspections in-house as Linda departs
meetings.summary: The Board of Assessors reviewed the principal assessor's monthly activity report (excise commitments, abatements, supplemental bills, GIS/server issues) and discussed how to reconcile the fixed annual Vision property card with a more frequently updated CI-based card. With principal assessor Linda departing at the end of June, the board line-edited a draft job posting and description for her replacement, emphasizing assessing (not just appraisal) experience and technology skills, and discussed pulling contracted services such as cyclical inspections back in-house. The board also received a detailed update on a neighborhood/waterfront reclassification project, recommended against the town purchasing a foreclosed Hollis Road property, and set the next meeting for June 3rd before adjourning to executive session.
