One additional bill was issued under this commitment number.
64 motor vehicle excise abatements were received and processed in the past month, awaiting payment by the tax collector.
All FY2026 real estate abatements have been processed; some granted, some denied including personal property/sole company items.
Supplemental real estate bills were prepared for three properties whose building value increased more than 50%, based on occupancy date.

The principal assessor gave an update on progress toward the town's new-growth estimate, noting the commercial/industrial figure so far and the equivalent tax bill value; said they may fall a bit short but remain in range.

budget_items.topic: Vision printing of CAI-style property cards
budget_items.what_was_said: A quote was given for Vision to print updated property cards annually instead of doing it in-house, proposed for next year.
A vendor quote was cited for continuously updating GIS layers such as catch basin data, discussed in context of townwide use of the CI/GIS platform.
The board signed and voted to approve the notice of commitment covering the three supplemental bills discussed earlier.
The chair reminded seniors of the circuit breaker tax credit and means-tested exemption, and noted the interest rate that applies if taxes are deferred.

decisions.decision: Board leaned toward keeping both the fixed annual Vision property card (as of January 1) and a CI-based card updated monthly, clearly labeled as to which is which.
Job posting language to be revised to require experience specifically in the assessing field, not just appraisal, and to add computer/CAMA/Munis/Microsoft Suite skills to qualifications.
Job posting/description to require current MAA designation or achievement of it within two years of hire.
Job description language changed from the assessor 'recommends' the tax rate to something like 'presents/estimates tax rate options,' since the assessor does not set the rate.
Add 'deferrals' alongside abatements and exemptions in the job description's duties list.
Narrow 'maintains the town's official maps' to specifically 'tax maps' in the job description.
Board intends to bring cyclical property inspections in-house going forward rather than continue contracting them out.
Next Board of Assessors meeting set for June 3rd.

minutes.headline: Commissioners reworked the pitch for a ~$47M PFAS treatment plant loan ahead of a town vote
minutes.summary: The Lunenburg Water District Commissioners spent most of this meeting line-editing the PowerPoint that will be used to ask voters to approve roughly $47 million in SRF loan and bond financing for a PFAS/iron-manganese water treatment plant, debating which points were fact versus hypothetical and cutting or adding slides. They also discussed a dispute with the Woodlands over a kayak rack (tabled), fielded a resident's pointed questions about how the SRF grant application was submitted months after the board had voted not to apply, and covered routine water-main leak repairs, a proposed PVC pipe cost-saving trial, and mailer logistics for the special town meeting.

what_happened.line: Commissioners revised the slide presentation for a special town meeting vote on financing a PFAS/iron-manganese water treatment plant, separating factual points from hypothetical ones and agreeing to finish edits by email rather than another meeting.
A commissioner found the loan amount cited for a 2024 zero-interest loan article did not match the figure shown on the current slide, and the presentation will be corrected before the vote.
A resident asked why the district applied for state revolving fund financing months after commissioners had voted not to, and why commissioners were not told until December; no vote followed.

Commissioners approved a one-time trial of PVC pipe instead of the district's standard ductile iron on a current installation, after staff quoted it at roughly half the cost.

why_it_matters: Residents will be asked at a special town meeting to approve loan and bond financing for the treatment plant, and the slides revised at this meeting are what they will be shown when they vote.

How that financing is structured (state revolving fund loan versus bonding) affects what water bills look like for years afterward, which is why commissioners were still correcting figures on the comparison slides.

The unresolved timeline question -- an SRF application submitted after a vote not to apply, disclosed to commissioners months later -- touches on how the board's own process is explained to voters before they're asked to approve the financing.

Revised acquisition criteria and any agricultural preservation restrictions would shape which private parcels the town moves to protect from development going forward.

what_happened.line: The Select Board held its last public comment session before Saturday's override election, and the chair stated personal support for a yes vote.
The board agreed to assign a police officer rather than the elected constable to cover election day, after members raised concerns about the constable's public remarks on the override.
Residents used the session to argue over how the town split new growth revenue among capital projects, a reserve fund, a new hire, and schools.
The board voted to sell two tax-title parcels on Hollis Road, contingent on a vote by the board of assessors.
The board approved an FY27 letter to Senator Cronin urging changes to state school aid, including circuit breaker reimbursement and local aid formulas.

why_it_matters: The override goes before voters at Saturday's annual town election; the chair's public position is one member's stance, not the board's decision or the vote's outcome.

Swapping the constable for a police officer at the polls is a change to customary election-day coverage, decided informally before the formal vote and tied to the override's politics rather than a stated procedural rule.
The advocacy letter and property sale don't change any resident's tax bill directly, but the letter is the town's on-record ask for state school funding changes that could affect future budgets.

Town manager's annual evaluation, targeted for completion the week after the election

meetings.headline: Trust Fund Commission publicly accuses town manager and select board of blocking release of funds to veterans and the poor
meetings.summary: The Trust Fund Commission chair used the meeting's public-comment period and most of the meeting itself to accuse the town manager and select board of stonewalling release of trust-fund money meant for veterans and the poor, and to read and rebut point-by-point a town counsel letter responding to the commission's breach notice on several trust funds (Nathaniel Day Worthy Poor Fund, American Legion Post 283 and Poor Funds, J&M Howard sidewalk fund, gazebo fund, Susan Howard fund). No cy pres filings were approved at this meeting; the commission agreed to request the drafted Nathaniel Day petition from counsel and to take up the school department's non-response to records requests at its next meeting, and it approved its prior meeting minutes before adjourning.

budget_items.topic: Trust fund cy pres money for underserved residents
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair said the select board has refused to authorize the cy pres filings needed to release this money, split mainly between the American Legion Poor Fund, Post 283 Fund and the Worthy Poor Fund, to veterans and poor residents.

budget_items.what_was_said: The chair said money Susan Howard gave to the town in 1905 no longer appears in the ledger and the town cannot locate it, and he wants it investigated.

budget_items.topic: Proposed override's tax impact on residents
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair argued the proposed override would raise typical tax bills by roughly this much a month, which he said makes trust fund assistance more necessary for seniors on fixed incomes.

figures_as_heard: million and a half$2 million dollars
budget_items.what_was_said: Richard recalled a roughly 20-year-old town decision to spend far more than a trailer park's assessed value on water and sewer service there, offering it as precedent for valuing people over a pure cost comparison.

budget_items.topic: Town's legal fees responding to the commission's breach notice
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair estimated the town is spending several thousand dollars on its attorney to answer the commission's 55-page filing rather than releasing the funds.

budget_items.topic: Cost of legal response versus cost of requested investigation
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair said the commission does not need to ask town meeting for this amount, but that the town may spend as much fighting the commission legally as it would cost to fund the requested investigations.

budget_items.topic: Nathaniel Day 1901 Worthy Poor Fund cy pres petition
budget_items.what_was_said: Town counsel's letter states this is the only fund currently requiring action and that a cy pres petition has been drafted for the commission's review and vote.

budget_items.topic: Hypothetical funding for fund investigations from the assistant town manager position
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair said he would take this amount from money requested for a new assistant town manager position to pay for investigating the trust funds instead.
The chair said at this salary level the town manager should not need an assistant and should handle more of the workload herself.

Counsel's letter argues the fund is not obsolete because Lunenburg veterans eligible for Legion membership can still receive funds; the chair called this unworkable given the veterans agent's limited authority.
Counsel's letter states this fund has no found devise and is not eligible for administrative cy pres, and would require costly judicial action instead.

budget_items.topic: Potential litigation/expert costs for American Legion Poor Fund
budget_items.what_was_said: Counsel's letter cites the Woodward School for Girls case to say expert testimony for judicial cy pres litigation could cost this much over the life of a case.

budget_items.topic: J&M Howard sidewalk and grounds fund
budget_items.what_was_said: Counsel's letter cites a 1931 town meeting record showing a devise for this fund and says cy pres is not currently required; the chair said no formal devise document has actually been provided to the commission.
Counsel's letter says the fund's purpose is not obsolete because a gazebo exists on town land, so cy pres is not required; the chair asked why a formal devise has still not been drafted.
Counsel's letter says any 1972 recordkeeping questions are now moot under the statute of limitations and that the town holds no funds under this name requiring action.

decisions.decision: The chair will personally call town counsel to request the cy pres petition document for the Nathaniel Day Worthy Poor Fund before the commission votes on it.
A draft compliance/investigation-request letter concerning the school department's non-response on scholarship and trust records will be reviewed at the next meeting.
Next meeting set for May 21.

The board also voted to bar equipment access through the water supply protection zone for a tree removal, discussed an unresolved dispute over a kayak rack sited in that same zone, authorized spending on postcards and social media to publicize the June 3rd vote, and heard public comments criticizing the board's conduct during a heated exchange and a resident's request for a long-pending agenda item.

Agreed to hold weekly Wednesday meetings leading up to the June 3rd vote, deciding meeting-by-meeting whether each one is needed.

minutes.headline: Water Commissioners set a June special vote on a large loan to fund PFAS and manganese treatment.
minutes.summary: The Lunenburg Water District board spent most of the meeting with its engineer reviewing how State Revolving Fund financing and bidding works for a combined PFAS and iron/manganese treatment project, and finalizing warrant-article language and cost-to-ratepayer estimates ahead of a June 3rd special district meeting where voters will be asked to fund the project. The board also voted to bar equipment access through the water supply protection zone for a tree removal, discussed an unresolved dispute over a kayak rack sited in that same zone, authorized spending on postcards and social media to publicize the June 3rd vote, and heard public comments criticizing the board's conduct during a heated exchange and a resident's request for a long-pending agenda item.

The board authorized spending with a marketing contractor on postcards and social media to publicize the June 3rd vote.
The board agreed to keep the existing tiered water rate structure and model debt service across usage tiers before publishing a cost estimate.

why_it_matters: Residents will be asked at the June 3rd special district meeting to approve loan funding for PFAS and iron/manganese treatment, which will show up on water bills through the rate tiers.
A per-household or per-tier cost estimate has not yet been published; the board said it wants that worked out on the district's billing software before the vote.
A separate, unresolved dispute over a kayak rack sited in the same water supply protection zone remains open, with a variance letter to the state whose outcome was not clearly recorded.

minutes.headline: Town meeting passed the FY27 budget and sent two Prop 2½ overrides to a townwide ballot vote.
minutes.summary: Lunenburg's annual town meeting passed a full slate of warrant articles, most consequentially the FY2027 balanced town/school budget and a two-tier Proposition 2½ override package that, if approved by voters at the ballot in two weeks, would restore cut positions and programs in town departments and schools. Extensive public debate covered the balance budget's cuts to school staffing, the library, recreation, and public safety, a new assistant town manager position, and an alternative permanent-investment-trust proposal, before the body voted to approve article 10 and both override tiers under article 11, along with capital, PEG, salary-schedule and union-contract articles.

watch_next: The townwide ballot vote on the two Proposition 2½ override tiers
Outcome of article 24 (TCP building decommissioning / assessor's office funding), not captured on this recording

what_happened.line: Town meeting approved the FY27 town and school budget, then sent two Proposition 2½ override tiers to a townwide ballot.
The override votes followed debate over cuts to school staffing, the library, recreation and public safety in the underlying balance budget.
A proposal to fund town operations through a permanent investment trust instead of recurring overrides was raised but not adopted.
Town meeting also approved capital funding, PEG cable funding, the non-union salary schedule, and first-year contracts for the fire, municipal employees' and DPW unions.
The final article, covering TCP building decommissioning costs and a special assistant position in the assessor's office, was still under discussion when the recording ended with no vote captured.

why_it_matters: The two override tiers now go to a townwide ballot; that vote decides whether cut school and town positions and programs are restored and affects the property tax bill.
The FY27 budget that passed is a balance budget built around the cuts described at the meeting, so its effects take hold unless the ballot overrides pass.
The union contracts and salary schedule approved at the meeting affect town and school staff pay regardless of how the override vote turns out.

meetings.headline: Town meeting passed the FY27 town budget and sent both Prop 2½ override questions to a townwide ballot.
meetings.summary: Lunenburg's annual town meeting adopted a level-services FY27 town/school budget requiring deep staff and program cuts, then separately approved (for the ballot) a tier-one $2.4 million and tier-two $3.3 million Proposition 2½ override, each restoring cut positions in town departments and schools if voters approve. The meeting also acted on dozens of other warrant articles covering capital funding, union contracts, free-cash transfers to reserve funds, the closure and decommissioning of the TC Pacios building (displacing the food pantry, PEG studio and gym), a new assistant town manager position, a revised town-meeting notice policy, and transfer of Kids Kingdom playground land to the select board.

minutes.headline: Town meeting passed the FY27 town budget and sent both Prop 2½ override questions to a townwide ballot.
minutes.summary: Lunenburg's annual town meeting adopted a level-services FY27 town/school budget requiring deep staff and program cuts, then separately approved (for the ballot) a tier-one $2.4 million and tier-two $3.3 million Proposition 2½ override, each restoring cut positions in town departments and schools if voters approve. what_happened.line: Town meeting adopted a level-services FY27 town and school budget that requires cuts to staff and programs.
Town meeting separately approved two Proposition 2½ override questions, sending both to a townwide ballot; either would restore some of the cut positions if voters approve.
Town meeting approved closing and decommissioning the TC Pacios building, after ruling a floor amendment to fund food-pantry relocation costs outside that article's scope.
A new assistant town manager position was created and the current post retitled HR director, and future town-meeting notices move to a postcard/opt-in system.
Care and custody of part of the Kids Kingdom playground land was transferred from the school committee to the select board.

why_it_matters: Residents will be asked to vote yes or no on the two override questions at the ballot; the outcome decides whether staffing and programs cut from the base budget are restored.
TC Pacios housed the food pantry, the PEG public-access studio and a gym, and the building's closure means those users need a new location before it is decommissioned.
The new administrative position and the switch to a postcard/opt-in mailing change both the cost of town administration and how residents learn about future town meetings.

meetings.headline: Commissioners split over locking in state loan funding for the PFAS treatment plant ahead of a May resident vote
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Water District board spent most of this meeting refining a joint PowerPoint on funding options (SRF loan and bond) for a combined PFAS/iron-manganese treatment plant and transmission-main project, ahead of a special resident meeting set for late May. Commissioners disagreed sharply over whether to secure the full SRF loan amount now versus waiting for firmer design-stage cost numbers, with no vote taken on that question; the board also voted on a special-meeting date, amended shutoff/collections rules, and directed a letter to MassDEP over a condo association's kayak rack.

budget_items.topic: Baseline cost for PFAS/iron-manganese treatment plant and transmission mains
budget_items.what_was_said: The board set a baseline construction estimate combining the Hickory Hills SRF-funded portion and the Keings project, to be presented as a single combined vote for residents.

budget_items.topic: SRF vs. bond interest rates for the two project components
budget_items.what_was_said: Commissioners discussed borrowing the larger Hickory Hills/Lancaster portion under the SRF at one rate and financing the smaller Keings portion separately at a higher rate.

budget_items.topic: SRF principal forgiveness and possible emerging-contaminant grant
budget_items.what_was_said: The board debated whether a percentage of principal forgiveness applies automatically under the SRF application, and whether a separate emerging-contaminants grant pool might add further funding; they agreed to seek clarity.

budget_items.topic: Engineering design-services line within the SRF application
budget_items.what_was_said: A commissioner calculated that the budgeted design-services fee, at an assumed hourly engineer rate, implied an unreasonably large number of full-time-equivalent engineer-years, arguing the true design cost is much lower; another commissioner noted the figure is the maximum SRF allows, not the actual cost.
The same commissioner compared the budgeted construction-oversight fee to what one engineer working the full construction period at an hourly rate would cost, arguing a large gap between the two.

budget_items.topic: Capital cost per gallon of treatment capacity, compared nationally
budget_items.what_was_said: A commissioner presented national cost data for similar-sized PFAS and iron/manganese treatment plants and argued the district's estimated building cost is several times higher than comparable plants elsewhere.

budget_items.topic: Residential vs. commercial water-use figures behind the cost allocation
budget_items.what_was_said: The clerk/treasurer explained a spreadsheet used for the annual statistical report that breaks down usage by connection type, used to check the numbers behind the funding slides.

budget_items.topic: Cost of the Keings-to-Lancaster transmission main
budget_items.what_was_said: A commissioner noted the transmission-line cost estimate has varied widely across different reports and design assumptions (pipe diameter), and said the true number awaits final design.

budget_items.topic: Total project cost and impact on resident water bills
budget_items.what_was_said: A resident said the plant, financing and operating costs over the loan term would roughly triple a typical household's annual water bill, and warned many customers are already behind on payments.

budget_items.topic: Delinquent accounts and collections behind new shutoff rule
budget_items.what_was_said: The clerk described the number of bills sent, second notices issued, and accounts running behind, used to justify adding formal payment-plan and shutoff language to the rules and regulations.

budget_items.topic: Resident survey response rate on funding options
budget_items.what_was_said: The board noted only a small share of water takers had responded to the survey and decided to extend the deadline and publicize it further before the special meeting vote.

decisions.decision: A commissioner will draft a letter to MassDEP requesting a variance to allow the Woodland Condo Association's kayak rack to remain, to be reviewed by the absent third commissioner and voted on at a future meeting.

The two commissioners agreed to merge their separate PowerPoint drafts into one combined presentation on PFAS/water treatment funding options, using one commissioner's visual diagram and the other's cost detail.
The board agreed to hold a public presentation at town hall, recorded for local TV, ahead of the special meeting vote.
Extend the resident funding-options survey a couple more weeks and promote it via social media before closing it.

Clarified that the planned SRF/bond vote authorizes funding for the Hickory Hills-to-Lancaster plant and transmission main and, separately at a different rate, the Keings transmission main, and either portion could later be declined if not needed.
Agreed to add discussion of the board's own agenda-item process to the next meeting's agenda.

The board voted to hold a special resident meeting in late May, choosing between two possible dates depending on school-space availability.

meetings.headline: Board took only routine votes; public comment sharply disputed override claims of fire and police service cuts
meetings.summary: The Select Board handled routine business -- a class 2 motor vehicle license, a one-day liquor license, lifeguard/beach director appointments, a videographer resignation, and setting a July 1 start date for the new sick leave bank policy -- alongside a town manager update on IFBs, recruitments, and town meeting logistics. The most substantive content was extended public comment in which a resident challenged claims that the FY27 balanced budget and override option cut fire and police services, followed by another resident promoting property-tax relief programs; the meeting closed by voting to enter executive session over firefighter and AFSCME collective bargaining strategy.

budget_items.topic: Fire department Sunday shift staffing cost, PDM coverage vs. career firefighters
budget_items.what_was_said: A public commenter said last year she pointed out the cost difference between PDM ambulance coverage and hiring career firefighters for the Sunday shift. She suggested the Sunday shift could again be added without an override, as is being done this year.

budget_items.topic: FY26 school department level-services budget request
budget_items.what_was_said: A commenter recalled the school department requesting an increase for level services in the FY26 process and said she raised concerns the numbers did not align.

budget_items.topic: FY25 override funds left unspent by the school department
budget_items.what_was_said: The commenter said a portion of the FY25 override went unspent due to lack of tracking under the former superintendent, which she said hurt students.

budget_items.topic: New assistant town hall manager position
budget_items.what_was_said: The commenter said the town manager's balanced budget adds a new assistant town hall manager position at an added cost, while eliminating one existing position.

budget_items.topic: Town reserve account vs. financial policy threshold
budget_items.what_was_said: The commenter said the balanced budget sets aside a reserve amount well above what the town's financial policy calls for.

budget_items.topic: New revenue used for capital expenses including vehicles
budget_items.what_was_said: The commenter said new revenue is being used for capital expenses including vehicles rather than drawing from an existing reserve account.
The commenter listed the band concert as a small service being eliminated in the balanced budget.
The commenter cited the town beach's net cost as another small service affected by budget choices.
The commenter framed the eliminated small services as insignificant relative to the total town budget, but said they matter to affected families and seniors.

budget_items.topic: School reserve accounts vs. amount needed for current services
budget_items.what_was_said: The commenter questioned why school reserve accounts exceed what she said is needed to maintain current services, given warnings that schools would be devastated if the override fails.

budget_items.topic: 41A property tax deferral and circuit breaker eligibility thresholds
budget_items.what_was_said: A resident described income and home-value thresholds under the state's 41A deferral and circuit breaker tax credit programs, saying eligibility is broader than residents realize.

budget_items.topic: State income tax circuit breaker credit
budget_items.what_was_said: The same resident said qualifying residents could also get an income tax break under the circuit breaker program.

budget_items.topic: Means-tested tax relief program income and asset limits
budget_items.what_was_said: The resident described household income and asset limits for a means-tested relief program, encouraging seniors to check eligibility with the assessors.

decisions.decision: Board held off formally appointing the AFSCME/SAP representative to the sick leave bank committee, since it was not specifically posted on this agenda; to be brought back on a future agenda.
Board agreed to hold the vote on 250 and 356 Hollis Road open until May 12th to allow time for input from planning, agricultural, open space/conservation, and assessors.
Board agreed the Hollis Road referral to those boards/committees can go out now rather than waiting for a future meeting.
Board agreed to wait until after annual town meeting before resuming work on the special event policy.
Board agreed members need more time to review the updated employee climate survey questions before approving them, aiming to issue the survey sometime in May.
Board agreed to ask town counsel (Adam) whether the FY27 budget/override open house needs to be posted as an open meeting given a possible quorum of members attending.

Commissioners approved a water main extension plan for a new Round Road-area development and voted to explore a state growth grant toward it.

Unanswered questions about how and when a loan application was submitted without a board vote go to whether residents can trust the numbers presented before any financing vote.

meetings.summary: The Finance Committee re-voted a batch of previously split or 5-member warrant-article recommendations so the chair's vote could be added, and worked through remaining deferred articles for the May town meeting warrant, most consequentially the FY27 omnibus balanced budget and the two-tier Proposition 2½ override. One member repeatedly argued the balanced budget under-documents new positions (an assistant town manager and HR director) and cuts services in a way designed to pressure voters toward the override, while other members defended the process and voted to recommend both override tiers. The committee also approved its FY27 annual report for inclusion in the mailed warrant and set its next meeting for April 23.

what_happened.line: Both the FY27 public-access budget shortfall and an aging broadcast-system replacement will go to town meeting as warrant articles, partly funded from retained earnings, without a committee vote.
A shortfall in this year's salary line was covered by shifting money out of the equipment, advertising, and maintenance lines rather than a new appropriation.
The committee decided to keep optional add-ons, including a mobile app and a branded streaming channel, in the broadcast-system quote for now and reassess after a year.
A vote on committee policy was tabled because a required member was absent.
A discrepancy in the health-insurance cost estimate for next year's budget was left unresolved, with the manager assigned to follow up.

why_it_matters: Town meeting will be asked to approve warrant articles drawing on the cable fund's retained earnings for both an operating shortfall and new equipment.
Covering this year's salary line by moving money out of equipment and advertising shows the budget already running tight before the fiscal year closes.
A new ADA-mandated audio description requirement and an unsettled health-insurance figure could add to what the FY27 budget needs to cover.
watch_next: Town meeting warrant articles for the FY27 PEG budget shortfall and the Castis system replacement
Next PACC meeting: the tabled policy vote and the enterprise fund investment status report

meetings.headline: Finance Committee set warrant recommendations but held its override vote for the full board
meetings.summary: The Finance Committee worked through the annual town meeting warrant article by article, recommending approval or no-financial-impact findings on most housekeeping, revolving-fund, capital and enterprise-fund articles, while deferring items still missing final numbers (FY26 closeouts, FY27 omnibus budget, PEG enterprise fund, three union contracts still in negotiation, and prior-year bills). The committee split on a new health-insurance stabilization transfer and on a new Assistant Town Manager/HR Director grade, and it postponed voting on its recommendation for the Proposition 2½ override so the full five-member board, including two absent members, could weigh in before the mailing deadline.

budget_items.what_was_said: A new revolving fund would let the economic development committee handle sponsorship money for events like the meet-and-greet without it passing through the town's general accounts. FY2027 spending cap discussed.

Spending limits were read for ambulance billing, timber rights, school custodial special details, Green Thumb, library, Council on Aging, storm water task force, electric/gas/plumbing inspector, technology, wetlands protection fees, COA meal site, and parks programming revolving funds.
Two outstanding invoices to Aeroseptic were named as the only known prior-year bills so far; recommendation deferred to town meeting since more may surface.

budget_items.topic: FY26 closeout / snow and ice deficit
budget_items.what_was_said: The current estimated operating deficit, driven mostly by snow and ice removal, was given; transfers will cover part of it and up to a stated amount was earmarked from free cash pending final snow and ice bills.
Two override tiers would go to voters as separate ballot questions, with only the highest approved amount implemented; the Finance Committee deferred taking a position pending the full board.

An accounting error had moved the same unspent FY23 capital funds through two prior votes (TCP roof repair, then FY26 capital); this article unwinds both so the money returns to the FY26 capital plan cleanly.

Individual capital items were read out including DPW bridge completion, a police cruiser, a fire engine/brush truck, primary school entry/driveway and playground design, public safety building roof and boiler work, door security intercoms at Turkey Hill and the primary school, and a DPW front-end loader.
The planned motion would transfer this amount from solid waste enterprise revenue to operate the program for FY2027; the fund does not cover recycling costs.
The fund would use enterprise revenue to pay Fitchburg for water and recoup a percentage under an intermunicipal agreement; figures were based on usage estimates.
A transfer toward the sewer enterprise's share of retiree health benefit liability; a member asked why the PEG/PAC enterprise carries no similar contribution.
Total FY2027 operating budget figure for the sewer enterprise fund.

budget_items.topic: SAP salary schedule / cost of living adjustment
budget_items.what_was_said: A cost-of-living increase for non-union salaried employees would be funded from the salary reserve; a member clarified it is not tied to any federal COLA figure.

budget_items.topic: Special appropriation: TC Pasio and assessor position
budget_items.what_was_said: Funds requested for TC Pasio operating and decommissioning costs and for a special assistant to the assessor position.

budget_items.topic: Free cash to OPEB trust fund
budget_items.what_was_said: Ten percent of certified free cash was described as being transferred to the OPEB trust under the town's financial policy.
A second consecutive year of a small deposit was proposed to build a cushion against retirement buyout costs exceeding the operating budget line.
Funds requested for activities marking the town's 300th anniversary; some members felt the amount was too large given past reliance on volunteers.
A standard annual transfer from free cash to the general-purpose stabilization fund, distinct from the vehicle/special purpose fund.

A new deposit was proposed as a cushion against a future spike in health insurance costs; total town and school insurance costs across active and retiree accounts were estimated. One member asked for defined trigger criteria for using the fund before supporting it.

budget_items.topic: Vacation accrual system transition liability buyout
budget_items.what_was_said: The town proposed buying out the full accrued-vacation liability at current dollar value ahead of a transition to a continuous accrual system, covering SAP employees and settled/near-settled union groups.
A member recalled roughly this figure as the cost of printing and mailing full warrant booklets to every household, cited in favor of switching to a postcard notice.

reconciliation.what: Our minutes against the minutes the town published. caption_error = the same fact the captions rendered badly, resolved by the official reading shown beside the as-heard one; discrepancy = a substantive difference, flagged and not resolved. Neither record is treated as the referee.
reconciliation.summary: The two records agree closely on the mechanics of nearly every vote (motion, outcome, and any split count) once articles are matched up, but they diverge in two ways worth flagging: the official minutes record every dollar figure zero times (they give motion/seconder/roll-call only), so almost none of "ours" many dollar amounts can be checked against them, and there are several real vote-outcome conflicts — Article Q (300th anniversary) is unanimous in the official record but "4-1" in ours, Article P (compensated absence reserve) has a Jay Simeone nay the official record shows but ours omits, and two articles ours marked "not audible" (O, Z2) the official record shows were unanimously approved. A reader should check the actual warrant to resolve which SAP article (N vs. EE) corresponds to the "Assistant Town Manager/HR Director grade" item ours describes, since the two records' SAP-related outcomes don't cleanly line up.

meetings.headline: Committee voted to keep charging the student bus fee despite members calling it unfair, citing budget desperation.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg School Committee heard public comment on an override, a student proposal to credit after-school sports as PE, and updates on capital projects and grant-seeking, then worked through a long list of votes: continuing the bus fee, discontinuing the lifelong learning program, approving a $300,000 federal earmark request, and endorsing a letter to legislators on Chapter 70 funding. Facilities updates covered an energy-efficiency program at the high school, relocating a generator from the Pacios building, solar array repairs, and Turkey Hill bathroom renovations, alongside several retirement and new-hire announcements including a new Turkey Hill principal.

public_comment.topic: Advocated that participation in after-school sports count as PE/gym credit for high schoolers, citing a student survey and studies on mental health benefits.
Raised concerns about the override not being a permanent fix, wanted long-range financial projections, and described rising need at the local food pantry and community mutual aid.
Reminded residents that the override must pass at both the May 2nd town meeting and the May 16th ballot, and urged attendance at both.
Raised concern that unified sports/arts opportunities for students with disabilities are shrinking and asked for a fuller committee conversation on options.

budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager approved three capital requests: two feasibility studies for the primary school (playground and drive/playground) and camera systems for building entrances. Other requested items were deferred for later in the year due to funding and the Pacios building situation.

The district is seeking one-time federal earmark funding to build a district-wide instructional framework and offset a projected cut to Title One funding; the district would not have to make up any shortfall if the full amount isn't awarded.
Funds previously voted to be accepted from the scholarship fund were not actually transferred from the estate to students due to a legal/executor issue; the district will bring it back once resolved.
As of month-end the district was at 66.1% of budget expended, rising to 68.6% once a payroll posted; last year the district was at 67% at the same point, having spent less overall.
The collaborative tuition line is overspent because circuit breaker reimbursement money has not yet been posted back into it; this is described as a normally hard line to budget.

Electrical spending is running over budget due to a colder winter and last year's underbudgeting; gas/heating has money remaining, and next year's electrical budget was adjusted based on recent actuals.
Legal expenses are running hot this year and the FY27 budget has been adjusted upward as a result.

The district described fee revenue collected over two periods and the fee schedule by family size and reduced-fee eligibility, and members debated the fairness of the fee against the roughly $70,000 it raises given the district's financial situation.

Chapter 70 does not include transportation costs at all, and regional districts get 75% of transportation reimbursed while Lunenburg does not, which a member said could be worth a large additional sum if reimbursed similarly.

The adult men's basketball program generated minimal revenue per player and relies on unpaid volunteer facilitators; the adult health and fitness program is a pass-through to a private vendor with the district retaining no financial benefit, supporting the recommendation to discontinue the district-run program.

A draft letter to legislators notes Lunenburg ranks near the bottom statewide for per-pupil spending while spending well above the state-required minimum, which members attribute to flaws in how Chapter 70 categorizes districts.
A building-controls efficiency study at the high school may be covered up to 100% by the program, addressing malfunctioning thermostats and actuators causing temperature problems.
The existing landscaping contract for the district's three athletic fields has expired and is going out to bid; costs under the prior contract were described as escalating over the years.
The PTO reported raising a significant amount at a recent dance fundraiser, plus a separate Great Wolf Lodge fundraiser.

decisions.decision: Bring Eden Fry's proposal on counting after-school sports as PE credit to the appropriate staff member (Mr. Sanders) and put it on a future agenda.

If the larger override passes and the town hires a full-time recreation director, the committee will coordinate with that person on facility scheduling and possible partnership on adult/community programs.

what_happened.line: The committee voted to continue charging the student bus fee for another year, despite members calling it unfair, citing the district's financial situation.
Members voted to end the district-run Lunenburg lifelong learning program effective June 1, citing minimal revenue and reliance on volunteers or a pass-through vendor.
The committee authorized the superintendent to pursue a one-time federal earmark to build a district-wide instructional framework and offset an expected cut to Title One funding.
Members endorsed a letter to state legislators arguing Lunenburg's Chapter 70 funding formula undercounts its per-pupil spending and excludes transportation costs.
The FY26 monthly budget report showed spending running ahead of the same point last year, with the electrical and legal lines over budget.

why_it_matters: The bus fee stays in place for families who use it, separate from and regardless of the outcome of the townwide override vote in May.
Ending the lifelong learning program removes a district-run adult offering, though students already enrolled will finish the current session before it closes.
The letter to legislators is an ask, not a change in funding -- any shift in how Chapter 70 treats transportation or per-pupil spending depends on action in Boston, not this committee.

meetings.headline: Board set the FY27 town meeting warrant and voted a two-tier override question onto the town election ballot
meetings.summary: The Select Board worked through the annual town meeting warrant article by article with town counsel, deferring several items (prior-year invoices, FY26 budget adjustments, the snow-and-ice closeout, and union contract funding) to town meeting itself, and declining -- after individual members stated concerns -- to include a Trust Fund Commission legal-fees article or a quorum bylaw article that counsel flagged as legally uncertain. The board voted to place a two-tier Proposition 2½ override question on the annual town election ballot, rounding the tiers to clean dollar figures and choosing a "Question 1/Question 2" ballot format, while one member stated ongoing concerns about the override's affordability. It also discussed but did not finalize where the override and other articles should sit in the warrant order and consent agenda.

public_comment.topic: Asked the board to randomize/lottery the order of non-fixed warrant articles at town meeting to stop "vote stacking" around the override.

Clarified the "rule of necessity" legal doctrine behind the trust fund quorum article and said the commission has filed a breach-of-fiduciary-duty notice against the town with a 30-day response request.

what_happened.line: Board voted 5-0 to place a two-tier Proposition 2½ override question on the annual town election ballot, pending town counsel's final edits.
Board members individually declined to put two Trust Fund Commission articles, on legal fees and a quorum bylaw, on the town meeting warrant.
The board deferred several FY27 warrant items, including prior-year invoices and union contract funding, to town meeting itself.
A Trust Fund Commission representative told the board the commission has filed a notice of breach of fiduciary duty against the town.

what_happened.line: The Finance Committee closed its public hearing on the FY27 school and town budgets without voting on the budget, an override, or any warrant article.

The superintendent laid out a level-funded budget with cuts to teaching positions, music, and athletics, against two override scenarios that would restore and add staff across schools, police, fire, DPW, and the library.
Draft warrant articles, including the override article itself, were walked through but not voted on.
The committee scheduled an additional virtual meeting for April 6 to vote on the warrant articles and finalize its report before the town meeting deadline.

why_it_matters: Whether voters pass a tier-1 or tier-2 override in May decides whether class sizes rise and positions such as teachers, a custodian, and an occupational therapy assistant go unfilled.
The warrant articles still being drafted will set exactly what residents are asked to vote on at town meeting and on the override ballot.
Town departments including police, fire, DPW, and the library face the same level-funded-versus-override choice as the schools.

meetings.headline: Trust Fund board voted to notify the Attorney General of a 50-year town breach managing charitable trusts
meetings.summary: The Board of Trust Fund Commissioners (two members, John Bowen and Richard Howard) spent nearly the entire meeting on a detailed breach notice alleging the Town of Lunenburg has failed for over 50 years to properly administer, document, and distribute numerous charitable trust funds, including missing donor declarations, an entirely missing fund, and unresolved American Legion fund eligibility requirements. The board voted to send a letter and submission packet to the Attorney General's Division of Public Charities and to the Town Manager and Select Board, giving the town 30 days to act, and also voted to amend the operating policy for the American Legion funds and adopt signature-page documents to formalize the filings. Chair Bowen also raised in commission comment concerns about the town's proposed override and his own re-election filing for the board.

budget_items.what_was_said: The chair said the trust funds have taken in a substantial amount of income, citing a total figure with a portion of it available to distribute out of that total.
The chair said he had proposed a smaller tax increase two years ago than what is now being sought, arguing the town wasted two years of investment income by not acting sooner.

budget_items.topic: Warrant article request for trust investigation funding
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair said the commission should not have had to request funding via warrant article for the town to investigate and administer the trust funds, arguing the town already has a fiduciary duty to fund this.

budget_items.topic: Repayment of improperly dispersed trust funds
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair said a past dispersement from the Worthy Poor fund to a landlord needs to be repaid to the board by the town, not by the individual who received it.

budget_items.topic: Woodward School for Girls v. Quincy case liability
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair cited a Massachusetts case where a town was held liable for failing to manage a charitable trust, used as precedent for the town's liability here.

budget_items.topic: 1901 Nathaniel Day trust gift, present-day value
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair displayed a 1901 donation receipt and said the amount would be worth much more today, illustrating funds that currently cannot be distributed.
The letter to the Attorney General states the town has allowed a sum in earnings to accumulate without lawful distribution across the charitable trust funds.

decisions.decision: Review and approval of the January 8th, January 29th, February 12th, and March 12th meeting minutes was tabled to the April 9th meeting agenda.
Chair will follow up with the town (Carrara) on posting the fund application manual to the website, which has stalled.

meetings.headline: Back-lot cemetery expansion cost estimate came in far above the $50,000 budgeted, forcing redesign before bidding.
meetings.summary: The Cemetery Commission approved routine minutes, Memorial Day flowers, a $20,000 transfer from sale-of-lots funds, a Fish Street plaque design, and a lot exchange recognizing a donor family. Most of the meeting was spent on the DPW director's report that the engineering estimate for the South Cemetery back-lot expansion came back far higher than the $50,000 placeholder budgeted, prompting discussion of cost-cutting (reusing town millings, cheaper gravel, dropping engineering-during-construction costs) and funding options (sale-of-lots balance, rate increases, possible non-resident burials) before the project can go out to bid.

budget_items.what_was_said: After applying the planned $20,000 transfer and assumed $600 flower cost, the commission worked out roughly how much would remain for the rest of the year.

The DPW director presented a new engineering cost estimate for the back-lot cemetery expansion that came in far above the original placeholder figure, calling it a shock, and outlined ways to bring it down.
The director proposed eliminating this line since he could answer bidder questions himself, paying an engineer hourly only if needed.
A line for moving contractor equipment onto site was discussed as an area that might be trimmed or folded into unit prices.

budget_items.topic: Sale of lots and perpetual care account balances
budget_items.what_was_said: Members discussed the sale-of-lots balance after the planned transfer and a separate, larger perpetual care account whose interest only can be used.
It was suggested that allowing non-residents to be buried in the cemetery, as some other towns do, could bring in additional revenue toward the expansion.
A per-stump estimate was called unrealistically low given hauling and documentation requirements, with a revised total suggested to be much higher.
The department is rehiring two part-time seasonal helpers from last year, within a limited budget that must last through the end of the fiscal year.

transfers.description: $20,000 from the sale-of-lots account to fund cemetery care, improvement and expansion

decisions.decision: Going forward, the commission will submit written authorization to the town treasurer/accountant to transfer sale-of-lots funds rather than seeking a town meeting warrant article each year.
The commission agreed it does not want to drain the sale-of-lots account to a low balance and will revise the expansion cost estimate before deciding how much of the project to bid.
The commission cannot solicit donations from town residents directly since it is a town body, though it could accept unsolicited gifts or support a resident-formed 501(c)3.
The commission will not go out to bid until the funding amount is confirmed; the DPW director will first revise the cost estimate and reduce scope where possible.
Board members will take home the revised cemetery rules and regulations document to review before discussing changes at the next meeting.
Next meeting set for April 23rd.

meetings.headline: Board defended SRF/PFAS funding against a resident group's bid to block it; a 29-year commissioner's last meeting
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Water District heard a developer's petition to expand the district for a 17-lot Birch Street subdivision, headed to a vote at Saturday's special district meeting, and discussed hiring Tighe & Bond to pursue a state grant for a Lancaster Shirley Road water main extension. meetings.headline: Commission found unpermitted tree removals at several properties and continued four hearings to April
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Conservation Commission opened with a resident's storm-water complaint that led into review of a related unpermitted tree-cutting and driveway violation at his property, then heard several notices of intent (Hickory Hills ADA dock/ramp, a new home on Flat Hill Road, an addition at Hemlock Drive, a DPW culvert replacement, and a floodplain-fill project), most of which were continued to April pending storm-water calculations, revised plans, or site walks. Along the way the commission discovered unpermitted tree removals at two more properties, ratified an administrative tree-removal determination at 100 Hemlock Road, discussed outstanding violations at Highland Street and Middle Lane, and planned an Earth Day event for April 22.

budget_items.what_was_said: The chair explained the storm water task force's goal is establishing a storm water utility, collected separately like the sewer commission, to fund storm water infrastructure improvements town-wide. No figures were given.

budget_items.topic: Tree removal fine, 922 Flat Hill Road

The agent said it would be her recommendation to issue a formal violation fine if the property owner does not resolve the matter by the next meeting.
The agent asked the commission for about a month before providing concrete budget figures, citing unresolved issues with fund allocation since the office combined with land use.

decisions.decision: No vote needed on the 1147 Massachusetts Avenue violation; the agent will arrange a site inspection with the property owner and advise on required filings for the removed tree.
Applicant at 922 Flat Hill Road to tabulate and plot the removed trees on an updated plan rather than an immediate fine being issued.
Required plan revisions set for the Catales project at 189 Hemlock Drive: no enclosed porch, no new retaining wall, removal of the carport, and additional plantings, ahead of a site walk.

The four dead trees at 100 Hemlock Road may be cut with stumps left in place to preserve slope stability; no replacement plantings required given existing canopy, though understory plantings were encouraged.
The agent will continue bringing administrative determinations before the full commission while she becomes familiar with local regulations, rather than deciding them independently.
Commission will hold off on any formal violation or fine for 314 Highland Street until the property owner appears at the April 1 meeting.
Commission agreed to give the agent about a month before presenting concrete budget figures.

meetings.headline: Committee picked one override number (core "Scenario C") and, if it fails, will cut athletic transportation to save a teacher and a therapy aide
meetings.summary: The School Committee spent most of a long meeting building two FY27 budgets: an override ask (core "scenario C," roughly $1.5-1.6 million) that it voted to send to the Select Board as a single number, and a "balanced" no-override budget that cuts classroom teachers, an assistant principal, a custodian, an occupational therapy assistant, and other positions through attrition. After extended debate over cutting athletics versus classroom staff, the committee voted to accept the balanced budget minus the athletic transportation line, directing the superintendent's team to decide how to reallocate that cut to restore a teacher and an occupational therapy assistant. Members also voted to formalize the town's PEC health-insurance opt-out enhancement, approved a scholarship payout, an international trip, and childcare-program handbook changes.

budget_items.what_was_said: The business office reported the period's warrant total for approval; no line-item transfers were reported this period.
A scholarship already awarded to two graduates needed a payment-voucher and signature process clarified with town hall due to a new donation-form requirement.

Current opt-out incentive is a one-time $2,000/individual or $4,000/family after two years of enrollment; the proposed new program pays $3,000/individual or $6,000/family annually after one year, with each side (town or school) covering its own employees' payments.
FY25 and FY26 opt-out participation across town and school was reported as very low.
A company's price for outsourced custodial work, not including supplies, was reported as higher than current in-house costs, so the superintendent does not recommend pursuing it.

budget_items.what_was_said: The superintendent listed a series of expense reductions from the originally posted FY27 budget, including high school admin, middle school special educators, maintenance lines, transportation (offset by bus/school choice fees), athletic transportation, trash removal, and fire-safety furniture repair, based on actual spending patterns.
Legal expense line was increased due to anticipated legal bills related to contentious records requests.

budget_items.what_was_said: Members debated and ultimately agreed to add back a small music-teacher position that preserves fifth-grade band, calling it a very small cost relative to the budget.

Members discussed whether to ask the select board for one override number or two tiers, weighing a restoration figure (1.9) against a lower core figure (1.5/1.6), with reference to a schools' target share of a combined town override around 54-57%.
A member compared the cost of the high school interventionist position to what was spent on athletic transportation the prior year, questioning spending priorities.
Various figures for the athletic transportation contract were cited repeatedly during debate over whether to cut it to restore staffing positions.

budget_items.topic: Total athletics and band transportation cost

budget_items.topic: Balanced (no-override) budget total gap to close
budget_items.what_was_said: Multiple running totals were cited during negotiation over which staffing positions and program cuts (athletics, transportation, attrition positions) would close the balanced-budget gap.
Extending the device replacement cycle from three to four years and switching to smaller/cheaper Chromebooks were proposed as small savings for the balanced budget.

budget_items.topic: Out-of-district special education placement cost risk
budget_items.what_was_said: A member warned that cuts risking noncompliance could push students into costly outplacements, citing this figure as illustrative of placement cost.

Every high school student pays a flat activity fee regardless of how many clubs they join; a per-additional-activity fee was floated but called impractical since fees are far below actual program cost.
Members debated whether cutting athletics in half would be a meaningful 'haircut' given it is roughly 2% of the total budget.
Cited as the share of high school students participating in at least one sport, used to argue against cutting athletics.

budget_items.topic: Prior override's approximately $600,000 lost to competitive grant accounting
budget_items.what_was_said: A resident asked whether money 'found' after a prior override was recoverable; the superintendent explained it was unspent competitive grant money that reverted to town free cash under an accounting irregularity now corrected, and that roughly a million dollars of that override is embedded in the current and next budgets.

decisions.decision: Send the select board a single override number rather than a tiered ask, while keeping a second, higher restoration-level number in reserve if the select board wants a tier.
Add the 0.2 FTE music teacher position (preserving fifth-grade band) back into the core override budget.
Adopt the superintendent's core budget ("scenario C") as the school committee's override ask to the select board.

Accept the balanced (no-override) budget as proposed, except cut the athletic transportation line, with the superintendent's team to decide how to use that cut to restore one classroom teacher position and the certified occupational therapy assistant position, and report back.
Revisit the PEC health-insurance opt-out agreement roughly every three years, aligned with the PEC's contract term.

what_happened.line: The committee voted to send the Select Board one override number, built from a "core" budget option, instead of asking for two tiers.

It also voted to accept a no-override "balanced" budget but cut athletic transportation instead of a teacher, and told staff to find a way to restore that teacher and an occupational therapy aide position.
Members added back a small music-teacher position to the override budget to preserve fifth-grade band.
The committee voted to move forward on a richer health-insurance opt-out incentive for employees who decline coverage.
A resident in public comment asked, without answer in the minutes, what happened to money left over from a prior override.

why_it_matters: Town meeting voters will be asked to approve a single override figure built from this "core" budget, so this is the number that reaches the ballot.

If the override fails, whether a classroom teacher and an occupational therapy aide keep their positions now depends on how the district reallocates the athletic-transportation cut, a decision still pending from the superintendent's team.
The health-insurance opt-out change affects what the town and school pay employees who decline coverage, on both the town and school side of the budget.
watch_next: Town meeting, May 2
Superintendent's team report on reallocating the athletic-transportation cut to restore a teacher and OT aide position

meetings.headline: Board included nearly all FY27 warrant articles; TC Passios' safety issues leave the food pantry's future unresolved.
meetings.summary: The Select Board worked through most of the draft FY2027 annual town meeting warrant, voting to include (and in some cases recommend) dozens of articles covering capital cleanup items, union contract funding, an OPEB trust appropriation, a vacation-buyout liability reduction, and several bylaw changes, while holding off on the override placeholder, trust fund commission articles, a stormwater bylaw, and the Central Mass Mosquito Control article pending more information. The board also heard an extended, unresolved presentation from the Lunenburg Community Food Pantry about the deteriorating TC Passios building, where the food pantry currently operates, and closed a public hearing on opting out of mail-in early voting before entering executive session to discuss a collective bargaining agreement.

meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Planning Board acted on several site-plan and ANR matters, including continuing a 20-unit townhome project on New West Townsend Road pending fire department and peer-engineering review, approving de minimis changes for a solar array and a garage rebuild, and declining the town's first right of refusal on Chapter land. minutes.summary: The Lunenburg Planning Board acted on several site-plan and ANR matters, including continuing a 20-unit townhome project on New West Townsend Road pending fire department and peer-engineering review, approving de minimis changes for a solar array and a garage rebuild, and declining the town's first right of refusal on Chapter land. what_happened.line: The board settled on four zoning amendments to bring to the next annual town meeting: inclusionary zoning, senior housing, minor site plan review, and cluster development.
The 20-unit townhome project on New West Townsend Road was continued to mid-April pending fire department review of the driveway and engineering review.

meetings.headline: Select Board leaned toward a two-tier (core + restoration) joint town/school override, no vote taken
meetings.summary: The Select Board spent a line-by-line workshop walking through every department's FY27 budget changes since the February 19 preliminary budget, flagging cuts (police clerk, second SRO, fire per diem, recreation director, communications/IT, animal control, town clerk staffing) as candidates to restore if an override passes. By the end the board leaned toward a tiered override structure (a core/level-service budget plus a separate restoration ask, for both town and school) but took no formal vote on it, and set a deadline of Thursday for the town's restoration number and Wednesday for the school committee's numbers.

what_happened.line: The Select Board leaned toward a two-tier override structure -- a core budget plus a separate restoration ask -- for both town and school, without taking a formal vote.

Board members worked line by line through department cuts made since the February 19 preliminary budget, flagging items such as a police clerk position, a second school resource officer, fire department per diem coverage, the recreation director post, communications/IT staffing and animal control funding as candidates to restore if an override passes.

The town manager was asked to produce the town's restoration budget number by Thursday, and Thursday's planned Tri-Board meeting was flagged for cancellation or reconsideration so the school committee's core and restoration figures could come in by Wednesday instead.

The board also settled smaller line items along the way, including pursuing a town engineer position in the restoration budget regardless of storm water compliance funding and leaving the snow and ice budget unchanged rather than risk a later cut.

why_it_matters: This is the shape of the override question residents may eventually vote on -- a base town/school budget plus a separate restoration ask, rather than one combined number.
The restoration list touches police staffing, a school resource officer, fire coverage, recreation programming and animal control -- services that stay cut if no override passes.

meetings.headline: Finance Committee reviewed FY27 department budgets amid a large town-school funding gap, with an override now expected.
meetings.summary: The Finance Committee heard FY27 budget presentations from DPW/sewer, land use, and general government departments, plus a trust fund commissioners' warrant article seeking money to legally investigate several neglected municipal trust funds, which the committee suggested moving to a special town meeting for a firmer estimate. No budget votes were taken; the committee recapped a prior tri-board session where all members agreed an override belongs on the ballot, split on whether it should be one or two amounts, and rescheduled its public hearing and a tri-board meeting for the following weeks.

budget_items.what_was_said: The general fund free cash was certified this week; Karen Brochu was thanked for putting together the free cash submission to the state.
Bill Bernard presented an overall DPW budget higher than previous years, covering mandatory work, a new part-time clerk, restored pavement management, and MS4 storm water compliance money.

Bernard's budget restores pavement management to $650,000 'where it should be,' while the town manager's preliminary budget shows only $279,000; a committee member said they will not support the restoration in the final budget.
Street light electricity costs were estimated at $30,000 originally, came in just over $30,500, then rose further; the line moved into DPW's budget after conversion to LED lighting.
Bernard requested a $340,000 increase in the storm water line item to get closer to MS4 permit compliance, covering catch basin cleaning and street sweeping.

budget_items.topic: Catch basin cleaning and sweeping performance
budget_items.what_was_said: In-house work over the last three years has completed about 30% of catch basin cleaning and 22% of street sweeping, well short of what is mandated.
Bernard estimated it would cost about $100,000 less per year to contract out catch basin cleaning and sweeping than to hire three additional staff.
Bernard modeled a 3% annual increase for DPW, clerical union, and himself across FY25-27 to estimate roughly $52,000 in added salary cost, pending ongoing CBA negotiations.
The snow and ice budget is being increased 2.5% per year to close the gap between budget and actual spending, currently around $800,000.
Vehicle repair costs sent out to contractors exceeded the budgeted line significantly last year, prompting a requested increase.
The recycling budget was reduced after a closer look at actual spending; last year's budget was much higher than what is actually being spent.
The trash program is described as roughly self-funding at about $500,000 per year.
DPW cited a small bridge grant for the Flaill road bridge, a storm water asset management grant from the Mass Clean Water Trust, and a pending Mass Community Cover grant for engineering on a culvert.
Bernard plans to apply for a Complete Streets grant and has a cost estimate of about a million dollars for sidewalk construction and repair between the high school and Marshall Park.
Chapter 90 funding for FY27 is expected at a higher level than the typical amount; continuing at the higher level over several years would add nearly $1.7 million versus normal funding.
The sewer enterprise fund budget is just under $2 million, with expenses and revenues nearly balanced showing an estimated small surplus.
The town pays Leominster and Fitchburg to treat sewage since Lunenburg has no treatment plant of its own; this is the largest driver of the sewer budget.
The engineering line was budgeted at $30,000 last year but actual cost was $80,000 after DEP required additional engineering work; the line is being increased again.
Money is set aside to replace aging pumps, controllers, and pipe as the sewer system approaches the end of its design life.

Without a rate increase, user charge revenue was estimated to leave a large deficit; with the proposed rate increase the budget shows only a small surplus, avoiding further draws on retained earnings.
The proposed sewer rate increase is about 16%, driven by Leominster and Fitchburg raising their own disposal charges.

The per-unit user rate would rise from its current level to a higher figure (about 16% increase), while the minimum charge rises only about 5%, intended to soften the impact on lower-usage households.

budget_items.topic: Sewer grant indirect cost line (health insurance)
budget_items.what_was_said: This line, which covers the sewer enterprise's share of health insurance and treasurer/collector office costs, was questioned for how it compares to prior years' actuals and budgets amid an 8% health insurance increase.
Total sewer expenses were compared across FY25 actual, FY26 budget, and FY27 request.
The combined conservation, building, and planning/economic development budget request represents a modest increase, driven mainly by step and cost-of-living increases.

budget_items.topic: Land use mapping purchase of services line
budget_items.what_was_said: A new line item funds mapping for zoning changes and proposals that previously had no dedicated funding mechanism.
About 16% of land use funding comes from the general fund, roughly 75% from building permit fees, and about 4% from specialty permits.
Some shovel-ready projects have not yet pulled permits; the building department has roughly this much in expected but uncollected permit fee receivables.

budget_items.topic: Trust funds legal investigation warrant article
budget_items.what_was_said: The trust fund commissioners requested this appropriation to fund roughly 40 hours of professional legal investigation into several long-neglected municipal trust funds.
The requested amount was calculated as approximately 40 hours of investigation at $350 per hour, covering all five flagged trust funds.

budget_items.topic: Total trust fund dollars at stake
budget_items.what_was_said: John Bowen said the funds under dispute total in this range, currently unable to be distributed to Lunenburg residents and veterans without a legal investigation.

budget_items.what_was_said: The 1901 donation establishing the worthy poor fund is estimated to be worth this much in today's dollars.
The town manager cited the school budget figure under full restoration as part of the overall FY27 budget update.
The presenter stated an overall projected budget deficit split between town and school portions.

budget_items.topic: Property tax levy and revenue estimates
budget_items.what_was_said: Property tax levy and total revenue estimates were cited, along with adjustments to motor vehicle excise and investment income revenue lines.
The overall general government budget changed slightly from the preliminary figure to the current figure presented tonight.

budget_items.topic: Town manager's office budget / assistant town manager position
budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager's budget rose substantially to fund a new assistant town manager position for a full year; restructuring by eliminating the communications/IT director position reduced the net new cost from $120,000 to $60,000.
Audit costs are rising because the town's former auditing firm was absorbed into a larger firm (CBIZ) at greater cost, and a competing firm lacked capacity to take on the town.
Small reductions were made to the treasurer and collector office budgets based on actual spending, including contracted services covering the deputy tax collector and Unibank services.
The assessor's budget is nearly level; a temporary special assistant position is being moved out of the operating budget to one-time funding; abatement counts have declined from a 2023 spike.
FY26 and FY25 real estate exemption counts and total dollar amounts were compared; the senior means-tested exemption was not approved for FY2025.
The town clerk's overall budget is roughly level, but the elections line rises sharply because 2026 is an election year with a September primary and November general election.
The APDC physicals budget was increased due to under-budgeting, and a new economic development committee line funds an annual town official meet-and-greet event.
The town report/printing line rose sharply because it had not been properly budgeted, covering the annual report, town meeting booklet, and special town meeting warrant printing and mailing.
The reserve fund is level funded; the town manager raised the idea of increasing it given department budgets are being tightened, citing prior years' transfer amounts.
The salary reserve has not been adjusted for FY27 pending outcomes of ongoing DPW, clerical, and firefighter contract negotiations; an anticipated 3% COLA for non-union (SAP) employees is assumed.
Central purchasing, which now includes consolidated postage costs, is level funded.
The veterans budget is largely driven by Chapter 115 benefit payments currently serving seven residents; the town receives trailing state reimbursement the following fiscal year.
This line rose almost entirely due to the non-discretionary Worcester County retirement assessment.
The unclassified budget, covering liability, workers comp, health, life insurance, unemployment and Medicare, increased from the preliminary figure due to a correction in Medicare supplement counts.
Liability insurance covers property/casualty with a rate guarantee through FY27, plus a separate injured-on-duty policy for police and fire and a small risk-management training line.
Workers compensation was reduced based on conversations with the town's insurance representative, applying available credits.
Group health insurance, the largest piece of the unclassified budget, increased; a separate line funds employees who opt out of coverage.
Retiree health insurance covers town and school retirees at estimated Medicare Blue and Medex rates, plus a Medicare supplement paid twice yearly.

reconciliation.coverage: official minutes are a summary only
reconciliation.summary: The two records agree closely on the headline figures the town chose to write down — free cash, the deficit, the school restoration number, the DPW and sewer budget totals, the land use budget, the trust fund warrant amount — and several of the "differences" are just caption garbling of the same digits (e.g. $3,25,5124 for $3,205,051.24). But the official minutes are a condensed summary: they omit the entire town-manager's-office restructuring decision, the board's agreement to put an override on the ballot, dozens of discussion-level figures (pavement management, sidewalk grant, sewer engineering/capital lines, real estate exemptions, town report costs), and several committee members' names outright — while a few figures that do appear in both (group health insurance, treasurer's budget reduction, salary reserve, town report) disagree by amounts too large to be a misheard digit and should be checked against the source budget documents.

what_happened.line: Finance Committee recapped a tri-board session where all members agreed an override belongs on the ballot, but remained split on whether it should be one amount or two.

DPW's proposed FY27 budget came in higher than prior years, restoring pavement management funding the town manager's preliminary budget had cut, though one committee member said they will not support that restoration.
The town manager's office is being restructured: the communications and IT director position would be eliminated and a new assistant town manager position funded starting July 1.

The committee recommended moving a warrant article seeking money to legally investigate several neglected municipal trust funds from the annual town meeting to a special town meeting, so a firmer cost estimate can be developed first.
The FY27 budget public hearing was pushed back one week to March 26, with a tri-board meeting taking the committee's March 19 slot instead.

why_it_matters: An override, once the ballot format is settled, would raise property taxes for residents and the one-question-versus-two split changes how they vote on it.
The DPW budget still has to be finalized, and whether pavement management funding is restored affects road paving work and how storm water permit compliance gets funded.
The town manager's office restructuring changes which staff position handles human resources and IT/communications duties going forward.

meetings.headline: Commission votes it and the Select Board lack the expertise to decide Legion trust fund eligibility questions
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Trust Fund Commission discussed a warrant article to fund roughly 40 hours of outside legal investigation into trust fund donor intent (particularly the American Legion fund, whose eligibility language proved unworkable on close reading), and a bylaw to let the Select Board temporarily manage trust distributions if the commission lacks a quorum. The commission adopted a citizenship/residency verification policy and passed a motion declaring that neither it nor the Select Board has the professional expertise to decide these trust-fund legal questions without hiring outside investigators.
