budget_items.topic: Age and size thresholds affecting which funds need review
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair said most trust funds are under a certain age and value, meaning most can be handled under the town attorney's existing retainer rather than needing separate investigation.
The chair cited a fund declaration limiting annual disbursement for sidewalk work near town hall.
A 1931 town meeting article set aside a memorial fund with interest to be spent annually on public grounds and sidewalks within a mile of the town center.

budget_items.topic: Estimated hourly cost of outside legal investigators
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair said the attorney indicated investigation work is billed hourly by outside firms, and used that rate to back into the requested warrant article total.

budget_items.topic: Hypothetical use of a sidewalk fund balance
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair used a hypothetical balance to illustrate how much could be spent on sidewalks and trash barrels near town hall if funds were freed up.

budget_items.what_was_said: The chair read the fund's current balance and a rule allowing a larger annual percentage payout once the balance exceeds a stated threshold.

budget_items.what_was_said: The chair read the 2013 declaration's annual disbursement cap, the balance threshold above which more can be released to veterans' benefits, and the post-threshold interest-based cap.
The chair restated the warrant article figure as roughly covering 40 hours of legal work, acknowledging the true cost could run higher.

budget_items.topic: Town's broader investment interest as a possible funding cushion
budget_items.what_was_said: A member noted the interest earned on the town's overall invested funds this year as a much larger pool than the warrant article amount, suggesting perspective on affordability.

decisions.decision: The proposed bylaw will not be submitted to the finance committee for funding review because it carries no cost.
No amendment to the American Legion fund eligibility language will be pursued until the cy pres investigation and any required court filing are completed.
Rewriting trust declarations through the Attorney General's office of public charities is being put on hold for now.
Overview of new research and fund documentation pushed to the next meeting.
Two remaining sets of meeting minutes will be reviewed at the next meeting.
Next commission meeting set for March 26, 2026.

meetings.headline: Sewer Commission weighed extending sewer service for a proposed duplex development via town meeting warrant article
meetings.summary: The Sewer Commission spent most of the meeting on a developer's request to extend sewer service up Pond Street to serve a planned duplex subdivision, discussing a possible town meeting warrant article and whether the commission would support it once engineered plans are ready. The commission also reviewed FY27 user rate and budget updates, ongoing infiltration/inflow and manhole repair work, a minor sewer bylaw wording change tied to the new ADU bylaw, and the pending storm water utility warrant article, approving prior minutes and adjourning by roll call.

budget_items.what_was_said: The commission reviewed the proposed FY27 rate, keeping the minimum charge increase at 5% while raising the regular usage charge more (about 16%), shifting more of the burden to higher water users. Staff said the rate is driven by what Leominster and Fitchburg charge Lunenburg for sewer treatment.
Demand fee notices will be mailed the week of March 16th; residents who have not paid their sewer bill were asked to pay before Friday, in person or online.

The commission recapped that it had already voted the FY27 budget in at a prior meeting so it could go out with the town warrants; a budget presentation was scheduled for Thursday night before FinCom. The budget avoids using retained earnings this year, with capital gains funding slightly reduced.

Members noted betterment revenue is slowing down as fewer new betterments come in, which is part of what is pushing the rate increases; the goal was described as trying to keep rates level rather than see dramatic swings.

budget_items.topic: Capital projects - Pump 2 and manhole covers
budget_items.what_was_said: Upcoming capital work includes work at Pump 2 and resetting manhole covers; the wrong size covers had been ordered but the correct size is in the warehouse and ready to install, targeted around April 15th.

An existing manhole repair contract is targeting manholes previously inspected and suspected of having inflow and infiltration (I&I); a member pushed for a more proactive approach to find and fix leaks rather than just tracking rising charges from Fitchburg/Leominster.

If a storm water utility is established, residents would be billed separately, similar to a sewer bill, with revenue used to fund street sweeping, storm drain cleaning and other work needed for federal storm water permit compliance.

budget_items.topic: Cost of special permit / engineering for duplex proposal
budget_items.what_was_said: The developer said he did not want to spend roughly two years and about $100,000 pursuing a special permit, preferring an as-of-right ANR approach; he said he is open to spending tens of thousands of dollars on engineered plans and to commission review of them.

meetings.headline: TriBoard split near evenly on one FY27 override vs. two tiers, but agreed unanimously to put one on the ballot.
meetings.summary: The Select Board, Finance Committee and School Committee met jointly to debate how to structure a Proposition 2½ override for next year's budget, weighing a single combined ask against tiered options. Every member present favored putting some override on the ballot, but the group was closely divided over one number versus two, and no final figure was set that night. meetings.headline: Task force outlined a proposed stormwater utility fee; bylaw goes to spring town meeting, fees start later.
meetings.summary: An engineering consultant presented the Stormwater Task Force's plan for a stormwater utility to fund MS4 federal permit compliance, explaining how fees would be based on impervious surface area rather than property value. No fee, budget, or bylaw vote was taken at this meeting; the plan calls for the enabling legislation and bylaw to go before spring town meeting and the storm water budget before fall town meeting, with residents raising questions about state roads, tax-exempt and agricultural properties, and credit caps.

The task force is considering a credit of up to a stated share of the assessed fee for properties managing their own stormwater on site, based on other Massachusetts communities' practice.

meetings.headline: Finance Committee warns a large school 'restoration' override could fail, as one did in 2012.
meetings.summary: The committee heard FY27 budget presentations from the Council on Aging (level-funded), the Library (a modest increase plus a push for above-level programming funding), and Public Access Cable, which described a widening deficit from declining Comcast franchise fees and a forced studio relocation. The bulk of the meeting was a debate over the upcoming Proposition 2½ override: members worried that bundling the town's mostly level-service requests with the school committee's much larger 'restoration' budget into a single ask risks a failure like the town's 2012 override, which passed by roughly two-to-one against and led to a decade of cuts.

what_happened.line: The Parks Commission voted to raise 2026 Town Beach season and day pass rates, aiming to shrink the town's subsidy of the beach program.
The Commission also voted, 3-0, to raise 2026 swim lesson rates, with a per-family cap for both residents and non-residents.
Staff said the new rates are still projected to fall short of covering the beach's costs, with the Parks revolving account as a possible backstop for the gap.
The Commission adopted an amended park facilities signage policy that removes the Commission itself from sign-approval authority, shifting it to staff.
Field-use rules and a proposed vendor-fair partnership were held off until a recreation director is hired, a position still vacant.

why_it_matters: This sets what residents and non-residents pay for beach passes and swim lessons in 2026, and it comes up in the context of a possible town override vote on covering town costs.
The rate increase is presented as narrowing, not closing, the gap between beach revenue and beach costs, so the shortfall may still draw on other town funds.
Sign approval at town park facilities now rests with staff rather than the elected Commission, changing who signs off on that kind of decision going forward.

budget_items.what_was_said: A shopping complex in Dennis, MA was cited as paying a very high storm water fee under that town's tiered structure, used as a comparison point.

budget_items.what_was_said: The task force discussed capping credits/abatements at a percentage of the fee, based on what other Massachusetts communities with utilities offer.

budget_items.topic: Assumed revenue loss from abatement program
budget_items.what_was_said: A rule of thumb from other communities assumes a portion of revenue will be lost to abatements once the credit program is in place, and some towns budget higher in year one to compensate.

budget_items.what_was_said: A wide range was initially used to estimate the value of the town's storm drainage network; the task force agreed to use the higher end on the slide.

budget_items.what_was_said: Rough estimates of pipe and road mileage were used to size the infrastructure-value slide; a member said these need to be verified with the DPW's own figures.

budget_items.topic: Infrastructure valuation framed as a park comparison
budget_items.what_was_said: The estimated value of the storm water network was compared to a large capital asset to make the scale tangible to residents.

budget_items.topic: Number of properties and parcels in the fee dataset
budget_items.what_was_said: The rate-structure analysis covers a defined subset of properties out of the town's full assessor's parcel list, with impervious area to be entered for each.

budget_items.topic: DPW operating budget request for storm water items ahead of the utility
budget_items.what_was_said: Bill said an extra amount was added to the DPW operational budget this cycle in case the utility fee is not approved in time, though he expects it may not survive budget cuts.

Using the state's override calculator, the group modeled what an increase to the general tax levy (covering basin cleaning, sweeping, and added engineering needs) would cost an average homeowner, as an alternative to the flat utility fee.

decisions.decision: Bill agreed to bring hard copies of the FAQ document to hand out at the public meeting.
Keep the residential/commercial fee-impact comparison slide (with the added revenue column), to be refined once real numbers are added.
Add a caveat to the presentation noting the fee is not guaranteed to stay flat, given uncertainty from a pending new EPA stormwater permit.
Keep the 50% cap on credits/abatements in the presentation, consistent with other Massachusetts communities.
Leave fee-structure governance with the select board for now rather than pursuing a combined sewer/storm commission, since that would require a multi-year legislative process.
Remove the 'drainage improvement projects' line item from the funding-use slide since it is not currently budgeted through the utility.
Bill's GIS team will go back and delineate impervious area for previously miscoded properties (e.g., Jaclyn Drive) that lacked a proper land-use code.
John will independently build his own spreadsheet model from the impervious-area data to test rate-structure trade-offs, in parallel with the consultant's team.
Someone will contact the library the next day to confirm the room and whether a screen/projector will be available for the presentation.
Hold audience questions until after the full slideshow is presented, given the likely larger turnout for this meeting.
The FAQ document will not be further revised for now; Jarice will send a final revised slide deck by end of day the next day.
Meeting adjourned at 8:26 p.m. on March 3, 2026.

meetings.headline: PACC approved its FY27 budget for FinCom, showing a shortfall to be covered from retained earnings
meetings.summary: The Public Access Cable Committee reviewed its manager's monthly report, walked through a detailed FY27 budget presentation destined for FinCom (salaries, new equipment, legal fees for upcoming Comcast contract negotiations, and Comcast franchise-fee revenue projections), and voted to approve the amended presentation and authorize the manager to present it. The committee also worked through a policy-book cleanup (an obsolete job title/policy to be formally removed), discussed early-stage talks about sharing studio space with FATV in Fitchburg, and voted to appoint two of its members to a newly approved town Cable Advisory Committee that will eventually handle Comcast franchise renewal.

budget_items.what_was_said: The manager said current-year salaries are on pace to exceed budget and will need a line-item transfer, and gave the FY27 salaries figure.
Videographer pay is budgeted to rise from FY26 to FY27.
Combined salaries and videographer costs rise from the FY26 to FY27 figure, an increase the manager characterized as double digits.
Both lines are unchanged from the prior year.
This line rises because the bulletin administrator's hourly rate was raised after it was found to be below minimum wage.
This line, used for video and peripheral equipment purchases via Amazon and B&H, is proposed to increase.
The large increase is to buy a new switcher and Castus program server plus installation, leaving a small remainder for emergencies.
A new legal fees line was added ahead of Comcast franchise negotiations, based on differing attorney fee estimates.
The insurance-driven indirect cost estimate was revised down after an initial higher estimate.
Revenue from Comcast fees was discussed amid concern about subscribers dropping Comcast; the quarterly basis used to project the year was revised downward after a lower recent quarterly payment.
Investment income was carried forward at the same level as FY26 because the finance department's interest postings are far behind.
The total PEG access revenue figure was corrected during discussion.
The manager gave a total expense figure and the resulting shortfall figure that would need to come from retained earnings, both to be updated after the Comcast revenue change.

The committee discussed asking the town to draw the shortfall from retained earnings via the warrant, noting timing problems because retained earnings for the year are not certified until after town meeting.
The budget presentation's funding-sources slide splits revenue between investment income and the Comcast franchise fee.

decisions.decision: The FY27 budget presentation, originally prepared for a tri-board meeting, will instead be given to FinCom on March 5.
Comcast revenue projection basis lowered to a more conservative quarterly figure rather than the higher one previously used, to avoid overstating expected revenue.
The manager will try to keep the FinCom presentation date but acknowledged FinCom may need to move it to give itself time to prepare questions.

The obsolete "videographer editor" job title/policy, which does not correspond to any actual town job title, will be brought back for a formal removal vote at the next meeting (policy changes require prior announcement).

Not renewing Clear Gov software produces a savings that partially offsets other IT cost increases.

A committee member questioned the cost of the Code Red emergency notification subscription relative to how many residents actually subscribe.
A portion of OpenGov's cost is offset by technology fees paid by users of online permitting, funneled through the tech revolving fund.

The superintendent gave the FY26 baseline: salaries, expenses, and a total that included a one-time free cash allocation used to offset health insurance, unemployment insurance, salaries, and athletic transportation.
School choice revenue received by the district has fallen sharply over the years, shifting that burden to the local taxpayer.
Extended day, lunch, and sped tuition circuit breaker were called out as the largest revolving revenue generators; the school choice "other" line includes bus fees collected early.
A member argued athletic fees should be required to cover athletic transportation costs, noting that doing so would wipe out the athletic revolving account.
Title I funding is expected to change significantly for FY27 versus FY26, with the district unsure of the exact allocation.
Title II, the main professional development funding vehicle, is projected lower for FY27.
Title IV funding, for safe and supportive school environments, is anticipated to be very small for FY27.
The special education entitlement grant largely funds one very expensive out-of-district placement at the May Institute/May Center.
Circuit breaker reimbursement is generally around a set percentage of the prior year's out-of-district tuition, rarely fully funded.
This is the second and final year of a two-year Student Opportunity Act grant, previously used to fund a literacy coach and now redirected to early literacy materials and professional development.
The state delegation secured earmarks for one-time costs; the FY27 amount is unknown, with prior earmarks discussed for use toward unfunded capital projects.
Health insurance is budgeted at current staff plans plus a percentage increase, plus new restored positions budgeted at the highest family plan tier as a conservative assumption.

The business manager budgeted a percentage increase for busing pending confirmation from the bus contractor, citing a memo with the actual contracted rate; the district has had four consecutive multi-year contracts with only one bidder.

what_happened.line: The School Committee chair said a townwide operating override, not a smaller fix, is needed to avoid what he called "catastrophic" cuts.
The district's FY27 school budget presentation focused on restoring special education, literacy, and student-services positions cut the prior year.
No budget votes were taken; the schools will get a single line within the town's balanced budget, and the district must scale its ask down to that number if an override fails.
IT presented an FY27 request driven largely by the loss of one-time ARPA funding that had covered MUNIS software.
The business manager agreed to compile ongoing EPIMS staffing trend data for the Finance Committee and the tri-board.

why_it_matters: An operating override, if pursued, would go to voters and change property tax bills beyond the normal 2½ percent cap.
The positions under discussion -- special education, literacy, and student-services roles cut last year -- affect direct school services to students.
Override structure and size will be worked out at the March 11 tri-board meeting before going to the Select Board for a warrant.

March 12 Finance Committee review of smaller department budgets (Council on Aging, Board of Health)

meetings.headline: Committee advanced a "needs" FY27 budget it says the town cannot currently fund without an override
meetings.summary: The School Committee held its FY2027 budget hearing, presenting a restoration (not expansion) budget built around bringing back positions cut the prior year, and stressed repeatedly that this is a need-based budget requiring a town override, not one the town can currently afford. Members voted to send that budget to the finance committee, discussed the shape and size of an eventual override (around $1.8 million, unified and untiered), and separately approved several small grant proposals, a cap on virtual-school enrollment, and the FY26-27 school calendar.

public_comment.topic: Spoke in support of the restoration budget and the forthcoming override, cautioning that cuts are far harder to restore than to make and that the committee should wait until the actual need is known before alarming the public.

budget_items.topic: School choice net cost / chapter 70 loss
budget_items.what_was_said: The district receives a set per-pupil amount for incoming school-choice students but loses more in chapter 70 aid and tuition value for students choicing out, making it a net financial loss.
The business manager gave last year's revenue collected in the transportation revolving account from bus fees.
Combined revolving account revenues were estimated in this range, with most of it being state or federal money rather than locally generated funds.

budget_items.topic: Federal Title grants FY26 to FY27
budget_items.what_was_said: Title I, II, and IV federal entitlement grants are all projected to shrink substantially for FY27, with Title I facing roughly a 30% cut.
This was the final year of a two-phase Student Opportunity Act grant that had funded a literacy coach position; no further funding is expected.
Legislators secured one-time earmark funding this year, but the district cannot count on earmark funding recurring at the same level next year.
Health insurance costs are projected to rise 9% for FY27 due to reduced coverage rather than cost containment; the district expects to spend out its FY26 budgeted amount without significant overage.
The FY27 heating budget assumption was based on FY25 actual costs, which the presenter said may have been under-budgeted for FY26.

budget_items.topic: Utilities - electricity actual spend to date
budget_items.what_was_said: Actual electricity expenditures so far this fiscal year were given, described as rising along with residential utility costs.
General transportation costs were budgeted with an assumed increase pending final contracted rates from the bus vendor, benchmarked against other districts' business managers.
The district's third-party technology vendor recommended these annual increases for subscriptions and equipment respectively.

Supply cost increase projections tied to tariffs were revised down from an original estimate, though a member suggested the figure may need to rise again; principals say schools have already depleted stockpiled supplies.
After the budget was first posted, the superintendent and business manager cut this amount by moving the athletic director from full-time to half-time and trimming supply lines across schools.
This is the estimated total cost of all restoration and restructuring positions in the FY27 needs budget, assuming staff take the most expensive health insurance tier.
With the restoration additions the schools would represent roughly this share of the town budget; the committee's informal goal has been to keep the share closer to a lower figure.

budget_items.topic: Health insurance share of school budget
budget_items.what_was_said: Health insurance now makes up a larger share of the total school budget than the prior year, a trend the presenter called concerning.

Committee members discussed a possible override figure in this range to cover the restoration budget, while noting the town does not guarantee the school district retains that increment in future years.

The district sought approval to redirect previously awarded one-time funds, originally intended for the iReady program, toward decodable readers, high school math materials, and targeted professional learning.
A one-time state grant request to pay teachers hourly for planning time to build middle-school career exploration and high school pathway alignment, ahead of a state mandate.
A grant request for professional development and instructional coaching for PreK-5 educators to strengthen foundational literacy instruction.

reconciliation.what: Our minutes against the minutes the town published. caption_error = the same fact the captions rendered badly, resolved by the official reading shown beside the as-heard one; discrepancy = a substantive difference, flagged and not resolved. Neither record is treated as the referee.
reconciliation.coverage: official minutes are a summary only
reconciliation.summary: The official minutes confirm every vote our minutes captured and match on outcomes, but they record almost none of the dollar figures, percentages, or discussion detail our minutes pulled from the audio, and they add a few concrete facts (the half-time athletic director, two guest principals, an absent/vacant committee seat) that our minutes missed entirely. The one thing a reader should check first is the committee roster: our minutes list five members present (Tony, Laura, Mandy, Cara, Liz) plus "the chair" separately, while the official minutes show only three seats filled (Chair Sculimbrene, Vice Chair Brzozoski, Secretary Gilman) with one member absent and one seat vacant — "Cara" and "Liz" do not correspond to anyone in the official roster.

what_happened.line: The committee voted to send the finance committee an FY27 budget it says the town cannot fund without an override.
Members said they favor one unified, townwide override rather than separate amounts by school or grade.
The committee will not detail what gets cut to balance the budget without an override until its March 18 meeting.
The committee also approved several grant proposals, capped virtual-school enrollment, and adopted the FY26-27 school calendar.
A speaker during public comment urged the committee to hold off alarming the public until the actual funding need is known.

why_it_matters: This budget is described as restoring positions cut the prior year, and the committee says funding it depends on an override, a vote that would raise property taxes beyond the normal cap.

The grant, enrollment-cap and calendar votes are procedural and do not depend on the override outcome.

meetings.headline: Water District voters approved surplus-funded Medicare back-pay, smart meters, and a new excavator.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Water District held its special district meeting to elect a moderator and act on three warrant articles, all funded from the surplus revenue account: back IRS/Medicare payments, Neptune R900 remote-read water meter gateways, and a new rubber-tired excavator for in-house project work. Residents questioned the makeup of the surplus account, including how much derives from the PAS lawsuit settlement, and all three articles were reported as passing by voice vote.

what_happened.line: Voters approved a surplus-account transfer to pay past-due employee Medicare payments, by voice vote.
Voters also approved a surplus-account transfer for Neptune remote-read water meter gateways at two tank sites, by voice vote.
Voters approved a third surplus-account transfer for a rubber-tired excavator for in-house water main work, by voice vote.
A resident asked how much of the surplus fund traces to the PAS lawsuit settlement; a commissioner said none of the night's articles drew on settlement money.
A commissioner said doing the Rolling Acres water main project in-house rather than through a contractor saved money, citing prevailing-wage costs avoided by district crews.

why_it_matters: All three approvals draw on the district's surplus revenue account rather than the regular water rate budget, so they don't change water bills directly but do reduce reserves the district holds.
The settlement-fund question bears on how much of that surplus a resident should expect stays available for future rate relief or capital work, separate from the PAS lawsuit money.
The in-house equipment purchase reflects a district choice to keep more infrastructure work off contract, which affects future project costs and staffing needs.

The board voted to recommend the town not exercise its right of first refusal on one such property, discussed an incoming request for a PILOT agreement tied to a proposed battery storage facility (referred to the Select Board), reviewed senior tax-exemption deadlines and FY27 new-growth estimates, set upcoming meeting dates, and adjourned into executive session under the abatement-confidentiality statute.

meetings.headline: Commissioners approved the FY27 operating budget and set warrant articles, including a district expansion
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Water District Commissioners approved the FY2026-2027 maintenance and operating budget, describing it as largely unchanged from the prior year aside from minor increases, and voted on the warrant articles for the annual meeting including changed polling hours, equipment/mains funding, a new truck purchase, and a citizen-petitioned expansion of the district for a Bird Street development. The board also discussed backup power and fire protection questions and took one question from the floor on the budget's year-over-year increase before adjourning.

budget_items.what_was_said: The board reviewed the commissioner's report and the maintenance and operating budget breakdown ahead of a vote. It was noted the report itself does not require a vote, only the budget does.
A motion was made to approve the maintenance and operation budget for 2026-2027 as listed in the budget breakdown, with the total read aloud and questioned for accuracy.

budget_items.topic: Budget line changes year over year
budget_items.what_was_said: Most budget items were said to carry straight over from last year with only minimal increases; health insurance stayed the same while interest on some loan principals rose. The budget overall was described as close to last year's, roughly tracking inflation.
Article 4 was described as authorizing the commissioners' temporary borrowing, referenced as from something heard as "ASAV."

budget_items.topic: Warrant Article 5 - equipment and mains account
budget_items.what_was_said: Article 5 puts money into the equipment and mains account, which funds the rolling acres project.
Article 6 authorizes purchase of a new truck because one of the district's current trucks is in poor condition.
The proposed expansion of the district onto Bird Street was said to cost the district nothing, with any new infrastructure built at the developer's own expense.
Asked from the floor how much the budget increased from last year, a commissioner estimated the total increase at roughly a figure on a roughly two-million-dollar budget.

decisions.decision: Agreed the commissioner's report does not require a vote and simply goes into the booklet; only the operating budget requires a vote.
Agreed to change annual meeting polling hours to 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., opening the meeting at 10:00 a.m. and reconvening at 4:00 p.m. to announce election winners.
Agreed to invite the developer proposing the Bird Street district expansion to attend the annual meeting to answer questions.

budget_items.topic: FY27 projected deficit before rate action
budget_items.what_was_said: Without a rate increase the budget would run this deficit, which in past years was covered by drawing down retained earnings.
Betterment payments from 20-year financing plans taken out when the system was built are ending, so that revenue source is shrinking and can no longer be relied on.
Of about ten rate scenarios considered, the preferred one raises the minimum charge by 5% (described around $133 to $139) so low-usage customers subsidize large users less.
Along with the minimum-charge change, the regular user rate would rise 16%, together closing the funding gap.
With the combined rate changes the budget shows an estimated surplus rather than a deficit.

Estimated privilege fees were put at $40,000, partly anticipating more ADU tie-ins; the sewer connection charge line was set around 30,000 versus a recent three-year average near 48,000, which spiked in a prior year when rates rose and people paid early.

The sewer budget is independent of the town's general budget; as an enterprise fund its revenues must equal or exceed its expenses with no town subsidy, though the sewer pays the town for shared accounting services.

budget_items.what_was_said: The director cited pavement management, which had been growing $50,000 a year and should be $600,000 this year but was cut to $279,000, as evidence that money placed in the general operating budget is not guaranteed to be spent on its intended purpose.
A single-family home would pay under $100 per year under the proposed storm water utility; commercial properties would pay based on impervious surface area.

meetings.headline: Town Manager unveiled a preliminary FY27 budget that does not balance without a property tax override

minutes.headline: Town Manager unveiled a preliminary FY27 budget that does not balance without a property tax override
minutes.summary: The Finance Committee heard FY27 budget presentations from the fire, facilities and police departments, each citing staffing, contract and equipment cost drivers, including a fire department fourth-shift staffing proposal and a police restructuring from two school resource officers to one SRO plus a second detective. The Town Manager then presented a preliminary town-wide FY27 budget that she said does not balance and currently relies on a Proposition 2½ override, walking the committee through revenue sources and expenditure categories in detail; no votes were taken on the budget or the override. She also reported that FY25 books were closed out late, risking a hold on state aid, though the town secured a filing extension.

reconciliation.what: Our minutes against the minutes the town published. caption_error = the same fact the captions rendered badly, resolved by the official reading shown beside the as-heard one; discrepancy = a substantive difference, flagged and not resolved. Neither record is treated as the referee.
reconciliation.summary: The two records overlap heavily on the FY27 financial summary (revenue, levy, expenditure-by-category totals, deficit/override math) and agree there, once you allow for digit-grouping/decimal-point caption garbling on our side — dozens of figures are the same fact rendered badly. But the official minutes are themselves a curated summary: they omit almost every granular departmental line our transcript captured (radio maintenance, sprinkler, drainage, IT contractor, etc.), while we're missing the police compensation table, mutual-aid stats, and cruiser count the official minutes include; a reader should specifically check the TCP revolving-fund balance ($6,000–24,000 heard vs. $33,500 official), the police lockup line ($125,000 heard vs. $20,600 official), and whether the SRO-to-detective move and next week's meeting topic were actually decided as our minutes state.

meetings.headline: Task force preps stormwater fee bylaw and March 5 info session; still undecided on override size, engineer hire
meetings.summary: The Stormwater Task Force reviewed how recent FinCom and Select Board meetings went, and spent most of the meeting stress-testing whether to hire an in-house engineer/admin versus outsourcing billing and inspections to keep overhead down. Members worked through sample commercial-property fee calculations, a town-budget-versus-utility cost comparison, and logistics for a March 5th public information session ahead of the town meeting where the stormwater bylaw is the only article; no substantive votes were taken, only routine approval of minutes and adjournment.

budget_items.topic: Overhead share of proposed stormwater budget
budget_items.what_was_said: FinCom flagged the overhead portion of the initial proposed budget as too large and pushed to outsource work to reduce it.
Group discussed replacing the project manager/engineer position with an outsourced percentage of the sewer business manager's role or a consultant, debating what share of salary that would be.
Members compared the proposed engineer salary to what entry-level civil engineers are actually paid, defending the estimate as reasonable.

budget_items.topic: Sewer business manager taking on stormwater billing
budget_items.what_was_said: Idea floated that the sewer business manager could absorb stormwater billing for a percentage of his salary/time, since he already runs Munis billing four times a year.
Members looked up their own UniPay transactions to estimate what a per-payment fee would cost the town if used for stormwater billing.

budget_items.topic: Enterprise fund subsidy for office space/equipment
budget_items.what_was_said: It was noted the town currently subsidizes enterprise funds for office space and equipment like computers, and stormwater would only owe a fraction of that.
Members each calculated, using different methods (DLS override calculator vs. their own tax-rate math), what an average single-family home currently contributes toward the stormwater line.

budget_items.topic: Override calculator projection for added funding
budget_items.what_was_said: Using the Prop 2½ override calculator, members estimated how much an average single-family tax bill would rise if the added stormwater money were structured as an override.
For public messaging, a member argued the town's stormwater infrastructure is worth roughly as much as the middle-high school, to help residents grasp its scale.
The group agreed to clarify publicly that the money being requested is not eligible for Chapter 90 reimbursement, since Chapter 90 doesn't cover maintenance.
A spot-check showed the Walmart-anchored parcel's current tax-based contribution to stormwater versus what a tiered utility fee might collect from it.
The task force cited a consultant-provided ERU value and noted 700 parcels are being analyzed by Weston & Sampson to assign ERUs for large properties.
Members compared what the utility company currently pays toward stormwater via property tax against what its share would be if distributed under the new fee.
Several other commercial properties (a church, a lumber yard, a fitness club) were checked to see how little they currently contribute compared to their impervious footprint.

budget_items.topic: Emerald Place / Carousel Lane apartment complex assessment
budget_items.what_was_said: The group examined how a 150-unit apartment complex is assessed and discussed whether to bill it as one integrated property.

budget_items.topic: Line-item budget scenario (town budget vs. utility)
budget_items.what_was_said: A chart compared the current town-budget line for stormwater against a proposed scenario that strips out the engineer/vendor costs, showing the resulting per-resident change either way.

budget_items.topic: Utility scenario resident vs. commercial burden split
budget_items.what_was_said: Under a stormwater utility funded by ERUs, the commercial/industrial/other share was estimated to cover a portion of costs, shifting the residential share down from the town-budget scenario.

budget_items.topic: Annual consulting cost from CI (current engineering contractor)
budget_items.what_was_said: Members tried to total what the town currently pays CI for consulting work, to compare against hiring an in-house engineer.

budget_items.topic: In-house engineer full cost with benefits
budget_items.what_was_said: The group estimated the fully-loaded cost of an in-house engineer including benefits, to weigh against outsourcing.
Specific outsourced tasks and their costs were pulled from a CI contract to see what could move in-house, including a report, BMP design, and plan updates.
Members noted town meeting had approved paying an engineering firm despite not unanimous support, as a precedent for getting the stormwater bylaw approved.

budget_items.topic: Paraprofessional salary and health benefit comparison
budget_items.what_was_said: As an aside on the cost of benefits driving hiring reluctance, a school paraprofessional's salary was compared to the cost of a family health insurance plan, which reportedly exceeded the salary itself.

meetings.summary: The Select Board heard the town manager's report that the FY27 budget is not balanced and will require an override, with a shortfall estimated at over $3 million pending school figures, alongside healthy FY25 free cash and a health insurance rate increase. The board also spent most of the meeting reviewing and amending its FY26 goals objective-by-objective and working through a long list of warrant articles for the 2026 annual town meeting, deferring several (appointment policy, legislative earmarks, trust fund/open space bylaws) to future meetings.

meetings.headline: FinCom previews FY27 budget: a level-service plan likely still needs an override, possibly again next year.
meetings.summary: The Finance Committee heard that the town's actual FY27 health insurance increase came in at 8.85% (down from over 20% after eliminating GLP-1 weight-loss drug coverage), and that a level-service town/school budget is unlikely to be balanced without an override. Members discussed how DPW, police, fire and school budgets will be presented in coming weeks, agreed to formally request the school department align its FY27 budget presentation with prior years and show FTEs and a consolidated athletics budget, and began a recurring discussion of how to structure a possible Proposition 2½ override, including the risk of needing another one next year. The committee also approved the January 8th minutes and adjourned by roll call vote.

budget_items.what_was_said: The actual health insurance rate increase came in at 8.85%, described as the actual (not estimated) figure just received.

Eliminating GLP-1 weight-loss drug coverage (voted by the insurance trust/'Maya') brought the increase down from an original estimate of over 20% to 8.85%; diabetes prescriptions for GLP-1s are still covered.

A committee member recalled that in a past budget year an extra $140,000 was paid toward transportation because it was being counted against the athletics revolving account, cited as a reason to want a consolidated athletics budget.
The chair explained that the level-service budget the committee will hear is likely not a balanced budget, and above-level-service or restorative requests will also be presented separately.

The chair described three possible budget scenarios the committee is dealing with: level service (likely requiring an override), increased/restorative service (a larger override), or a balanced budget reached through cuts.

The finance director said the level-service budget she is presenting already includes some cuts regardless of the override outcome, citing as an example a reduction from 5 days a week to 4 days a week of an unspecified service.
The chair opened discussion on a likely FY27 override or overrides, with no amount yet determined; a member argued level-service and restorative/enhanced requests should not be blended into one ask.
A member asked that the school present one consolidated athletics budget including expenses paid from the revolving account, a practice she said stopped around 2020.
The committee agreed to formally request that the FY27 school budget be presented in the same format as FY26 and FY25, clearly showing level service versus extra items and FTE per salary line.
A member raised concern that the Capital Planning Committee is reviewing a turf field replacement project that was never a ranked priority submitted by the school department, questioning the process.

The chair warned there is a high likelihood that even a level-service override passed this year could be followed by another level-service override next year, and floated setting the levy limit higher than taxed in year one to build headroom.

decisions.decision: DPW, police, and fire/facilities budgets are judged firm enough to present next week even though some union contracts (e.g., DPW Teamsters) are not yet finalized.

A committee member will draft and send the school business manager a written list of requests for how the FY27 school budget should be presented (aligned format with FY25/FY26, FTE per salary line, consolidated athletics budget, itemized approved budget changes).
The committee will consolidate all members' questions into one compiled list before sending them to the school business manager, rather than sending questions individually.

Because there will not be time to finish the full Finance Committee report before the warrant is mailed, the committee will include a high-level summary with a QR code in the mailed warrant and issue the full report about a month later.

meetings.headline: New Lunenburg planning director floated zoning fixes for small stores; Leominster briefed the committee on outreach.
meetings.summary: Leominster's economic development coordinator, Amanda Curtis, gave the Lunenburg Economic Development Committee an overview of Leominster's marketing, sponsorship, small-business grant, and infrastructure programs. Lunenburg's newly hired planning and economic development director, Stephen Wallace, introduced himself, proposed visitor-guide advertising and a business brochure, agreed to draft a "minor site plan review" process to ease zoning burdens on small storefronts, and, after consulting town counsel, confirmed non-restaurant businesses may allow BYOB without permission. No formal votes were taken except the roll-call adjournment.

budget_items.what_was_said: Leominster's economic development coordinator said the city runs over 50 events a year with a zero dollars budget for those events, relying on sponsorships and donations.

A newsletter sponsor's funds have been redirected into small grants to local businesses, described as $250 grants so far, with hope the fund grows.
The coordinator said she keeps newsletter print runs conservative, printing about 200 copies to avoid waste, distributing the rest online.
The brook and culvert reconstruction project is under construction and grant-funded; FEMA reportedly prioritized it after the 2023 flood.

decisions.decision: Stephen Wallace to draft a 'minor site plan review' process so simple changes of use in small existing storefronts (no parking increase, no building alterations) would not require full planning board site plan review; would need zoning language amendment for annual town meeting, or a planning board regulation amendment any time via public hearing.
Committee offered to form a sub-quorum working group (two members plus the ex officio member) to assist Stephen Wallace on the site plan review work if helpful.

After consulting town counsel, determined that non-restaurant businesses (e.g., a nail salon, hardware store) may allow customers to BYOB without needing town permission, since Lunenburg has no BYOB regulation for non-restaurant businesses.
Committee noted Lunenburg lacks an advertisement in the North Central Massachusetts visitor guide and should consider adding one to promote town events.

meetings.headline: State Reps Kushmerick and Scarsdale briefed the COA on caregiver legislation, grants, and school/healthcare funding fights.
meetings.summary: State Representatives Mike Kushmerick and Margaret Scarsdale visited the Council on Aging to discuss caregiver reform legislation, funding sources for home modifications and senior programs, the Nashoba Valley Medical Center closure, and Lunenburg's school funding and reading-proficiency struggles. The board also covered routine business including personnel hiring updates, a telehealth hub project, calendar of upcoming programs, and a lengthy, unresolved-then-resolved debate over how the council should support a proposed seniors-reading-to-students program at the schools, ultimately agreeing to limit its role to organizing volunteer readers.

Rep. Scarsdale described a T-Mobile Hometown grant she wrote for community-centered improvements such as gazebo alterations.

budget_items.what_was_said: A board member said small towns must write many separate grant applications for modest amounts and asked the state to make funding easier to access directly.

budget_items.topic: School funding gap addressed by delegation earmarks
budget_items.what_was_said: Rep. Kushmerick said each delegation member secured a separate earmark for the schools, together addressing a portion of last year's budgetary gap through direct funding.
Rep. Scarsdale noted the governor's FY27 budget had just been released and the House was reviewing it, including the per-person line item for senior centers.
Rep. Scarsdale described conversations about shifting some state funding into the flexible UGGA bucket so the town could decide how to spend it, rather than restricted grants.

decisions.decision: The council agreed to send a letter of support for Rep. Kushmerick's and Rep. Scarsdale's caregiver reform legislation, currently before the Committee on Revenue.
The chair asked members to return with thoughts on criteria for creating honorary/emeritus board member status, suggesting roughly four terms of service as a starting point.
The board agreed to have someone look into trying the 'Plaud Note' AI recording/transcription tool to assist with minutes, without it replacing the work of watching and revising the meeting record.
A flyer time error for the WEAR 365 breakfast presentation (listed as 10am, actually 9am) will be corrected, and Lucas will make a new flyer to be emailed out.
The bylaws subcommittee will hold its first meeting Thursday, using examples from other towns, with discussion to follow at a future council meeting.

The council agreed its role regarding the schools' reading proficiency issue should be limited to organizing volunteer seniors to read with children at the discretion of school educators, not presenting itself as fixing the reading problem.

meetings.headline: Monty Tech's FY27 assessment to Lunenburg would jump sharply, and the town manager warned an override is likely.
meetings.summary: The Finance Committee opened FY27 budget season by hearing Monty Tech's proposed budget, whose per-town assessment formula would raise Lunenburg's cost significantly more than Monty Tech's own budget grew; then heard a storm water task force pitch to create a dedicated storm water utility, which several committee members criticized as inefficient compared to funding it through the regular operating budget; and closed with a preliminary, free-cash-dependent FY27 capital plan and a town manager's report describing ongoing finance department turnover, an unclosed FY25 books, and a likely need for an override or cuts in FY27. No budget or override decisions were made; this was described as an early, non-binding discussion.

budget_items.topic: Monty Tech FY27 total proposed budget
budget_items.what_was_said: The business manager presented Monty Tech's total FY27 proposed budget as a 2.53% increase. She said most of the increase was driven by required net school spending and transportation costs.

budget_items.topic: Monty Tech total assessment to all 18 communities
budget_items.what_was_said: The total FY27 assessment to all member communities was presented, described as a 6% increase over FY26.

budget_items.topic: Lunenburg's FY27 assessment to Monty Tech
budget_items.what_was_said: Lunenburg's proposed FY27 assessment to Monty Tech was presented as an increase driven almost entirely by the state's required minimum contribution formula.
The business manager walked through the chapter 70 formula, noting Monty Tech's foundation aid calculation produced only a small increase, so the state applied a hold-harmless $75-per-pupil minimum.

budget_items.topic: Monty Tech capital budget cut to offset athletic complex lease
budget_items.what_was_said: The business manager said Monty Tech cut its capital budget to offset the new operating cost of the athletic field/track and bleacher tax-exempt municipal lease.

budget_items.topic: Monty Tech budget cuts from initial request
budget_items.what_was_said: The business manager said Monty Tech had to cut its initial wish-list budget request by this amount to reach the proposed FY27 budget.

budget_items.topic: Monty Tech excess and deficiency (E&D) use
budget_items.what_was_said: Monty Tech's certified E&D (similar to free cash) was presented, with portions proposed to offset the operating and capital assessments to towns.

budget_items.topic: Storm water utility proposed FY27 budget
budget_items.what_was_said: The DPW presenter proposed a storm water utility budget to reach MS4 compliance, versus continuing to fund storm water only through the existing DPW operating line.

budget_items.topic: Storm water project manager position cost
budget_items.what_was_said: A new storm water project manager position was costed out including salary, fringe benefits, and a share of the DPW director's salary and benefits.
Vendor costs for engineering, catch basin cleaning and roadway sweeping were presented as the largest share of the proposed storm water utility budget.
The task force proposed a flat annual fee for single-family homes, citing comparable towns' fees as a benchmark.
Twenty-two capital projects were submitted for FY27 across departments, ranked by the capital planning committee.
The town manager said the preliminary capital plan is funded using a conservative free cash estimate, level taxation, and the special purpose stabilization fund, pending free cash certification.

budget_items.topic: Free cash history used to estimate FY27 capital funding
budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager cited 10-year and 5-year free cash averages and medians as the basis for a conservative FY27 free cash estimate.
The town manager described the special purpose stabilization fund, created in 2017 for vehicles/equipment, noting its current balance and that it has never been used.
The town manager reported the town is deficit-spending on snow and ice, already well over budget with much of winter remaining, which affects free cash available for other uses.
The town manager said TC Pacios building carries unbudgeted annual operating costs and that decommissioning half the building produced far less utility savings than expected.
The town manager flagged the FY27 mosquito control program assessment as a possible town meeting article given the town's financial condition.
The town manager reported a grant application for design funding for the Goodrich Street culvert.
The town manager reported a grant application for network infrastructure upgrades at the Adult Activity Center, a project unlikely to be funded within the FY27 capital plan itself.

decisions.decision: An additional capital planning committee meeting was scheduled for the following Wednesday to discuss initial reactions to the preliminary FY27 capital plan.

The chair asked department heads to include in their FY27 budget presentations: a summary of key services, a status-quo vs. proposed-changes summary, funding sources outside taxation, and an organizational chart.
A committee member agreed to collect finance committee members' detailed budget questions for each department and forward them to the town manager/finance director in advance of presentations.
The public schools budget presentation to the Finance Committee was set for February 19.
Warrant articles for the May 2 annual town meeting are due by March 16.
The town manager will begin meeting with TC Pacios building stakeholders (including cable access and the food pantry) starting the next day about winding down operations there.

what_happened.line: The town manager said an override or cuts are likely for FY27, citing budget pressure across departments.
Lunenburg's FY27 assessment to Monty Tech would rise mainly because of the state's minimum contribution formula, not Monty Tech's own spending growth.
A storm water task force proposed a dedicated utility funded by a flat homeowner fee; several committee members argued the operating budget would be more efficient.
The finance department reported ongoing staff turnover and FY25 books still not closed, complicating FY27 budget preparation.
A preliminary FY27 capital plan listing ranked projects across departments was presented, pending free cash certification.

why_it_matters: An override, if it goes to a town-wide vote, would raise property tax bills beyond the normal cap and residents would decide it directly.
A separate storm water utility, if adopted, would likely show up as a new fee on homeowners rather than as part of the existing tax-funded budget.
Monty Tech's assessment increase and Lunenburg's own department budgets both feed the same FY27 town budget that goes to the May 2 annual town meeting.

meetings.headline: Superintendent warns prior budget cuts are pushing more students toward costly out-of-district special ed placements
meetings.summary: The committee heard a superintendent's report mixing a new DESE-funded reading tutoring grant with a warning that last year's cuts to in-district special education have left the district unable to serve some students, raising the risk of more out-of-district placements. The board discussed FY27 budget level-service figures, decided to stop applying for two small state family-engagement grants and hand them to a regional partner, voted to relocate meetings to the accessible middle-high school, gave the superintendent permission to explore redirecting a legislative earmark from passenger vans to ADA-accessible bathrooms at Turkey Hill, and heard principals describe strained staffing from prior cuts during school improvement plan updates.

First earmarked funds approved this week are going to touch-view screens at the primary school, middle school student needs, and safety improvements (sander attachment and harnesses) across all three campuses.

meetings.headline: School officials call the FY25 surplus a budgeting failure, not lost money, and warn FY27 will be tight
meetings.summary: School committee members, the superintendent, the business manager and the town manager held a public forum to explain how the district ended FY25 with an unexpectedly large surplus, attributing it mainly to a competitive grant that freed up already-budgeted paraprofessional funds that were never reallocated, plus austerity measures imposed on a mistaken sense of scarcity. No formal votes were taken; officials described new oversight practices already adopted (regular budget updates, grant pre-approval, a new stabilization fund for out-of-district placements) and residents pressed on transparency, MCAS reading scores, and whether another override will be needed.

budget_items.what_was_said: The business manager gave the total surplus figure after the chair estimated it roughly.
The largest driver of the surplus was a competitive grant for paraprofessionals whose already-budgeted funds were never reallocated once awarded.
A surplus also built up in the utilities line that could have easily been spent under austerity measures if caught in time.
Out-of-district placement costs vary widely year to year and can shock the budget when a child moves into town after the budget closes.
A speaker noted the district asked for an override and then returned more than half that override amount as surplus the same year.
Inflation outpaced the maximum allowable tax levy increase over the period, described as the fundamental budget problem.
The district said it just learned from the state of an expected cut to Title I federal grant funding for the coming budget.
The special stabilization account for out-of-district costs is established but currently unfunded; the operating budget line it backstops was estimated at this figure.
A resident used a hypothetical grant amount to question how the town would know a budgeted line item was instead covered by a grant.
The business manager cited an example of a workbook supply line that went entirely unspent under austerity measures.
The business manager reported the current fiscal year's percentage of budget expended so far.
A resident compared Lunenburg's per-pupil spending against Acton, Groton and Fitchburg, saying Lunenburg spends less per pupil than its neighbors.
A resident compared Lunenburg's student-teacher ratio unfavorably to Ayer and Fitchburg.
A resident cited MCAS results showing a majority of young students not meeting or exceeding reading expectations.

decisions.decision: In the FY27 budget, anyone currently paid through an entitlement grant will be fully removed from grant funding, with entitlement grants used only for one-time expenses going forward.
The district will discontinue the practice of budgeting a line item for something it is also seeking a competitive grant to cover, to avoid the appearance of double-budgeted funds.
Once the current budget season concludes, the new budgeting practices will be memorialized in a written budgeting handbook.

meetings.headline: Assessors keep the FY27 overlay at its proposed level and set a September deadline for the new senior tax exemption
meetings.summary: The Board of Assessors welcomed the town's new financial director/accountant and walked through how the senior means-tested tax exemption, overlay, and MUNIS issues have been handled. Most of the meeting was routine business: signing excise and abatement paperwork, correcting and approving a backlog of minutes, fixing errors in the draft annual report, and reviewing ongoing problems with parcel mapping, chapter land, and sewer betterments. The board decided to keep its proposed FY2027 overlay unchanged, set a fixed annual deadline for the senior means-tested exemption, and adopted a board code of conduct policy.

The board voted to set the senior means-tested tax exemption application deadline as the first Wednesday in September, going forward.
The board voted to adopt a code of conduct policy for its members.

why_it_matters: The overlay is the reserve set aside to cover abatements against the tax levy, so holding it steady rather than shrinking it affects how the tax rate is set even though fewer abatements were requested this year.
Homeowners who qualify for the senior means-tested exemption now have one fixed annual deadline, the first Wednesday in September, to file their application.
Dropping the mapping/GIS software upgrade may leave known parcel-mapping accuracy issues unaddressed for another year, which can affect individual assessments.

meetings.headline: Parks Commission voted to pay for an independent peer review of the skate park's roughly $1.14M cost estimate.
meetings.summary: The Parks Commission met to settle on a final project price for the privately-funded skate park so the nonprofit could proceed with bonding, reviewing an estimate of roughly $1.14 million from the skate park's consultant, Dillis and Roy. After extended discussion of risk, procurement law, and how a bond/security would actually function, the commission voted to authorize an independent peer review of the estimate (up to $6,000) and then heard a new skate park proposal to use a privately-backed cash escrow instead of a traditional bond, with details on renegotiating the lease agreement's security terms left to be worked out offline before returning to a public meeting.

meetings.headline: Town manager warns an FY27 override may be needed while unreconciled FY25 books risk losing state local aid
meetings.summary: The Select Board heard a lengthy town manager report warning that FY27 budget cost drivers exceed revenue growth and an override is likely, while the town's unsubmitted FY25 Schedule A risks the state withholding local aid and free cash remains uncertified. The board also honored a school resource officer for a cryptocurrency fraud recovery, marked a police officer's retirement, approved two peddler's licenses, voted to retain labor counsel under his new firm, and began discussing FY27 legislative earmark requests and warrant articles for town meeting.

budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager said health insurance, retirement assessment and school transportation are major cost drivers exceeding revenue growth, and that absent service reductions an override is likely required.
The town has not submitted the Schedule A to the Division of Local Services; failure to do so by February 13th risks the state withholding local aid.
Free cash has not yet been certified, which directly affects planning for town meeting including the capital plan, reserve transfers, and the snow and ice deficit.

A preliminary capital plan was delivered but is conservative pending free cash certification; two large projects, the Flatill road bridge and the public safety roof, are consuming much of the available funding.
The town is in deficit spending for snow and ice after 18 snow events this season; this is legally permitted deficit spending.
The DPW director and stormwater task force will present a proposed budget for a new storm water utility to the finance committee and later to a joint board meeting.
The town now bears full TCP building operating costs after the school department vacated; expected energy savings from partial decommissioning have not materialized.
The town applied for a MassDOT grant to fund design of the Goodrich Street culvert over Easterbrook Brook.
The town believes moving with Attorney Terry to his new, more public-sector-focused firm will be a cost savings over time; there are no hourly rates cited.
The board reviewed past state earmarks received by the town, mostly for schools, and discussed shifting focus toward town-side requests for the FY27 state budget.
A draft warrant article proposes a multi-year allocation for the town's 300th anniversary.
A second draft warrant article would establish a gift fund for donations and sale of anniversary merchandise.
The school committee discussed using funds originally for a new literacy coach position instead to build internal capacity by paying existing skilled staff stipends.
The school committee added a five-day preschool option alongside 2, 3, and 4-day options, with an annual tuition increase; this passed.
The school committee had discussed the school budget using certain healthcare figures, but has since learned those healthcare numbers are lower and will need to adjust the budget accordingly.

meetings.summary: The Parks Commission approved funding for a replacement Fitzgerald Field sign and approved a private-donation project to demolish and rebuild two dugouts at Powell Field. It also opened discussion, without voting, on roughly doubling town beach fees to make the beach self-sustaining amid town budget pressure, and began reviewing draft field-use, signage, and non-resident field-fee policies to bring back at the next meeting.

A member cited a local country club's non-resident and resident family and individual pool membership prices as further comparison.

meetings.headline: Town, school and finance officials agree Lunenburg likely needs a property-tax override to close a large FY27 budget gap
meetings.summary: This joint "tri-board" meeting of the Select Board, School Committee and Finance Committee opened with extensive public comment from firefighters and school staff describing understaffing and burnout, followed by a Town Manager presentation showing updated state aid and revenue figures leaving a large projected FY27 deficit once health insurance, retirement, transportation and a fourth fire shift are covered. The boards debated how to communicate the gap without "scare tactics," discussed override structures and cost-saving options (recycling, school choice, mosquito control), sparred over whether school staffing has actually been cut, and set a February 9th follow-up meeting without settling on an override amount.

budget_items.what_was_said: Starting from new FY27 revenue and subtracting health insurance, retirement, transportation and the fourth fire shift in sequence, the Town Manager walked the board down to a negative balance.

The Town Manager said the deficit shown covers only four items and does not include utilities, vendor contracts, TCP carrying costs, pavement management restoration, the actual Monty Tech assessment, or collective bargaining increases, putting the full deficit higher.
A school committee member stated the total level-service school budget figure and how much it is over FY26, including the 20% health insurance assumption.
A board member noted school-choice revenue on the cherry sheet has fallen sharply from what it used to bring in, shifting that cost onto taxpayers.
A board member argued the recycling program's cost has grown substantially since the start of COVID with no action taken to address it.
The Town Manager again floated eliminating the mosquito control assessment as a savings option, noting past public pushback.

decisions.decision: The tri-board agreed it needs to settle on an override number in time to be placed on the ballot by the town's April 10th deadline.
The school committee agreed to supply updated staffing data including last year's layoffs, which were missing from the FY16-FY25 headcount chart presented.
The tri-board set its next joint meeting for February 9th, to be held at the middle-high school.
The school committee agreed to hold a separate session addressing the outstanding FY25 questions (the prior override whose funds had to be returned) before the wider public forum.
The Town Manager agreed to send the board members the state's Prop 2½ override-options guidance and the campaign-finance rules for elected officials discussing an override.

what_happened.line: Town, school and finance officials agreed Lunenburg likely needs a property-tax override to close a projected FY27 gap, without settling on an amount or structure

meetings.headline: Commissioners set a Feb. 25 special town meeting for data collectors, an IRS bill, and a new excavator.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Water District Commissioners set a special town meeting for February 25, 2026 to fund two data collectors, a new excavator, and an IRS bill, deferring a more contested well-testing article to the annual meeting. Most of the rest of the meeting covered PFAS treatment compliance deadlines, aging pipe infrastructure and in-house repair savings, a public engagement survey going out in late January, and a recent main break, closing with a vote to adjourn into executive session.

budget_items.what_was_said: The board discussed appropriating money now, ahead of a July 1 billing-company switch, to buy two radio data collectors so they are running before the transition. Figures for the cost were given inconsistently in the captions.

A commissioner clarified the cost is the fee to acquire and install the collectors, separate from the operational/billing part that would be in next year's budget; money would be pulled from a reserve.
The board discussed replacing aging excavation equipment (a 1996 tractor and 2008/2009 machines); pricing for a rubber-tired excavator was cited, with attachments adding to the cost.
A commissioner said the new equipment purchase could be funded from surplus, the same source the PFAS-related money had gone into, to be used on water line and plant work.

A commissioner asked how much the district currently budgets each year for main replacement; the figure given was described as the current annual allocation, which barely covers engineering when using outside contractors.

budget_items.topic: Rolling Acres in-house repair cost vs. contracted work
budget_items.what_was_said: Doing the Rolling Acres main replacement in-house was said to have cost a fraction of what a contracted job of that scope would have cost, illustrating the savings of in-house work.

budget_items.topic: Water rate impact of Massachusetts Avenue main project
budget_items.what_was_said: A resident noted his quarterly water bill rose by a stated amount after the Massachusetts Avenue main project and asked whether that increase applied to all customers.

decisions.decision: Two items (data collectors and new excavator/equipment) plus an IRS bill were settled as special-meeting articles; a well-testing/"Keings" article was set aside for the annual meeting instead, since it was seen as more controversial.
The special town meeting was set for Wednesday, February 25, 2026 at 6:00 p.m., timed to coincide with a regular commissioners' meeting.

The legal letter concerning a kayak rack in zone one (from an attorney named McGregor/on behalf of a Nathaniel Stevens) will be referred to the district's own attorney to respond, since it was addressed to the attorney.
The public engagement survey will be mailed to residents the last week of January, accompanied by a flyer with a QR code and a story in the Lunenburg Ledger.
The district will transition staff email addresses from the old Verizon.net address to new .gov addresses.
The district plans to move to a new analog radio alert system so crews are notified of a broken water main independent of cell phones.

meetings.headline: Board declined to endorse a 35-lot Parmentor Road ANR over Fire Road 15's inadequacy, waiving refiling fees
meetings.summary: The board spent most of the meeting on an ANR for 10 Parmentor Road, ultimately declining to endorse it because Fire Road 15 (proposed frontage for a number of the lots) was found not to have sufficient width, grade or construction, while agreeing to waive filing fees if the applicant resubmits a revised plan within six months. meetings.headline: Officials warn the FY27 budget leaves almost nothing after health insurance, pointing toward an override
meetings.summary: This was a joint Select Board / Finance Committee / School Committee ("tri-board") session in which the Town Manager walked through preliminary FY27 general government, debt, intergovernmental and revenue figures, including a new assistant town manager position, a large Munis/IT cost increase, and a steep audit-cost jump. The revenue walk-through showed that after health insurance is covered, almost no new money is left to fund any raises, cuts, or level services, and the group spent the second half of the meeting discussing operational efficiencies, the state and federal funding picture, and the likelihood that an override will be needed, without taking any substantive vote.

meetings.summary: The Stormwater Task Force met with its consultant (Weston and Sampson) to review contract progress on impervious surface data, rate structure, and public engagement materials, and spent most of the meeting building a detailed calendar of Finance Committee, Select Board and public information session dates leading up to the March 16 warrant closing and May town meeting. The group decided to bring forward only the enabling bylaw establishing the utility framework this spring, holding the fee/rate structure and budget vote for a later town meeting, and reviewed a draft stormwater budget with the DPW representative covering Chapter 90 and residential/commercial funding splits. meetings.headline: PACC to seek a meeting with the town manager after being shut out of two warrant changes

meetings.headline: Chair flags a possible large historic shortfall in old trust funds, pushing a bylaw for no-quorum releases
meetings.summary: The Trust Fund Commission (chair John Bowen and vice chair Richard Howard, the only two present) spent most of the meeting reviewing decades of historic trust fund records ahead of drafting a bylaw that would let the select board release trust fund money when the commission lacks a quorum. In the process the chair identified an unresolved 2017 loan redetermination, a fund from 2017 with no discoverable records, and a large apparent gap between what a 1931 sidewalk/memorial fund should be worth today and its current balance, all of which he committed to investigate further. No formal votes were taken except the roll-call vote to adjourn.

budget_items.what_was_said: The chair reviewed a 2017 dispersement from the worthy poor fund's earnings to a resident, structured as a loan with a six-month redetermination that was never followed up on. He said this board will now have to take up that redetermination.
Reading a 1966 record at the Worcester Savings Institute, the chair cited the fund's total, its original principal, and interest recorded as of a 1965 date.

budget_items.topic: Nathaniel Day fund and missing Treasury bond
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair read the Nathaniel Day fund's savings balance and noted a 90-day Treasury bond in that fund that he cannot locate; he wants to find where it is and whether it was cashed.

The chair said Susan Howard's separate fund (distinct from the sidewalk fund) held Treasury bonds, and estimated informally what decades of compounding might now be worth if the bonds were never cashed.

budget_items.topic: Sidewalk (John and Mary Caldwell Howard) fund, 1931
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair read the 1931 warrant article establishing the fund with a stated principal and annual interest amount, to be spent on sidewalks and public grounds within one mile of town center in perpetuity.

A commissioner asked why the fund shows a much lower current balance than what decades of interest at the stated rate should have produced; the chair said he has to find where the money went and will pursue it.
The chair read two 1931 warrant articles accepting sums for perpetual care of specific cemetery lots in the North Cemetery.

A 2013 letter setting up the fund specified that only annual interest could be dispersed, capped at a share of that year's interest, until the fund passed a threshold at which principal above that amount could also be used for veterans' benefits.

decisions.decision: Chair and vice chair will brainstorm a bylaw allowing the select board to release trust fund money in the absence of a quorum, to be drafted by the chair as a hard copy for the next meeting.
The commission wants a public comment period built into the process before finalizing bylaw changes and any cy pres filing, even though it is not legally required.
The chair will personally contact individuals named in the 2017 meeting minutes to recover missing trust fund records rather than wait for them to come forward.
The chair will investigate the unexplained 'Lind Saxon' fund from 2017 with the accounting department, since no records or dispersements for it can be found.
A cy pres court filing to update the American Legion veterans fund's restrictions will wait until after the next election cycle due to the town attorney's town meeting workload.
The chair will contact the U.S. Treasury to try to locate the Nathaniel Day fund's Treasury bond and determine its status.
The chair will investigate why the sidewalk (Howard) fund's current balance is far below what decades of stated interest should have produced.
Interns will not be used this year due to lack of a prepared curriculum; it may be revisited next year.
The commission has an open vacancy and is inviting interested residents to come forward.
