what_happened.line: The Commission halted a volunteer's mountain-bike trail grooming at the Town Forest until he submits a mapped trail plan and gets its approval.
Four wetlands hearings -- Mopus Road, Summer Street, a Northfield Road culvert, and Fire Road 15A -- were continued to January 7 for more information.
The Commission voted to cover Hollis Road property costs from the Hollis fund, including a heating-service contract, back bills, and a remote monitoring device for the vacant building.
The order of conditions for Zero Shirley Reservoir Road was extended to August 2029 ahead of the project going to bid.
Members discussed moving the bylaw's consultant-fee cap into an easier-to-change regulation rather than the bylaw itself.

why_it_matters: Anyone using the Town Forest's mountain-bike trails will see grooming paused until a plan is on file, a condition tied to volunteer maintenance work residents praised in public comment.
The four continued hearings mean the property owners at those addresses face another wait before any wetlands permit is decided.
The town-owned Hollis Road property is now drawing recurring costs from its dedicated fund, and its longer-term use is set to come back as a full agenda item.

A future agenda item on the long-term use of the Hollis Road residence.

meetings.headline: Water Commissioners tabled a vote on new well testing, deferring it to a future special meeting
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Water District commissioners approved paying a Tighe & Bond engineering invoice and reviewed results of exploratory test wells near the Keing well site, but tabled a decision on further well investment until a special meeting can be called for public input. They also discussed Neptune meter-reading upgrades, a DEP non-compliance notice on PFAS sampling, hiring an additional operator, upcoming commissioner elections, and revisions to a resident survey comparing well-source options and their loan costs.

meetings.headline: Capital Planning Committee unanimously adopted a tentative order-of-merit ranking of 22 FY27 capital requests
meetings.summary: The Capital Planning Committee reviewed members' individual rankings of 22 FY27 capital requests, resolved several ranking ties (including flipping the order of a DPW dump truck and an IT network upgrade), and discussed funding constraints given roughly $3.3 million in requests against a typical $1-1.5 million annual funding capacity. The committee voted unanimously to adopt the resulting order-of-merit list as a tentative recommendation, to be revisited once the town manager's financial picture is clearer, and tentatively scheduled its next meeting for January 28; it also discussed unused ClearGov budgeting software costing about $20,000 a year and outyear capital request planning.

budget_items.topic: Total FY27 capital requests vs. likely funding
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair noted requests total roughly $3.3 million while the town typically funds between $1 million and $1.5 million a year from raise-and-appropriate, non-expended capital, or free cash.

A member described a DPW business case showing savings from buying a six-wheel dump truck versus contracting the work, at a cost noted in captions; the town currently has six of seven trucks of that class after recent ARPA investment.

budget_items.topic: Relative sizes of dump truck vs. IT/network items
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair contrasted a large dump truck cost against a much smaller IT activity center network upgrade and school items to illustrate how a funding cutline could reorder priorities.
A member said the network upgrade items seemed cobbled together just to clear a stated capital threshold and said he didn't want to reward that.

A member argued that funding design money alone, rather than full projects, could let the town scope larger items before committing, citing a small design spend as an example of avoiding a bigger unnecessary project.
The town manager said the ClearGov software, currently unused, costs about the figure heard annually and she has not yet decided whether to pause or terminate it.
The town manager said a ballpark free cash number should be available roughly a week before the January 31st closing, accurate to within the figure heard.

budget_items.topic: Prior year outyear request example (stone fence)
budget_items.what_was_said: A member noted relief that this year had far fewer extreme outyear requests, citing as an example a prior year's request for a cemetery stone fence at roughly the figure heard, which did not recur this year.
figures_as_heard: a third or almost a half million dollars

decisions.decision: The committee will submit a tentative/provisional order-of-merit ranking tonight to meet the year-end charter deadline, and revisit it in late January or February once the town manager is closer to a formal capital plan recommendation.
The committee agreed to flip the order of the DPW six-wheel dump truck and the IT/Activity Center network upgrade in the ranking.
The committee kept the supervisor cruiser replacement ranked above the public safety building roof repair, despite one member preferring the reverse.
The committee tentatively set its next meeting for Wednesday, January 28, pending confirmation once free cash figures are closer to being known.

what_happened.line: The committee voted unanimously to adopt a tentative order-of-merit ranking of the 22 FY27 capital requests.
The ranking is provisional because requests add up to far more than the town's typical yearly funding capacity from raise-and-appropriate, non-expended capital, or free cash.
Members resolved several ranking ties by discussion, including flipping the order of a DPW dump truck and an IT network upgrade.
The committee plans to revisit the ranking once the town manager's financial picture is clearer.
The next meeting was tentatively set for January 28, pending confirmation once free cash figures are known.

why_it_matters: This ranking shapes which capital purchases -- vehicles, IT upgrades, building repairs -- the town manager and town meeting are likely to fund first next year.
Because requests exceed what the town typically funds in a year, items near the bottom of this list may wait, get scaled to design-only funding, or be cut.
The order is explicitly tentative and tied to the free cash certification, so it can still change before it reaches a town meeting warrant.

meetings.headline: Parks Commission tables the roughly $14 million Marshall Park project until town finances are clearer.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Parks Commission, meeting with only three of its members present, decided to replace the storm-damaged Fitzgerald Field sign and handed the long-stalled beach house dedication sign project to a newer member. Most of the meeting concerned deferring a decision on the large Marshall Park project until the town's overall financial picture is clearer, along with ongoing struggles to fill the vacant recreation director position and a plan to draft written field-use policies and forms, with no change to youth sports field fees this year.

budget_items.what_was_said: The storm-damaged Fitzgerald Field sign will be replaced using parks funds; the chair said she asked Chris Ruth the cost but he had not given her a figure.

A local company (Dillis) had agreed roughly two years ago to cover the cost of a new sign naming the beach house after Genevieve Nass; the chair said the project stalled and is handing it to Maryanne.

Dillis and Roy produced a prevailing-wage estimate for the skate park that came in around figures_as_heard, but it omitted town administrative/bid costs that were part of the original ballpark figure; final decisions expected in January.
The chair said she thought about figures_as_heard remained but it turned out closer to a lower figure; remaining money comes from ARPA (a smaller amount) and from town-meeting-approved capital funds.
A board member said the town needs to understand its finances before pushing a project of that scale forward again at town meeting.

The vacant rec director position is a 19-hour-a-week job with no benefits; a member said covering the paperwork duties falls outside the volunteer commission's purview and suggested a stipend for whoever takes it on.

budget_items.topic: Youth sports per-player field use fee
budget_items.what_was_said: The commission charges youth leagues a flat per-player fee for a season rather than an hourly rate like the school uses; figures were recalled for comparison but the board confirmed no fee change this spring.

decisions.decision: Chair will tell Chris Ruth to go ahead and replace the Fitzgerald Field sign as long as the price is reasonable, aiming for a more permanent design.
Maryanne will take over the beach house sign and dedication project from the chair, who will forward prior graphics and pricing information.
No decision on Marshall Park tonight; the chair will bring information back to the town manager in January rather than deciding in December.
The board will table further discussion of recruiting/electing new commission members and the Marshall Park path forward until closer to January.
Chair will bring a formal vote to the January agenda seeking permission to personally process field-use paperwork if the recreation director position remains unfilled.
No change to youth sports per-player field use fees this spring season.
Chair will draft revised field-use forms and bring them to an upcoming meeting in January or February.
Next meeting set for January 28th (the fourth Wednesday).

meetings.headline: Committee says it won't choose between a full-time athletic director and reading interventionists in FY27.
meetings.summary: The School Committee heard a select-board letter on tri-board communication, extensive public comment on reading support and the athletic director's workload, and then held a long FY27 budget workshop covering health insurance, a paraprofessional undercount in FY26, reading interventionists, EL staffing and the bridge program. Members declined to choose between funding a full-time athletic director/trainer and reading interventionists, agreed to make no further staffing cuts, planned to vote their own budget before the town manager's number arrives, and approved (pending edits) an official statement on FY2025 budget variances.

what_happened.line: The committee said it cannot sustain further staffing cuts and would not choose between a full-time athletic director/trainer and reading interventionists in the FY27 budget.
Members plan to vote their own FY27 school budget before the town manager sets her budget number, a change in sequencing from past years.
Any override request would go to the May town meeting rather than a November special town meeting, because November needs a higher approval threshold.
The committee voted to finalize its FY2025 budget variance statement, pending edits sent to the superintendent that do not change its message.
Officials disclosed a paraprofessional staffing gap in the current FY26 budget that had gone unaccounted for, but said the year should still close out okay.

why_it_matters: The choice between a full-time athletic director and reading interventionists is left open, so families may not know until later in the FY27 process which program gets funded.

An override, if requested, would appear on the May town meeting warrant rather than a November special vote, and this cycle's cuts would be discussed in broad categories rather than naming specific positions.
A paraprofessional undercount already found in the FY26 budget is a data gap worth watching for whether it recurs or grows in the FY27 numbers that underlie any override ask.

meetings.headline: Select Board rehired retired town accountant Karen Brochu as interim finance director amid a stalled recruitment.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Select Board ratified Stephen Wallace as the new planning and economic development director, heard a clean FY24 audit from CBIZ that flagged behind-schedule cash and receivable reconciliations and an unresolved ~$90,000 Fitchburg water-billing issue, and approved bringing retired accountant Karen Brochu back part-time as interim finance director after the posted position drew no viable candidates. The board also approved several license renewals, an interim finance director's contract, and a letter to the Governor urging significantly more state local aid (citing a $351 million statewide UGGA ask) ahead of the FY2027 budget process, and opened discussion on the future redevelopment of 925 Mass Ave, appointment policy revisions, and opioid settlement fund planning.

attendees.role: director of planning and economic development (newly appointed), presenter

public_comment.topic: Asked whether the audit and Wallace introduction were public hearings, pressed for a public hearing on the $90,000 owed related to the Fitchburg water billing issue and on school department financial concerns, and criticized lack of interaction during public comment.
Asked what an 'intermittent heavy equipment operator' position is, and suggested the letter to the Governor should also press the state to fund unfunded state mandates.

votes.motion: Ratify the town manager's appointment of Steven Wallace as director of planning and economic development.
Ratify the town manager's appointment of Brandy Oul as meal site manager.
Ratify the town manager's appointment of Joseph Davis as intermittent heavy equipment operator.
Approve the annual license renewals as printed on the agenda, with contingent votes for the applicants with outstanding items (excepting Smokestack, addressed separately).
Approve an additional annual common victualler license renewal that had been omitted from the agenda.
Approve the employment agreement for Karen Brochu as interim finance director/town accountant.
Approve the letter to Governor Healey on local aid and the FY2027 budget, and send copies to the Governor, legislators, the school committee and the finance committee.
Adjourn.

budget_items.what_was_said: The auditor reported the total general fund balance, with portions set aside for encumbrances and free cash used for the FY25 budget, leaving an unassigned balance that rose from the prior year.
The auditor listed balances in the general, zoning, vehicle and equipment, health insurance, and opioid stabilization funds, noting the general stabilization fund has grown steadily since 2013.
The auditor said real estate and personal property tax collections remained strong.
The auditor described a revenue surplus and underspending across departments, offset by use of free cash to balance the FY24 budget.
The town's OPEB trust contribution and investment income grew the fund, while the net OPEB liability fell, tied partly to a higher blended discount rate.

budget_items.topic: Net pension liability, Worcester Regional Retirement System
budget_items.what_was_said: The auditor reported the town's net pension liability rose slightly while the system's funded ratio improved.
Capital asset additions for general government, mainly road paving and equipment, were reported; none for the sewer enterprise.
Short-term debt outstanding funded the capital plan and a land purchase; required long-term debt payments for governmental and sewer funds were noted.
The town exceeded the federal expenditure threshold requiring a single audit, with the education stabilization fund selected for testing and no findings.
A resident and board members discussed money owed related to the town not raising water rates or billing timely when Fitchburg raised its rates; described as an FY25/26 issue outside the FY24 audit.
The town manager reported the MMA is calling for a statewide increase to UGGA to restore pre-recession local aid levels.

budget_items.topic: Finance director recruitment / recruiting agency fee
budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager said Robert Half would be engaged to help recruit a finance director and payroll/benefits administrator, with a fee only if a hire results.
The board approved contingent votes for several license applicants with outstanding paperwork, inspections, or landlord issues.

budget_items.topic: Employment agreement, interim finance director Karen Brochu
budget_items.what_was_said: A retired former town accountant/finance director agreed to return on an hourly, part-time basis with no additional benefits, capped by retiree earnings limits.
A board member found the MMA's report basis for its ask, benchmarking UGGA against historical local tax share, yielding a similar but not identical figure to what was cited.
A board member reported a one-time reimbursement grant amount for Lunenburg from a fund tied to a regional hospital closure, based on a base amount plus a call-volume formula.
The planning board report noted a completed lot posted a performance guarantee bond, after which the certificate of occupancy could be issued.

decisions.decision: The town will engage CBIZ again for the FY25 audit once FY25 is closed, targeted for around January 31st, with a contract signed before work begins.
When engaging the auditor for FY25, the town manager will request special attention to issues including the Fitchburg water billing matter.
Board members indicated comfort proceeding with contingent votes on pending license renewals, including Lunenburg Gas, rather than delaying or calling a special meeting.
Board members will review the prior Mass Development presentation video (June 11) on 925 Mass Ave before the next discussion.
If any board member wants Mass Development's representative to give a follow-up presentation, they should tell the town manager before the following week.
The board's focus at the next 925 Mass Ave discussion will be the evaluation criteria on pages 16-17 of the draft RFP.
Board flagged for further consideration in January whether/how to structure a subcommittee to screen or interview appointment applicants, given open meeting law implications.
The appointment policy's key dates section will read simply 'June' rather than 'first and second Tuesday in June.'
A future agenda item will be scheduled to decide how the town will approach expenditure of opioid settlement funds.
Board members will coordinate signing the letter to the Governor via DocuSign or in person on another day, since it was not yet printed and a board member was absent.

meetings.headline: Committee met its energy-reduction goal but remains stalled awaiting building energy audits needed for Turkey Hill decisions.
meetings.summary: The Green Community Task Force reviewed its FY26 annual energy report, which showed the town hit its energy-reduction goal, with Turkey Hill and the old elementary building flagged as the largest energy users. Most of the meeting covered stalled progress: a National Grid building-energy audit and analysis six months overdue, no reserve fund for future LED streetlight maintenance, an unsuccessful styrofoam-recycling grant push, and broader town indecision on Turkey Hill, Town Hall and other building needs. No substantive votes were taken beyond routine approval of minutes and adjournment; the group discussed renaming itself an energy/sustainability committee and pursuing Tyler's appointment to a soon-open seat.

budget_items.what_was_said: The committee reported total municipal energy consumption fell versus the baseline, meeting the green-communities reduction goal, with the largest drop in buildings.
The annual report narrative stated total municipal, building and vehicle energy use all decreased while water and sewer energy use increased.
The chair reported the November streetlight bill was high but far below what the town paid before it owned its own streetlights.

budget_items.topic: Streetlight savings and a proposed maintenance reserve fund
budget_items.what_was_said: Members said savings from lower streetlight bills have just been absorbed into the general budget with nothing set aside for future LED maintenance, and discussed creating a reserve or special revolving fund instead.
A member said the town badly needs an experienced grant writer, and noted a budgeted grant-writer line had gone unspent before.

budget_items.topic: PPP energy audit and comprehensive building analysis (CBA)
budget_items.what_was_said: National Grid was to provide a free preliminary audit and a comprehensive building analysis of all twelve town buildings, but the committee said it has waited months with no result.

budget_items.topic: Capital outlay override for building projects
budget_items.what_was_said: A member described how the town of Ashby used a one-time capital outlay override to fund and pay off building projects in a single year, and suggested Lunenburg consider it for its aging buildings.
A member said current incentives make an electric riding mower roughly half the price of an equivalent gas model, but the town would need duplicate equipment for separate departments.

budget_items.topic: Capital planning equipment list / mower purchase
budget_items.what_was_said: A member said the school department's capital plan includes buying a new zero-turn mower and the group discussed pushing for an electric model.

A member relayed that capital planning discussed a perceived risk that hybrid police vehicle batteries could be costly once out of warranty, and that gas vehicle quotes may be sought for the next replacement round.

decisions.decision: Committee agreed to consider renaming itself from a Green Community committee toward something like an Energy or Energy and Sustainability Committee.
A member agreed to update the committee's Facebook page with the annual energy report the chair would send.
Chair agreed to push for Tyler's official appointment to an upcoming open committee seat.
Next meeting set for roughly mid-January, once the PPP building audit results are available.

meetings.headline: APDC voted to press the Select Board to act on town meeting's directive to sell or lease the Brooks House.
meetings.summary: The Architectural Preservation District Commission (three members present, no public) received updates on 50 Main Street's office condo, the Lunenburg Municipal Building Design Committee's plan to consolidate town offices in the Ritter building using GSA space standards and an elevator rather than the existing chairlift, and the nearly-finished 10-year master plan covering housing pressure from state law, excluded debt, and priority facility projects (Town Hall, Ritter, Turkey Hill, Marshall Park). The commission voted to have a member raise the long-unaddressed Brooks House sell-or-lease town meeting vote with the Select Board, and deferred approval of prior meeting minutes to January.

budget_items.topic: Master plan steering committee consultant work
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair said that had Kim Duffy not taken over managing the master plan steering committee's work after it had gone unmet for almost a year, the process would have been a waste of the town's money. He cited the cost as a figure in the captions.

budget_items.topic: 2004 town meeting Ritter addition project (May town meeting project)
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair described a prior, larger proposed addition to the Ritter building that the design committee has now decided not to pursue, in favor of modifying the existing 1963 addition instead.
The design committee is adopting GSA space guidelines to size staff offices in a consolidated Ritter building, with different footage for managers versus staff.

The master plan will include an analysis of the town's excluded debt, showing it is declining as older capital projects from 2004 are paid down, which the chair argued creates capacity to take on new debt for facility needs.
The chair noted a prior town meeting vote directed the town to sell or lease the Brooks House, that this has not been acted on, and that he intends to raise it with the Select Board.

decisions.decision: Vote on approval of the October and November meeting minutes will be deferred to the January meeting since not all members had reviewed the November minutes.
Confirmed the next APDC meeting is January 8, correcting an earlier stated date of January 18.
Nathan will draft and send a letter to the owner of the 50 Main Street office condo over the holidays, a task carried over from the November meeting.
The chair will bring the Brooks House issue back up at the January APDC meeting regardless of the Select Board outcome.

meetings.headline: Committee finalized its ~22-item FY27 capital request list for members to rank, amid free-cash funding uncertainty

The committee also heard planning-department and downtown-business updates, approved its October minutes, and agreed to form a small subcommittee to draft a business-friendly bylaw ahead of the next meeting, without taking any other formal votes.

what_happened.line: The committee took no votes on town business, spending most of the meeting on a Chamber of Commerce presentation about business loans, tourism and advocacy programs.
Facing an expected loss of quorum, members postponed the master plan steering committee item and the EDC bylaw review to the January meeting.
An informal two-member subcommittee was formed to work with town staff on a draft bylaw covering a resident's request for a BYOB-type policy at a nail salon and on streamlining site-plan permitting.
The committee approved its October 14 minutes and set its next meeting for January 13.

why_it_matters: A bylaw addressing alcohol policy at businesses like nail salons and streamlining site-plan permitting could change what local business owners must do to open or operate, once a draft exists.
A member flagged a stormwater utility fee under consideration by the town as a possible burden on local businesses, though the committee took no position and made no request of the Chamber.
No resident action or vote is needed from this meeting; the substantive work (bylaw draft, master plan item) is deferred to January.
watch_next: January 13 meeting, when the bylaw draft, master plan steering committee item, and EDC bylaw review are expected to return.

meetings.headline: Committee ran a hands-on card-sorting workshop ranking Master Plan ideas on housing, zoning and infrastructure; no votes taken.
meetings.summary: This was an interactive public workshop for the Lunenburg Master Plan update, where a small group of attendees used a card-sorting exercise to rank draft recommendations (covering housing/zoning, economic development, facilities, and later transportation/infrastructure) by importance and urgency. No formal votes were taken; the session produced informal group consensus on which ideas seemed most important or time-sensitive, feeding into the consultants' effort to narrow a long list of recommendations to a short list for the draft Master Plan report.

consultant, RKG Associates (economic development, municipal facilities, transportation, housing)

public_comment.topic: A resident noted no Selectmen or Zoning Board members appeared to be present and remarked they would only see the video and could submit questions in writing.

A resident asked whether Lunenburg still requires a 2-acre minimum residential lot, prompting discussion of current Residence A/B minimum lot sizes and whether they should be reduced to ease housing costs for younger people.
A participant asked whether the card-sorting exercise could be expanded online so more residents could weigh in, since turnout was low.
Participants debated whether to expand farmers market hours, with disagreement over whether the market has historically drawn enough vendors or customers.
A participant argued that improving the town green behind the library/senior center, without disturbing the existing gazebo or fire lane access, was a feasible community gathering space.
Discussion of whether a business incubator on town-owned land, potentially at the Brooks House, was worth pursuing, including concerns the Brooks House needs significant, possibly high-cost repairs.
Discussion of prioritizing sidewalks and pedestrian infrastructure in commercial areas, noting MassDOT "Complete Streets" requirements are costly and space-intensive on state roads.
Debate over adding bicycle infrastructure between high-density housing areas and the town center, with mixed views on current demand versus future utility.
Discussion of traffic calming measures (speed tables) near Whalom Lake given pedestrian safety concerns for children and families.

budget_items.what_was_said: The consultant explained each recommendation card is rated by cost tier (dollar-sign icons) and time frame, to help gauge feasibility during the prioritization exercise.

A participant described a hypothetical inclusionary zoning scenario where a developer building a round number of apartments would have to set aside a percentage as deed-restricted affordable units, similar to what other communities require.

A card proposing a town-supported business incubator on town land was discussed, including reduced rent and shared facilities, but participants felt Brooks House repairs would likely exceed the card's stated cost/time tier.
Participants noted state (MassDOT) grant funding exists for sidewalk and Complete Streets projects, but design requirements make such projects expensive and land-intensive on state roads.

decisions.decision: The group agreed that upgrading school facility accessibility (discussed in reference to Turkey Hill) belongs in the very important/very critical category of recommendations.
The group agreed to pause and relocate to the community room at 8:00 when the current meeting space closed for the evening.

The facilitator proposed, and the group agreed, to run the card-sorting exercise again at other public gatherings, such as the senior center, to gather broader input for the short list of recommendations.

meetings.headline: FY2026 tax rate awaits state approval; bills must be at the printer by December 14
meetings.summary: The Board of Assessors welcomed and began onboarding a new member while the principal assessor walked through the statutory report: the tax classification hearing had set a single tax rate, the FY2026 rate was resubmitted to the state for approval, and staff described the tight timeline to get billing files to the printer. meetings.headline: Board will push legal action against Woodlands condo trust over kayak racks in the well's protected zone
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Water District Commissioners reviewed the in-house cost of the Roland Acres water main replacement versus hiring it out, discussed a near-final draft of a community engagement survey on water source options, and spent significant time on the Woodlands condo trust's refusal to remove kayak racks from the well's Zone One protection area, concluding they will pursue legal action if the racks are not voluntarily moved. The meeting also covered SRF grant funding status, a possible new hire and equipment purchase for future in-house projects, a proposal to explore alternative voting methods for ratepayers, and recognized the superintendent's 40th work anniversary, closing with extended public comment challenging the survey's cost estimates.

budget_items.topic: Roland Acres water main replacement — cost review
budget_items.what_was_said: The board reviewed two cost figures for the in-house replacement job: the materials-only cost and a figure that adds the value of crew labor, comparing both to an estimate of what it would have cost to hire the job out at current 2023-era bids.
A commissioner proposed reinvesting the savings from doing the water main job in-house into a rubber-tire excavator and tandem-wheeler to allow the district to keep doing similar projects itself.

budget_items.topic: Possible new hire for in-house main work
budget_items.what_was_said: Commissioners discussed bringing on another employee in late winter/early spring to continue in-house main replacement work, and agreed to start putting together the annual expense estimate for staffing and equipment to present at a future meeting.
A commissioner said pursuing the zero-percent-interest SRF loan option was estimated to save a large sum compared to conventional financing.

budget_items.topic: O&M cost differential between water source options (survey)
budget_items.what_was_said: A resident presented his own analysis arguing the operations-and-maintenance cost difference between two water-source combination options was understated in the district's consultant figures, using a baseline and a variable-cost percentage split; the district said its consultants (Tighe & Bond) were confident in their numbers but did not have them itemized as a line item.

budget_items.topic: Capital cost of the three-well treatment option
budget_items.what_was_said: A resident questioned why moving from a two-source to a three-source treatment configuration added several million dollars in capital cost; the superintendent explained it required a larger treatment plant and a raw water transmission main.

decisions.decision: Staff will begin putting together annual expense projections for hiring an additional employee and for equipment, to bring to a future meeting as part of a three-to-five-year plan.
The community engagement survey draft will be finalized and brought back to the board for approval before release, alongside a draft postcard mailer and website.

The district will continue pursuing removal of the Woodlands condo trust's kayak racks from the Zone One well protection area, through its attorney if necessary, and will seek to recover costs from the Woodlands if legal action becomes necessary.

The clerk/president will look into whether the district's bylaws allow shutting off a ratepayer for non-compliance with district regulations (not just non-payment), and report back at the next meeting.
The board will ask town counsel whether an alternative voting method (e.g., a paper ballot period before the meeting) could legally be offered to increase ratepayer participation.

meetings.headline: Commission ruled a proposed three-season porch sits entirely in the wetland no-structure zone, blocking it as designed
meetings.summary: The Conservation Commission held several wetlands permit hearings: it approved a restoration project at 199 Massachusetts Ave (twice, after rescinding to drop an erosion-control requirement), issued a positive determination against a proposed three-season porch at 13 Birch Island Way for sitting inside the 50-foot no-structure zone, and continued three other hearings to December 17th over unresolved landowner permission and boundary-measurement issues. It also reviewed the newly reclassified conservation agent job posting, voted a budget split for the Hollis property (Haw) fund, and got updates on the conservation trust fund and a recreational trails grant reimbursement and extension.

meetings.headline: Select Board voted unanimously to let the town manager sign a low-income community solar discount deal.
meetings.summary: The Select Board heard a presentation from the new LEAF education nonprofit and voted unanimously to authorize the town manager to sign onto a Colonial Power Group low-income solar (SMART) discount program. The board also reviewed a draft tri-board communication letter ahead of a budget season expected to be difficult, discussed the finance department's ongoing staffing transition, license renewals, and heard committee reports including the school committee's plan to build three FY27 budget scenarios, before voting to enter executive session on firefighter union bargaining.

The school committee increased the substitute teacher daily rate to try to attract more substitutes.

The district will produce three FY27 budget scenarios: a level service budget, a level funded budget, and a prioritized necessary increase budget.
The school committee discussed health insurance cost projections potentially rising significantly for the coming year.
A stretch of local road was noted as newly eligible for National Highway Freight Network funding, which could in theory fund improvements to a treacherous intersection.

meetings.headline: District previews FY27-29 outlook, asking to restore staff cut in FY26; no vote was taken.
meetings.summary: The select board, finance committee and school committee met jointly to hear a preliminary, forward-looking FY27-29 school budget outlook, explicitly deferring any FY25 questions to a later public forum. The superintendent and business manager walked through contractual assumptions (salaries, health insurance, utilities, transportation) and a series of requested staff restorations -- interventionists, a kindergarten paraprofessional, a world-language teacher, a music teacher, a bridge/TLC program, an ELL teacher, and a debated full-time athletic director/assistant principal split -- framed as restoring FY26 cuts rather than new expansion. No formal votes were taken on any budget item; the boards adjourned after discussion, with several follow-up items assigned to the administration for the next budget cycle.

Next Open Space Committee meetings set for December 10, 2025 and January 14, 2026.

meetings.headline: Town meeting reversed a failed vote to pay Fitchburg the water bills Lunenburg forgot to send for over a year
meetings.summary: This special town meeting worked through 17+ warrant articles, most contentiously a near-failed then reconsidered vote to pay Fitchburg for water bills the town had failed to send to 11 accounts for over a year, plus a $195,790.97 FY26 budget amendment driven by heavy finance-department staff turnover. minutes.headline: Town meeting reversed a failed vote to pay Fitchburg the water bills Lunenburg forgot to send for over a year
minutes.summary: This special town meeting worked through 17+ warrant articles, most contentiously a near-failed then reconsidered vote to pay Fitchburg for water bills the town had failed to send to 11 accounts for over a year, plus a $195,790.97 FY26 budget amendment driven by heavy finance-department staff turnover. Town meeting also funded a storm water utility consultant and a capital cost-estimating fund, created a special education out-of-district reserve fund, raised the senior tax-deferral income limit, adopted an MBTA Communities Act zoning overlay at Tritown, revised SAP personnel/benefit rules, passed over a Kids Kingdom playground transfer and a warrant-mailing change amid public pushback, and narrowly voted down eliminating the town's volunteer personnel committee.

what_happened.line: Town meeting rejected, then reconsidered and passed, paying Fitchburg for water bills the town failed to send to 11 accounts for over a year.
Town meeting approved a mid-year FY26 budget amendment driven by turnover of the finance director, assistant accountant, and payroll coordinator.
Town meeting created a special education out-of-district reserve fund over the finance committee's own recommendation against it.
Town meeting adopted a zoning overlay at Tritown to comply with the state's MBTA Communities Act.
Town meeting narrowly voted to keep the volunteer personnel committee rather than dissolve it.

why_it_matters: The Fitchburg billing lapse left the water enterprise fund short of budgeted revenue, which the finance director said could complicate setting the tax rate, and it is the reason a related capital-fund transfer needed town meeting approval at all.

The new special education reserve fund is a standing account town meeting still controls dollar by dollar, meant to absorb the swings in out-of-district placement costs that have come up in three straight budget seasons.
The MBTA Communities zoning overlay is a compliance vote, not a building proposal by itself, but it sets the multifamily density allowed at Tritown going forward.

The Zoning Board of Appeals held a public hearing on Safe Store Real Estate Company's application for a special permit to build a climate-controlled self-storage facility at 30 Summer Street, replacing a former auto dealership. The applicant's engineer presented site, parking, lighting, and fire department details, the board asked questions on height, materials, use classification, and buffering, and then voted to approve the special permit for the use before adjourning.</parameter>
</invoke>

what_happened.line: The Zoning Board of Appeals voted to approve a special permit for a four-story self-storage facility at 30 Summer Street.
The board chose not to table the matter for planning board review first, saying only the use, not dimensional requirements, was before it.
No members of the public attended the hearing, so no public comment was taken on the project.

why_it_matters: The permit lets a former auto dealership become a four-story storage building, a land-use change residents nearby may notice in scale and traffic.
The applicant's claim that the project will raise the property's tax revenue comes from its own petition materials and has not been verified by the town.

meetings.headline: Committee narrows to three priority capital projects and sets a Dec. 10 deadline for board feedback
meetings.summary: The Master Plan Steering Committee spent most of the meeting reviewing October facility tours of Town Hall, Ritter, and Turkey Hill, then debated how to present capital priorities without formally ranking them, converging on Town Hall/Ritter, Turkey Hill, and Marshall Park as the priority groupings. The consultant walked through feedback from town boards on the draft recommendations and a new implementation table, and the committee set December 10th as the deadline for final comments ahead of a late-January draft report, while also approving several backlogged sets of meeting minutes.

budget_items.what_was_said: A select board member recalled that an earlier version of the project, just rehabbing the existing workspaces in both buildings, had been estimated much lower, and said he'd have supported that scope paired with a Marshall Park project.

budget_items.topic: Scale of the rejected Town Hall project vs. other looming costs
budget_items.what_was_said: A member argued that spending on one large building project without disclosing other looming costs (like TC Pacios) to residents was unfair, citing hypothetical figures.

A member said an earlier discussion had floated a large cost for a PFAS treatment plant serving town water takers, plus ongoing annual maintenance, calling these affordability concerns comparable to building projects.
Cited as an example of another big-ticket, impactful item alongside PFAS remediation and building renovations, in the context of overall town affordability.
A member relayed a conversation with a town official that building sidewalks from Chestnut to Highland, even where the town already has right-of-way, was estimated to cost roughly this much.
A member said the town is currently trying to hire a finance director and argued that Town Hall's poor working environment makes it hard to recruit high-quality candidates.

decisions.decision: Committee agreed it is identifying priority capital projects, not formally ranking them numerically.
Consultant and committee converged on treating Town Hall/Ritter as one linked project, plus Marshall Park and the elementary school (Turkey Hill), as three priority project groupings.
Noted possible headroom for a third debt-exclusion project since older debt-excluded projects will be paid off before the new master plan's 10-year horizon, pending finance committee input.
Agreed to remove the recommendation to reduce minimum lot size for agricultural preservation, since the 5-acre threshold is set by the state and the town has no local authority to change it.
Agreed to revise the senior tax relief recommendation to focus on reviewing whether existing eligibility thresholds are set appropriately, rather than creating new relief.

Agreed to soften recommendation language from the town 'providing' marketing/space-advertising for businesses to 'establishing and maintaining a relationship with the Lunenburg Business Association' to support small business marketing.

Agreed to change recommendation language away from 'establish a town fund' for stormwater infrastructure to more neutral wording (e.g., 'managing'), since the town has not decided between a stormwater utility fund or traditional taxation.
Agreed to repeat/reference Turkey Hill specifically under the schools section even though it's already listed under municipal buildings, given it is the top facilities priority.
Set December 10th as the deadline for the committee's last round of comments/feedback to the consultant on the recommendations and implementation table.
Consultant indicated a realistic target of a draft final report by the end of January.
Committee members encouraged each other to attend the Marshall Park facility tour on Saturday, November 15th at 10:30am.

minutes.headline: Committee narrows to three priority capital projects and sets a Dec. 10 deadline for board feedback
minutes.summary: The Master Plan Steering Committee spent most of the meeting reviewing October facility tours of Town Hall, Ritter, and Turkey Hill, then debated how to present capital priorities without formally ranking them, converging on Town Hall/Ritter, Turkey Hill, and Marshall Park as the priority groupings. The consultant walked through feedback from town boards on the draft recommendations and a new implementation table, and the committee set December 10th as the deadline for final comments ahead of a late-January draft report, while also approving several backlogged sets of meeting minutes.

what_happened.line: Committee converged on three priority capital project groupings -- Town Hall/Ritter, Turkey Hill, and Marshall Park -- rather than a formal ranking.
Set December 10 as the deadline for boards to send final feedback on the draft recommendations and implementation table.
Consultant targeted a draft final master plan report for late January.
Dropped a draft recommendation to lower the minimum lot size for agricultural preservation, since that threshold is set by the state, not the town.
Approved several backlogged sets of minutes from earlier meetings, after a dispute over how abstentions count toward a quorum majority.

why_it_matters: The three grouped projects are the ones likely to come back to residents as capital spending or debt-exclusion votes, so this sets what gets asked for, not yet how much.
December 10 is the last open window for any town board -- finance, planning, school committee -- to change recommendation language before it is fixed in the draft report.
Dropping the agricultural lot-size recommendation means the master plan will not ask town meeting to change a threshold the town has no authority to set anyway.

meetings.headline: Board approved a special permit for a ground-mounted solar array at 560 Mulpus Road, plus a stormwater permit.
meetings.summary: The Planning Board closed out a continued hearing on a Sunny Hill Road stormwater/order-of-conditions matter, approving the stormwater permit with added inspection conditions, then held and closed a hearing for a ground-mounted solar array special permit at 560 Mulpus Road, approving it with conditions on Board of Health septic sign-off and interconnection paperwork. The board also heard from the Open Space Committee chair about adding an Agricultural Commission seat and about the committee eventually becoming an independent, bylaw-based committee, and closed with routine committee reports and board comment on housing and mixed-use financing.

budget_items.what_was_said: The task force is seeking a new stormwater contractor after being unhappy with the prior one and is waiting on the outcome of special town meeting to know whether it has a budget to hire someone new.
The solar applicant said they want approval before the new year so the project does not lose the federal incentives behind it.
A board member said CPTC classes are worthwhile and that the town has money to pay for members' training.

decisions.decision: The revised survey plan for the Sunny Hill Road property will be swapped in administratively with conservation; no new hearing or approval is needed since the lot-line change is minor and does not affect Wetlands Protection Act compliance.
The chair will raise with staff (Brian) getting the legal hearing notice added to OpenGov as standard practice going forward.
The pending Board of Health septic setback sign-off for the solar project will be handled as a condition of approval rather than delaying the hearing.

The Open Space Committee will draft a standalone bylaw, modeled on Medway's, for its own mission and membership, with the planning board remaining the appointing authority, and will bring it to the bylaw review committee before returning to the planning board for a vote.

Mike Tuhill will confirm with the Agricultural Commission and the town manager/town counsel before the planning board formally votes to add an Agricultural Commission seat to the Open Space Committee.
The December 15 meeting room is booked; the November 24 meeting will likely be cancelled if no new hearings are filed in time.

what_happened.line: Board approved a special permit for a ground-mounted solar array at 560 Mulpus Road, conditioned on Board of Health septic sign-off and interconnection paperwork.
Board also approved a stormwater permit for a Sunny Hill Road property, adding inspection conditions covering tree removal, erosion control, and the rain garden.
No members of the public spoke on either hearing.
Open Space Committee raised adding an Agricultural Commission seat and moving toward becoming an independent, bylaw-based committee; no vote taken yet.

why_it_matters: The solar permit sets conditions a developer must still clear before construction can proceed, and the board keeps a hook to revisit panel layout if septic requirements change it.
The stormwater permit's added inspection conditions are the mechanism the town uses to check drainage work actually gets built as designed.

A bylaw making the Open Space Committee independent, and adding an Agricultural Commission seat, would change who sits on it and how it is appointed — a governance change residents may see come back for a vote.

what_happened.line: The committee agreed to a staged, multi-meeting process for deciding whether to renovate or replace Turkey Hill Elementary, starting with building needs before cost or funding options.
Rather than have the facilities director attend the next meeting, the committee will first collect written feedback from Turkey Hill staff on what the building needs.

The committee took first readings on four policies -- advertising in schools, a Monty Tech pathway program, cashless payment at events, and competency determination -- and sent each to a second reading.

The Trust Fund Commission's chairman told the committee that school-related gifts and trusts are town property under statute and asked that scholarship and donor records be turned over to the treasurer's office for review.
The committee approved routine items: two line-item transfers, four donations, and a new scholarship named for James J. Larkin.

why_it_matters: The renovate-versus-rebuild choice for Turkey Hill will eventually come before residents as a building project and a tax question, and how much the state's MSBA program reimburses depends on which path the committee picks.

The four policies now headed to a second reading -- including cashless payment at school events -- will return for further debate before they take effect, and could change how families pay for or access school activities.
A request to catalog school-related trusts and scholarships touches funds set aside for student scholarships and could affect who has authority to approve them.

meetings.headline: Fire and DPW presented decade-long capital plans; committee weighed using the $2.5M stabilization fund for big vehicles
meetings.summary: The Capital Planning Committee heard detailed FY27-FY37 capital plans from the Fire Chief (apparatus, ambulances) and the DPW director (trucks, drainage, bridge, salt barn), including grant prospects and financing tradeoffs. No formal votes were taken on funding besides procedural adjournment; the committee agreed to submit written follow-up questions on the DPW plan and discussed how to weigh the special purpose stabilization fund, possible debt exclusions, and a new state zero-emission vehicle mandate against future requests.

votes.motion: Motion to adjourn

budget_items.what_was_said: Chief proposed replacing the 36-year-old light/medium brush truck, which has had repeated breakdowns; an assistance-to-firefighters federal grant was applied for but is almost certainly not awarded due to the federal shutdown.

budget_items.topic: AFG grant match figures for engine 2 and squad/brush truck
budget_items.what_was_said: Chief described the 80/20 federal match structure and what the town's share would have been for engine 2 versus the larger brush truck grant that was not pursued this cycle.
Chief proposed replacing the 2019 ambulance based on 5%-per-year escalation off the 2023 purchase price, with the retired unit kept as a mechanical spare rather than adding a vehicle to the fleet.

budget_items.topic: Fire: Car One (chief's vehicle), pushed to FY28/FY30
budget_items.what_was_said: Chief recommended delaying replacement of his own vehicle a year, noting good mileage and leaving the decision on vehicle type to his successor.

budget_items.topic: Fire: Squad 3 / heavy rescue pumper, moved to FY29
budget_items.what_was_said: Chief moved this big-ticket heavy rescue/pumper replacement out because engine 2 was the higher priority this year; a rough quote was given based on the vehicle as currently equipped, though new lighter equipment (battery tools) may lower the eventual cost.
Chief proposed spacing replacement of the first paramedic-era cardiac monitors over two fiscal years as they reach the 10-year mark, based on 5%-per-year pricing.
Planned replacement continuing the three-vehicle ambulance rotation, cost estimated on a 5%-per-year escalation from the prior purchase.

budget_items.topic: Fire: Heavy-duty brush truck replacement, FY33
budget_items.what_was_said: This AFG-grant-funded truck would be about 30 years old at replacement; chief suggested a possible future swap to a small tanker given town areas without hydrants.
Mutual-aid engine planned for replacement at a 20-year lifespan, cost based on 5%-per-year escalation from the prior engine purchase.
Another planned ambulance replacement on the 5%-per-year escalation model; committee members remarked on how high the projected price has become.

budget_items.topic: Storm water utility consultant work, warrant article
budget_items.what_was_said: A special town meeting warrant article would transfer old capital funds to finish consultant work needed before a storm water utility option could be presented to voters at town meeting.

DPW requested funds to complete the bridge project after the original contractor failed to follow through; existing grant and FY22 capital funds cover part of the anticipated construction cost, with more needed for engineering and construction.
DPW compared the cost of renting a loader for the winter versus purchasing, finding purchase cheaper over a 15-year life; last winter's four-month rental was costly.

budget_items.topic: DPW: six-wheel dump truck / salt spreader replacements
budget_items.what_was_said: DPW described replacing aging snow/salt trucks, noting the chassis is a fraction of the cost and the upfitting (plow, dump, spreader) is the larger expense; goal is seven trucks for seven snow routes.

budget_items.topic: DPW: one-ton dump truck replacement schedule
budget_items.what_was_said: DPW obtained multiple quotes for routine one-ton truck replacements and requested funding on the high end of the quoted range to buffer against future price increases.

budget_items.topic: DPW: New West Townsend Road drainage design consultant
budget_items.what_was_said: DPW requested funds to design fixes for roughly eleven undocumented, deteriorating drainage pipe locations along the road; design costs would let construction be phased.
A failing 72-inch pipe under Goodridge Street needs replacement; because of the stream width the project may effectively become a small bridge, raising the cost.

DPW requested design funds to replace the aging, damaged salt shed with a fabric-style structure, also enabling anti-icing liquid infrastructure and reduced salt spillage near the municipal water supply.
Two consultants gave rough cost estimates for engineering an anti-icing liquid system (storage tanks, saddle tanks, spray bars) to reduce salt use.
A member reported the fund balance as of annual town meeting, noting the town cannot expect to add to it soon and asking the committee to weigh which size of project should draw on it.
A member flagged that the track and field project would likely require regular borrowing with a debt service on the order described, over a term no longer than the turf's expected life.

transfers.description: Old capital funds transferred to fund remaining storm-water-utility consultant work, via special town meeting warrant article

decisions.decision: Chair accepted the finance committee's proposal to have a member (Jean Russell) sit in remotely on capital planning meetings while the finance committee chair is traveling.
Chair will build a consolidated spreadsheet covering FY27 requests and out-year requests for a broader prioritization discussion in December or January.
Rather than discuss DPW's full multi-year plan live, the committee will submit written questions (directly or through the chair) to be consolidated and read out at a future meeting.
Chair will share a soft/electronic copy of the annotated draft fiscal policy document and send it to the town manager for review, with the committee to bring back thoughts afterward.

meetings.headline: Town manager says finance-department transition is causing substantial, monthslong operational and financial disruption
meetings.summary: The Select Board heard a Lunenburg Snow Riders equipment gift, ratified three town-hire appointments, and voted to sign a Massachusetts Teachers Association-linked advocacy letter to the state legislature on FY27 school funding over one member's objection about scope and a resident's objection about partisanship. The board worked through special-town-meeting warrant articles (voting recommendations on two planning board articles), heard the town manager describe a difficult and costly finance-department staffing transition and a corrected new-growth figure, and set up scheduling for a pre-town-meeting session and a tri-board meeting with the schools before entering executive session on a non-union personnel matter.

budget_items.what_was_said: The Lunenburg Snow Riders donated a portable chainsaw for police/fire use; no vote was needed because it falls under the gift-acceptance policy threshold.
The Snow Riders said they have brought over $200,000 in RTP grants to the community over 15 years, an 80/20 grant with roughly $60,000 representing the club's volunteer match.
The town manager reported actual new growth over the estimated $400,000 as approximately $180,000, correcting a rumor it was over a million.
MassDOT agreed to extend the $600,000 small bridge grant through December 31, 2027, so the town will not lose the funding; construction is now expected to run October 2026 to June 2027.

The town manager listed open positions including a new library assistant hire at 19 hours/week, and vacancies for payroll and benefits (36 hrs/week), dietary aide (9 hrs/week), heavy equipment operator, land use director (40 hrs/week) and recreation director (19 hrs/week).
The town manager corrected the earlier new-growth figure, saying it is actually $118,000, not $180,000.
The town manager is working with the finance director toward roughly $150,000 in FY26 budget adjustments, mostly consultant costs and vacation buyouts tied to the finance department transition.
Retiree health insurance came in about $100,000 higher than budgeted; the town manager hopes to absorb it using contingency positions already parked in the active budget.

what_happened.line: The board voted to accept the LA4 assessment-to-sales ratio report, a step toward setting the FY26 tax rate.
The new-growth figure used for the LA13 report was corrected downward after duplicate entries were found in the state's Gateway system.
The principal assessor was asked to bring back a methodology for spreading the new senior means-tested exemption's tax shift onto other taxpayers.
The board will seek a joint meeting with the select board to consider appointing a new assessor board member.
Review of Clause 18 and a possible GIS vendor change was pushed from November 19 to the December 3 meeting.

why_it_matters: The LA4 report and the corrected new-growth figure are inputs to how the FY26 tax rate gets set, which affects every property tax bill in town.

The senior means-tested exemption removes tax burden from approved applicants and shifts it onto everyone else; how that shift is calculated is still being worked out and returns to the board on November 19.
The November 25 classification hearing is where the select board decides whether residential and commercial property are taxed at the same or different rates.

meetings.headline: Town manager found a capital fund already spent but never closed on the books, needing a town meeting fix
meetings.summary: The Capital Planning Committee heard FY27-FY37 capital requests from the police department (cruisers, hybrid-vs-gas fleet decisions, taser financing) and the school district (primary school driveway/playground, Turkey Hill repairs, technology, and an urgent, still-unscoped track and field project). The town manager reported free cash is not yet certified due to accounting office turnover, and disclosed she found a prior-year capital appropriation that had already been transferred to another project but never closed out on the books across two town meetings, which she is now moving to correct at May town meeting.

budget_items.what_was_said: The traffic car came in on schedule and on budget with money left over; the K9 car saved money because an Explorer hybrid was bought instead of an unavailable Expedition.

budget_items.topic: Hybrid cruiser battery failures / FY27 cruiser fuel type
budget_items.what_was_said: Three hybrid cruiser batteries failed this year; the chief proposed switching patrol cruisers to gas EcoBoost Explorers while keeping hybrids for single-use vehicles, citing battery replacement cost and a price gap between hybrid and gas.

Old tasers lose Axon support/liability coverage in 2029; a 5-year no-interest payment program covering batteries, software and repairs was quoted, versus paying the full cost upfront. The chair raised concern about obligating multi-year capital funds and the town manager explained financing options.

budget_items.topic: Primary school driveway/parking study and expansion
budget_items.what_was_said: A feasibility study and driveway/parking expansion were priced separately; the town manager and facilities director both suggested the playground estimate is likely too low.

Design services and new, smaller ADA/inclusive playground equipment were estimated; the town manager said a comparable rubber-surfaced playground could run far higher, and the facilities director cited an outside quote for surfacing alone plus a rough total.
Window film to reduce cooling costs and UV/impact resistance was requested as the last school to receive it; committee members pressed for actual (not "up to") savings data before ranking it.

budget_items.topic: Turkey Hill hot water tank replacement
budget_items.what_was_said: The nearly 20-year-old tank is beyond useful life and needs replacement.
A redundant server would preserve camera access during an outage or cyber incident.

Two competing quotes were presented for a generator to protect the building during outages; committee members noted this line item's estimate has fluctuated wildly for years and said it will not be appropriated without a reliable quote.

budget_items.topic: Primary school gas condensing boilers, FY29
budget_items.what_was_said: Aging boilers are failing intermittently; a replacement quote was obtained close to the budgeted estimate.

budget_items.what_was_said: Original single-pane windows need a full architectural replacement plan; may later qualify for MSBA accelerated repair funding if Turkey Hill remains a school 25-30 years.

budget_items.topic: Turkey Hill complete window replacement, FY31
budget_items.what_was_said: Full window replacement was estimated, potentially offset by MSBA accelerated repair program funding; the figure was called an older estimate likely to rise.

budget_items.topic: Middle high school projector replacement, FY31
budget_items.what_was_said: Aging wall-mounted projectors need replacement; committee suggested flat-screen displays may be more current technology by then.

The current firewall reaches end of life in FY30; a figure was given for the cost of restoring service after a cyberattack, and a member urged a joint town/school security review before this priority slips further.

budget_items.topic: Turkey Hill renovation or new build, FY32

meetings.headline: Commission tabled a 763 Mass Ave sewer easement to weigh extending service down Chestnut Street
meetings.summary: The Sewer Commission held two public hearings on Massachusetts Avenue sewer easement waivers. meetings.headline: Board votes to recommend MBTA Communities compliance via a density bump at Tritown, not new sites
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Planning Board endorsed a routine ANR lot-line adjustment for a Unitil substation expansion, then continued a contested storm water permit for 255 Sunny Hill Road to November 10 after abutters raised unresolved drainage-pipe and lawsuit concerns and outstanding taxes on the property surfaced. The board then closed public hearings and voted to recommend to town meeting both an MBTA Communities compliance bylaw (achieving compliance by raising the density cap at the existing Tritown development rather than opening new land) and a minor amendment removing a paving requirement from the common driveways bylaw, alongside routine committee reports and administrative votes.

In discussing development pressure, a board member cited the current median home assessment as an example of why builders want to build wherever they can.

The chair reported that Richard Harris is again being retained by the town as interim consultant/land use manager, after a prior gap caused by limits on his allowed hours, not any problem with the working relationship.
The chair noted the Capital Planning Committee begins hearing department requests this week and expects to function more as a ranking committee again this year given competing priorities.

Board agreed not to schedule a meeting three days before Christmas.

Chair will draft written material for the next meeting laying out why the zoning bylaw needs a full rewrite, to support future funding requests for a consultant.
Board directed the storm water applicant and the abutter to try to work out details of the pipe/culvert plan before the November 10 meeting.

The change to public comment practice affects how residents get an item onto a Planning Board agenda going forward.

reconciliation.what: Our minutes against the minutes the town published. caption_error = the same fact the captions rendered badly, resolved by the official reading shown beside the as-heard one; discrepancy = a substantive difference, flagged and not resolved. A reader should also check the sick-leave language change, since the official minutes note the terms were "harmonized" without saying which term ("doctor's note" vs. "doctor's certificate") was kept, and whether the three-consecutive-day threshold was actually changed or just discussed.

meetings.headline: Chair says town may owe money back to poor-fund accounts over unresolved 2008 and 2017 loans
meetings.summary: The Trust Fund Commission spent most of the meeting on the chair's legal review of municipal gift and trust law, including a disclosure that 2008 and 2017 disbursements from the Worthy Poor Fund were never followed up on for repayment, raising a question of town liability. The board also walked through a draft investment/operating policy line by line without voting on it, and ratified minutes from two prior meetings before adjourning.

budget_items.what_was_said: The chair explained that a trust document must be valued at no more than a stated dollar threshold and be older than a stated number of years to qualify for an administrative ruling from the Attorney General's Office of Public Charities to modify a vague declaration.

2017 meeting minutes documented a motion approved to disburse a sum from the earnings of the Worthy Poor Fund to a resident, with a planned six-month follow-up to determine ability to repay that the chair says never happened.
A 2008 letter signed by the then-chairman directed a sum in rent arrears be paid from the Worthy Poor account on behalf of a resident; no follow-up minutes on repayment were found.

budget_items.topic: Statutory investment limits on trust funds
budget_items.what_was_said: State law caps the share of trust funds that can be invested in bank or insurance company stocks once the trust exceeds a stated total value, and caps the share in any single bank or insurance company's stock.
The chair noted the state's municipal depository trust pool, which the town does not use, was recently paying a stated daily rate.

meetings.headline: Task force voted to approve a scaled-back, roughly half-cost stormwater utility study proposal from Weston and Sampson.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Stormwater Task Force reviewed a revised, scaled-back proposal from consultant Weston and Sampson for a stormwater utility feasibility study, after members had met with the firm to cut scope items including background data collection, a DPW capabilities assessment, and an ArcGIS online tool, in order to roughly halve the cost. The task force voted to approve the revised proposal dated October 10, 2025, discussed funding it via reappropriation of unspent old capital project money through a November town meeting warrant article, and received an update that earthwork on their demonstration BMP project is complete with a kiosk and drainage grates still to be installed.

budget_items.topic: Task 1 - background data collection and review
budget_items.what_was_said: The task force said this task was cut from the Weston and Sampson scope, though there was confusion in the room about which task number this was.
The online web application/tool, done mostly by communities tiered within SFH, was removed from the scope; the underlying GIS delineation of commercial parcels was said to remain.

budget_items.topic: Impervious cover GIS data layer - parcel count and cost
budget_items.what_was_said: The number of parcels to be covered by the impervious-cover GIS layer was discussed with several conflicting figures read off different copies of the proposal; the group settled that around 700 parcels, covering commercial and non-single-family properties, would be included.

budget_items.topic: Minimum square footage threshold for GIS parcel review
budget_items.what_was_said: The minimum square footage a property must have to be looked at was raised from the original Concord-based proposal figure to a higher figure in the new proposal.

The task force discussed removing most of the fee-structure work since they feel comfortable with what was already proposed for the town's own tiers, leaving Weston and Sampson to do a smaller review/advisory pass.

budget_items.topic: Task 2 cost - fee structure review, town vs. Concord comparison
budget_items.what_was_said: The cost for this task was compared to what Weston and Sampson charged Concord for similar work, and the new town figure was read out.
This task's cost was reported to have stayed the same as the prior proposal; printing and distribution costs are not included in the scope.

budget_items.topic: Meetings and project management scope and cost
budget_items.what_was_said: The number of small-group, public, and monthly progress meetings was cut roughly in half to a third, and the associated cost was reduced.

budget_items.topic: Total revised Weston and Sampson proposal cost
budget_items.what_was_said: The task force said the overall proposal cost was brought down substantially from the original figure after asking the consultant what budget they were targeting.

budget_items.topic: Task force's own budget vs. proposal cost
budget_items.what_was_said: A member said their current budget does not cover the new proposal cost and described a worst-case shortfall, noting the town manager has it covered but more money is still needed.

budget_items.topic: Reappropriation of old, unspent capital project funds
budget_items.what_was_said: Funding for the stormwater work is proposed to come from previously allocated but unspent capital project money, to be reappropriated via a town meeting warrant article.

decisions.decision: Task force confirmed removal of the background data collection task (Task 1) from the Weston and Sampson scope, per their prior meeting direction.

meetings.headline: Consultants presented Lunenburg's draft master plan -- 8 goals, ~80 recommendations -- ahead of a December report; no votes held.
meetings.summary: This was the sixth and final public information session on Lunenburg's master plan, led by the steering committee chair, planning board chair Matt Brener, and consultants from OverUnder. The consultants walked through eight community-derived goals (housing options, farmland protection, small business support, open space/recreation, community gathering spaces, municipal building prioritization, school facilities, and resilient infrastructure) and roughly 80 supporting recommendations, then described a three-part implementation strategy (an implementation committee, a filter checklist, and an implementation table) before residents asked about the adequacy of public input and how town government might respond; the session then moved into hands-on breakout activities with no formal votes taken.

public_comment.topic: questioned whether the process gathered the right public input and whether the eight goals accurately reflect the town, given low attendance at this session
public_comment.stated_role: a resident who has participated in the master plan steering committee process

public_comment.topic: asked how town government/municipal officials are likely to respond to the plan's recommendations

budget_items.topic: cost-tier framework for master plan recommendations (low/medium/high cost)
budget_items.what_was_said: The consultant proposed working cost categories for recommendations -- low, medium, and high -- to be tweaked with town staff feedback. Low and medium cost items were described as coverable within an operational budget, high cost typically not.

budget_items.topic: possible tax relief for senior citizens
budget_items.what_was_said: As property values and tax rates rise it becomes a greater burden for those on fixed incomes, so the plan may recommend the town consider tax relief for seniors. No figures were given.
A recommendation to establish an affordable housing trust was described as a clearinghouse to help identify funding opportunities for new homeowners, not a funding source itself.

A recommendation to create a fund to help preserve farmland when land goes up for sale, possibly giving the town a right of first refusal, so it stays open space rather than becoming developable land.
A recommendation to establish a town fund dedicated to stormwater infrastructure and maintenance.

decisions.decision: The consultants plan to hand the completed master plan report to the town in December.
The group agreed to move from Q&A directly into the breakout activity sessions, with further questions to be handled there.

meetings.headline: ZBA approved a special permit for a used-car lot at 149 Summer Street, capping it at 12 display cars.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Zoning Board of Appeals held a public hearing on an application by Philip S. Smith to operate a used/secondhand motor vehicle sales lot at 149 Summer Street, a site currently used as a gas-station-turned-repair-garage. Board put on the record that all repair work must be conducted inside the building.

what_happened.line: Select Board voted 3-2 to pull the APDC/Historical Commission merger article from the special town meeting warrant.
The vote followed extended public opposition and a town counsel review of legal questions the merger raised.
The board voted 4-1 to recommend the special education reserve fund article, after a member flagged a possible hidden future budget impact.
The noise ordinance article was deferred and will not appear on this warrant, pending further work.
The board voted to include and recommend the 41A senior tax deferral article, raising the decades-old income threshold for that exemption.

why_it_matters: Pulling the merger article means the Architectural Preservation District Commission keeps separate authority over historic-district reviews, at least until a future town meeting takes it up again.
The 41A article, if approved by voters at the November 18 special town meeting, would let more senior homeowners qualify to defer their property tax bills.
The special education reserve fund article changes how the town could set aside money for special-ed costs; it carries no budget impact yet, but a member noted it could down the road.

meetings.headline: Committee narrows town building priorities to Town Hall/Ritter and Turkey Hill; TC Pacios left undecided
meetings.summary: The Master Plan Steering Committee approved three sets of prior minutes and reviewed feedback from other town committees on its draft master plan recommendations. Most of the meeting focused on prioritizing major town building projects for the next decade, converging on Town Hall/Ritter and Turkey Hill as the top near-term priorities, with Marshall Park and TC Pacios as the next tier, while leaving the Brooks House slated for sale or lease rather than town investment.
