A member noted the town manager had asked the select board to put a roof repair project for TC Pacios before voters at a special town meeting, but no long-term use for the building has been established.
A member asked what dollar threshold was used to decide which building projects made the priority list, contrasting a smaller project size against the multi-million-dollar ones already listed.

A member said the list was built around projects that would cost more than the capital planning committee's annual budget could typically cover, describing that threshold as roughly a million dollars.
A member clarified that a prior town meeting appropriation for a specific section of the TC Pacios roof could not simply be redirected to other roof work without going back to town meeting.
A quote was obtained for repairing the entire TC Pacios roof, and the town did not move forward with it because it would need to go through the regular capital planning process.

decisions.decision: Keep the Brooks House and 925 Mass Avenue on the building list as slated for sale or lease, not for town capital construction spending.
Limit the near-term prioritized building list to roughly five projects: Town Hall/Ritter, Turkey Hill, then Marshall Park and TC Pacios as next in line.
Treat the middle/high school athletic field improvements as already moving forward as a separate submission to the May annual town meeting, off this prioritization list.
The chair will follow up separately with the planning board, and the library committee (meeting the next night) will relay any feedback on the Brooks House within a couple of days.

minutes.headline: Committee narrows town building priorities to Town Hall/Ritter and Turkey Hill; TC Pacios left undecided
minutes.summary: The Master Plan Steering Committee approved three sets of prior minutes and reviewed feedback from other town committees on its draft master plan recommendations. Most of the meeting focused on prioritizing major town building projects for the next decade, converging on Town Hall/Ritter and Turkey Hill as the top near-term priorities, with Marshall Park and TC Pacios as the next tier, while leaving the Brooks House slated for sale or lease rather than town investment.

what_happened.line: The committee narrowed its near-term building priority list to Town Hall/Ritter and Turkey Hill, with Marshall Park and TC Pacios ranked just behind.
Brooks House and 925 Mass Avenue stay on the list as candidates for sale or lease, not for town capital construction spending.
Athletic field improvements at the middle/high school are already moving forward as a separate item for the May annual town meeting, outside this list.
A roof repair project for TC Pacios may go before voters at a special town meeting, though no long-term use for the building has been settled.
The committee approved minutes from three prior meetings, with corrections, and reviewed feedback from other town committees on its draft plan.

why_it_matters: This priority list is an early step toward what capital projects the town could eventually ask taxpayers to fund, so where a building lands on it -- or off it, like Brooks House -- signals what kind of ballot question residents may see later.
A TC Pacios roof question at a special town meeting would be a near-term vote, separate from this longer-range prioritization.

The threshold discussed for what makes this list -- roughly projects beyond the capital planning committee's typical annual budget -- shapes which future building repairs residents vote on directly versus which are handled through routine capital planning.

meetings.headline: Commission voted to give its chairman broad authority to investigate town land sales and trust-fund handling.
meetings.summary: The Trust Fund Commission chair delivered an extended report on the commission's research into its fiduciary duties over gifted real estate, scholarships, cemetery funds and historical assets, citing case law (Woodward School for Girls v. Quincy, Cohen v. Lynn, Carol v. Select Board of Norwell) to argue the town may owe proceeds from sold trust land back to designated purposes. The commission adopted a distribution application, voted to give the chairman authority to contact state agencies on trust matters, voted to pursue college interns for research, ratified prior minutes, and voted to pursue a declaration-language change for American Legion funds; no land sales were found or reversed at this meeting.

The chair said a 2017 distribution from the worthy poor fund was structured with a repayment arrangement rather than an outright gift, plus another distribution in 2008, and he is still researching whether it was ever repaid or minuted.

decisions.decision: Rewriting the risk policy was tabled until the vice chair reviews and edits it, for discussion at the next meeting.
The chairman will keep revising the commission's proposed written policy as new case law is researched.

meetings.headline: Water Commission delays a vote on a roughly $90,000 PFAS pilot study, awaiting DEP input before a special town meeting
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Water District Commission spent most of the meeting debating whether to fund a Tighe & Bond pilot study, priced around $86,000-$90,000, testing pH effects of combining Kings and Lancaster Ave. well water before PFAS treatment; commissioners and residents disagreed sharply over whether the study was necessary and whether Hickory Hills should be included, and the board deferred a special town meeting vote to the next meeting pending word from DEP. The board also covered ongoing Rolling Acres water main work, a MassDOT drainage/paving fix, an unresolved Woodlands kayak rack zoning violation, and early discussion of replacing an aging backhoe, with no purchases decided.

budget_items.what_was_said: Tighe & Bond did not submit a full proposal but gave a budget number for a pilot study that came in about double what was expected; laboratory sampling was later reduced to lower the figure.
A commissioner recalled the district once had a large sum available that went unused, contrasting it with the current hesitation to spend on the pilot study.

budget_items.what_was_said: Including Hickory Hills in the combined-treatment plan would add the cost of a transmission main to Kings on top of the base plan.
A resident noted the PFAS master plan update figure coincidentally matched the pilot study figure, calling it a strange coincidence.
Commissioners asked for a hypothetical budget figure for a given length of pipe; a figure was given that did not include engineering costs, and a larger figure was also mentioned.
In discussing replacing the aging JCB backhoe with a wheeled excavator, a rough cost comparison between two machine options was mentioned.

transfers.description: appropriating money from surplus, via a special town meeting, to fund the PFAS pilot study

decisions.decision: Deferred scheduling a special town meeting vote on pilot study funding to the next commission meeting, to allow more time to hear back from DEP.

Agreed to set up a follow-up meeting between the superintendent, the Tighe & Bond engineer, and the vocal resident commenter to go through the cost/technical questions before presenting to the public.
Directed staff to request that the Woodlands' representatives provide a definitive written plan to remove the kayak racks from the Zone 1 area by the October 22 meeting.
Asked the superintendent to bring comparative budget numbers for water main replacement costs to the next meeting.
Directed staff to put together options and pricing for replacing the aging JCB backhoe, tying the purchase discussion to a broader capital improvement plan rather than deciding now.

meetings.headline: Board can't fund new means-tested tax exemptions in Munis; approved contingent on fixing that.
meetings.summary: The Board of Assessors reviewed routine assessing operations -- exemption and abatement processing, chapter land applications, removal of unsupported functional/economic obsolescence discounts, and pending vendor-supplied interim property valuations -- and worked through several minutes approvals. The most substantive discussion was that the town has no established mechanism to fund newly-authorized means-tested property tax exemptions, so the board planned to approve the current applicants contingent on resolving how the cost will be spread across taxpayers; the board also reviewed a GIS/mapping software proposal and discussed staffing and office-hours pressures. The meeting closed by entering executive session to discuss abatement/exemption applications under the statutory exemption for such proceedings.

budget_items.what_was_said: The office reported four abatement requests and 43 motor vehicle excise tax abatements processed in Munis for September, awaiting payment processing by the tax collector.
FY2026 real estate exemption applications were mailed September 1st with an April 1 deadline; applications received by mid-November will still be applied to the next tax bill.
The 41D exemption amount was increased with a cost-of-living adjustment, and income/asset limits were adjusted at town meeting for both 41D and 17E/F.

budget_items.topic: Social security income deduction for 41D eligibility
budget_items.what_was_said: After consulting DLS, the assessor confirmed a social security income deduction can be applied to 41D applications, which brings some previously-excluded applicants back into eligibility.
Chapter land applications for fiscal year 2027 are due December 1st, and the office is now requiring all supporting paperwork before processing.

budget_items.topic: Roll-back tax invoice, 222 West Townsend Road
budget_items.what_was_said: A roll-back tax invoice was prepared after a chapter land property lost its exemption; the select board reportedly declined right of first refusal.
The FY2026 smart-growth cost report covering motor vehicle excise and additional property tax revenue, largely tied to Tri Town Drive, was submitted to DLS and the state; growth funding is expected.

New growth in tax dollars for residential, commercial, industrial and chapter land was reported, with personal property growth from a vendor still pending and expected to exceed the town's original estimate.

budget_items.topic: DLS request to accelerate free cash reporting
budget_items.what_was_said: The board noted a DLS request to accelerate free cash certification and said it needs to check with the town accountant on timing.
Discounts removed after inspections or non-response totaled a stated tax-assessed value and tax-dollar impact, following a Department of Revenue order to remove unexplained discounts.
A separate set of economic obsolescence discounts (excluding commercial items handled by the vendor) was removed, with a stated assessed-value and tax-dollar impact.
The board noted the 41A income limit had been unchanged for exactly two decades at a stated figure, which had caused at least one prior applicant to be rejected.

budget_items.topic: 41A adoption/interest rate proposal from Council on Aging
budget_items.what_was_said: A warrant article submitted via the Council on Aging proposed adopting 41A (already state-mandated and previously adopted) and lowering its interest rate; the assessor called it unnecessary and duplicative.

budget_items.topic: Roll-back taxes, chapter land release (six lots)
budget_items.what_was_said: A chapter land parcel is being released from chapter status, generating roll-back taxes with interest, with the property expected to become six new house lots.

budget_items.topic: GIS/mapping software ("One Map"/Data Scout) proposal cost
budget_items.what_was_said: A proposed GIS mapping and field-data platform was compared against the town's existing CI/CAI mapping contract, with a net annual cost increase discussed for switching or adding the new service.

Eight applications for a means-tested exemption were reported as qualifying, representing a small share of the tax levy, but there is no method in Munis to implement the burden-shift the statute requires.

budget_items.topic: Overlay account as possible funding source for means-tested exemptions
budget_items.what_was_said: The board discussed whether the overlay reserve account could absorb the cost of the means-tested exemptions, noting that is not the account's intended purpose.
The board discussed wanting to increase the part-time inspector/assistant's hours, citing a backlog of roughly 500 needed inspections, ahead of the May town meeting.

decisions.decision: Assessor will apply the DLS-confirmed social security income deduction to 41D applications, restoring eligibility for some applicants close to the income limit.
Assessor asked the Town Manager's office to document the Select Board's declination of first refusal on 222 West Townsend Road in a letter for the file.
Board asked the assessor to have future sales reports sorted by percent change rather than by ratio, and broken out by neighborhood/site index.
Board agreed to hold off requesting a new sales report from the vendor until the Department of Revenue submission process is complete.
Revised 41A warrant article draft (with added income explanation) to be submitted to the Town Manager ahead of tomorrow's deadline.
No action needed on the Council on Aging's proposed 41A adoption/interest-rate warrant article, since 41A is already state-mandated and previously adopted; feedback given to the Town Manager.
Board will approve the eight qualifying means-tested exemption applications tonight contingent on later resolving how they will actually be funded/implemented in Munis.
Assessor will forward Westford's disabled-persons exemption criteria for the board to consider drafting a comparable local-option exemption.
Room reservation for the October 15th meeting will stand for now, to be cancelled if the date changes.

Two applicants (a deck project and a dock project) were told their work actually requires the more involved RDA process, not a simple administrative determination, with fees credited toward the new filing.

why_it_matters: The driveway approval sets wetland-protection conditions for a four-lot residential project, with two years of required monitoring.
Homeowners proposing tree removal, decks or docks near wetlands may be routed into the longer, costlier RDA review depending on how much ground work is involved.
Closing out a wetlands permit requires a stamped as-built plan on file; without one, the compliance certificate can be denied even after work is finished.

meetings.headline: Committee backed a special-ed reserve-fund warrant article but withdrew a separate bid for extra Chapter 70 money
meetings.summary: The committee voted to put a special reserve fund for unbudgeted out-of-district special education and transportation costs on the November town meeting warrant, approved two new paraprofessional positions and restoring a full-time IT support position, and heard quarterly budget, athletics, and facilities reports. After extended debate, a second proposed warrant article to immediately appropriate roughly $22,185 in additional Chapter 70 funding was withdrawn in favor of seeking it through the regular FY27 budget process, and a proposal for an outside comprehensive/forensic audit of FY25 finances was deferred pending further talks with the town manager; the committee also discussed what to do about football and soccer uniforms that had been purchased without proper authorization.

what_happened.line: The committee voted to place a special reserve fund for unbudgeted out-of-district special education and transportation costs on the November town meeting warrant.
A separate warrant article seeking additional Chapter 70 funding, an amount as heard, was withdrawn in favor of pursuing it through the regular FY27 budget process.
The committee approved two new paraprofessional positions and restoring a full-time IT support position, both drawn from the salary reserve line.
A proposal for an outside comprehensive audit of FY25 finances, funded from returned free cash, was deferred pending talks with the town manager.
Football and soccer uniforms bought without required purchase-order approval will not be penalized retroactively; undistributed soccer uniforms will be held for next year's replacement rotation.

why_it_matters: The reserve fund is a warrant article residents will vote on at November town meeting; it would let year-end school budget surplus automatically cover special education placement and transportation costs that come in over budget.
Withdrawing the Chapter 70 warrant article means any additional state aid this year would not be spent immediately but would instead be weighed against other priorities in the FY27 budget process.

The unauthorized uniform purchases and the salary-reserve-funded hires prompted the committee to signal it will develop a policy requiring pre-approval before staff spend outside the certified budget.

budget_items.what_was_said: The agreement's insurance clause for MART was holdover language never actually charged; town staff said it was a cleanup, not a substantive change.

budget_items.topic: DPW snow/ice: own equipment vs. hiring out
budget_items.what_was_said: Bill Bernard said an analysis showed it is cheaper to use town equipment and operators than to hire private vendors, based on the cost of the highest-paid heavy equipment operator.
The DPW director plans to request a new CDL-class dump truck in this year's capital request, noting the price has risen sharply since he first priced the same truck in 2022.
The DPW director said the department has run a deficit in the snow and ice budget over the last five years and plans a 2.5% annual increase to reduce, but not eliminate, it.
Failure to comply with the federal MS4 stormwater permit could carry penalties, though the director does not expect the town would actually be fined that amount.
The DPW director said the plan is a flat annual fee for residential properties, with a sliding scale for businesses based on impervious surface.

budget_items.topic: Storm water utility revenue target vs. current spending
budget_items.what_was_said: The DPW director said the target is to collect roughly a set amount annually through the new utility, well above what the current storm water/drainage budget spends.
The DPW director gave a preliminary multi-year capital outlook covering equipment replacement and drainage/bridge engineering and construction.

budget_items.what_was_said: The director said drainage and storm water line items would need to be higher in FY28 and FY29 if the utility is not approved, compared with if it is.

A board member asked whether fair share money promised when voters supported the tax would continue; the DPW director said that was uncertain.

The facilities director noted the building now carries a commercial internet cost, mainly for the public access studio, higher than he expected.

The chief summarized the combined increase across hiring and overtime lines needed to fund a fourth shift.

budget_items.topic: Fire Dept. total requested expense-line increase
budget_items.what_was_said: The chief gave the total requested increase across the department's expense lines.

budget_items.what_was_said: The chief said the new contract calls for salary increases over the next three years, with expenses otherwise level-funded.

meetings.headline: Superintendent signals schools want to keep the ACE program and central offices at Turkey Hill, shrinking the town hall project.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Municipal Building Design Committee interviewed new Superintendent Dr. Fortuna, who said the ACE program must stay collocated with the director of special services and that the superintendent's office does not need to be collocated with the town manager — a reversal of the prior superintendent's stated need that had driven significant square footage into the Ritter/town hall renovation plan. The committee treated this as a major finding that could shrink its project scope, discussed reduced need for a single consolidated town hall given growing online town services, set two Brooks House tour dates with the facilities director, and scheduled its next meeting for October 20th to get the town manager's input on collocation needs.

meetings.headline: Commission voted to draw an extra $10,000 from the sale-of-lots fund to cover hedge and grounds work.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Cemetery Commission approved three sets of prior meeting minutes, reviewed cemetery fund expenditures and balances, and voted to draw an additional $10,000 from the sale-of-lots fund to cover hedge trimming and grounds work. The board also received updates on the North Cemetery backlot expansion engineering survey, South Cemetery stone wall repairs, burial and niche-wall activity, grant options, and historical headstone repairs, and set its meeting schedule through the winter before adjourning.

budget_items.what_was_said: The board reviewed a spreadsheet listing recent expenditures already approved by motion, including flower plantings, a file cabinet, SIMS software maintenance, and North Cemetery hedge and stone wall work.

budget_items.topic: Remaining amount owed on approved projects
budget_items.what_was_said: After the backlot expansion (funded from the capital plan) was set aside, a remaining balance was calculated for the other approved but unpaid expenditures.

budget_items.topic: Perpetual care and capital transfer fund allocation
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair allocated last year's expenditures between the perpetual care fund and the capital transfer fund.
After subtracting the allocated amounts, remaining balances were calculated in both the perpetual care fund and the capital transfer fund.
The board worked through what total funds remained after the committed expenditures were subtracted, concluding they did not yet have enough for the remaining hedge trimming work.
The sale of lots fund was identified as an available source to draw additional money from.

budget_items.topic: Additional draw from sale of lots fund
budget_items.what_was_said: The board voted to request an additional amount from the sale of lots fund to cover the shortfall for hedge trimming and related work.

budget_items.what_was_said: The engineer's fee for the site survey and plan phase of the North Cemetery backlot expansion was discussed, funded from the capital plan allocation.
After the engineering cost, the board discussed how much of the capital plan allocation for the backlot expansion remained.

budget_items.topic: Hedge trimming and hedge planting expenditures
budget_items.what_was_said: The board distinguished between an already-approved amount for purchasing and installing new hedges and a separate, not-yet-approved amount for trimming existing hedges.

budget_items.topic: South Cemetery stone wall repair cost
budget_items.what_was_said: The board confirmed it had agreed to pay a set amount for a contractor to begin rebuilding a collapsed section of the South Cemetery stone wall, to be reassessed once that amount is used.
The board discussed pursuing a Massachusetts preservation projects grant but noted this cycle's deadline was too close to prepare an application in time.
The board agreed to get a price to repair damaged half-headstones for a historical family plot, using salvaged stone rather than new monuments.

budget_items.topic: Children's grave marker and plaque cost
budget_items.what_was_said: The board discussed getting a price from a monument company for a granite marker and bronze plaque to mark several unmarked children's graves, using stone Bill already has on hand.

decisions.decision: Backlot expansion bid work will be scheduled for summer rather than winter.
Hedge trimming will be done on a two-year cycle going forward.
South Cemetery stone wall repair will be completed before starting similar work at North Cemetery, done one section at a time.
Next meetings set for October 30th and November 19th, with a target of meeting again in the second week of December rather than skipping to February.
A SIMS software training session will be scheduled separately and will not be publicized or recorded as a regular open meeting.

meetings.headline: Task force to slash Weston & Sampson stormwater fee-study scope to fit budget, then bring it to the Town Manager
meetings.summary: The Stormwater Task Force reviewed a new, expensive scope-of-work proposal from consultant Weston & Sampson for a stormwater utility fee study and worked through cutting it down task by task -- excluding residential parcels from impervious-area assessment, dropping two tasks entirely, and reducing the number of public and progress meetings -- to bring a smaller cost figure back to the Town Manager. They also approved prior minutes by roll call, discussed funding the study via a Chapter 90 transfer instead of a special town meeting, gave input to the master plan steering committee, and set the next meeting for October 16.

budget_items.topic: Weston & Sampson stormwater utility feasibility study proposal
budget_items.what_was_said: The task force reviewed a new cost estimate from Weston and Sampson (successor to prior consultant CI) and said it "breaks the bank," prompting discussion of reducing the scope of work.
A member asked how much is left to spend on the storm water initiative; Bill said the demonstration BMP would draw further from that same pool, leaving little remaining.

Members questioned where CI's parcel counts came from, since the GIS database was updated more recently than CI's report; they discussed narrowing the number of parcels needing individual impervious-area review by excluding residential codes.
A member estimated that excluding residential parcels and other scope cuts to Task 3/Task 4 would save a meaningful amount.
Members discussed a target figure they are trying to reach for the overall consultant scope, referencing a number below what was originally proposed.
Members discussed whether bills should go out quarterly or twice a year to save printing/mailing cost, noting the per-bill amount would simply be larger if billed less often.

budget_items.topic: Revised total scope-of-work cost after cuts
budget_items.what_was_said: A member did quick math on cutting Task 6 meetings in half and eliminating Tasks 2 and 4, arriving at a reduced total to bring back to the Town Manager.

budget_items.topic: Comparison to prior consultant CI's pricing
budget_items.what_was_said: Members compared the new reduced estimate to what CI had charged for a comparable scope including BMP and storm water utility work.

budget_items.topic: Chapter 90 funds as possible funding source
budget_items.what_was_said: Rather than a special town meeting request, a member suggested transferring available Chapter 90 highway funds into the storm water study, noting the town may receive a larger Chapter 90 allocation this year that has not yet arrived.

budget_items.topic: Town budget capacity for the study
budget_items.what_was_said: A member noted the town's contact (Jen) does not have funds on hand to cover the study's cost either, reinforcing the need to reduce scope before returning to her.

decisions.decision: Modify Task 3 of the Weston & Sampson scope to exclude residential parcels (and related codes such as condos) from individual impervious-area review.
Remove Task 2 and Task 4 from the proposed scope of work, and reduce Task 6 to one small-group meeting, two public presentations, and five monthly progress meetings.
Take the reduced scope-of-work cost figure to the Town Manager before proceeding.
Explore transferring available Chapter 90 highway funds to cover the study cost rather than seeking money at a special town meeting.
Set up a call/Zoom with Weston & Sampson, with one or two task force members participating, to discuss reducing the scope of work.

Respond to the master plan steering committee's questionnaire identifying the storm water infrastructure fund item, and taking the position that storm water infrastructure also counts as a resiliency strategy for conservation land.
Produce a durable (tin/aluminum) sign for the storm water BMP kiosk describing what the demonstration BMP is and how it works, then hand the design off to be fabricated.
Set the next meeting date for October 16.

meetings.headline: Entire town finance department is turning over at once; a new finance director starts October 20
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Finance Committee heard that the town's entire finance department is turning over — the finance director, the payroll/benefits administrator, and the assistant accountant are all leaving, with a new finance director, Katie McKenna, hired to start October 20 and interim coverage in place. The committee also reviewed a master planning committee questionnaire (voted to send it), previewed the upcoming tri-board meeting and the town meeting warrant (including dropping a TC Pacios roof repair article and possible personnel board and pay-plan changes), and discussed ongoing efforts to reconcile school budget data, without resolving the underlying discrepancies.

budget_items.topic: TC Pacios roof warrant article / FY23 capital appropriation
budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager recommended not moving forward with a partial roof repair warrant article; the prior FY23 appropriation would stay attached to that year's capital projects and be reappropriated through the normal capital planning process rather than returned to free cash.

budget_items.topic: School budget $600k underrun / current fiscal year baseline
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair described ongoing questions to the superintendent and new business manager about a reported underrun and where money went relative to the current fiscal year's budget baseline.

budget_items.topic: School department purchase orders and encumbrances
budget_items.what_was_said: A member described how duplicate or unclosed purchase orders inflate apparent spending, citing figures that moved as POs were closed and money was freed up as encumbrances were resolved.

decisions.decision: Chair's completed master planning committee questionnaire responses would be sent to the master plan steering committee as filled in.

The partial TC Pacios roof repair will not proceed as a warrant article; the roof project will instead go through the normal capital planning process, with the prior FY23 appropriation left in place for reappropriation.
Finance committee will aim to review the Q1 FY26 Munis report at its October 23rd meeting.
Town finance policies review will be brought back onto the agenda in November rather than waiting until the end of the calendar year.

meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Water District Commissioners reviewed and signed the warrant, approved prior minutes, and discussed a proposal from Verdantis/a hydrogeologist to investigate potential bedrock well sites near 361 Mass Path, deciding to get test-well pricing before signing any agreement. They also voted on a policy formalizing employee use of district vehicles for on-call response, received an update on the Rolling Acres water main replacement project (including a failed-then-repeated bacteria test and future equipment needs like a skid steer, sweeper and trailer), discussed a poorly-executed private trench dig on Harbor Road that had to be redone to proper depth, and heard extended public comment from a resident challenging the necessity and cost of an additional DEP-driven pilot study on treating water from the Kedings well.

budget_items.topic: Cost to drill a bedrock test well
budget_items.what_was_said: After the site study, drilling and testing an actual bedrock test well was estimated as a further cost, separate from the site study.

what_happened.line: The Zoning Board of Appeals voted to grant a special permit reducing the minimum lot size at 32 Spring Street so a new single-family house can be built.
The lot-size problem surfaced after a zoning district split between RA and RB was found on the property, following an earlier ANR plan that had already been endorsed.
The board left the boundary of the septic-system area where the plan showed it, though the applicant's engineer said its exact placement had some flexibility.
No members of the public attended or commented on the petition.
The chair read the standard conditions and appeal rights attached to the special permit after the vote.

why_it_matters: The permit allows a smaller lot than the bylaw normally requires so a new house can be built, based on a septic system serving the neighboring house at 31 Spring Street sitting partly on this lot.

The case shows how a zoning district boundary running through a property can create a lot-size problem even after an earlier plan for the same land was already approved, which matters to anyone splitting or building on property near a district line.

meetings.headline: Committee tentatively ranks Turkey Hill/schools, Town Hall, and Ritter as the town's top three capital priorities.
meetings.summary: The Master Plan Steering Committee reviewed feedback trickling in from town boards (Open Space, APDC, EDC, Council on Aging, Capital Planning) and heard that the town lacks several statutory plans, including an unfinished emergency management plan. meetings.headline: Commission may lose unused recreational-trails grant money if a Dec. 31 deadline isn't extended

budget_items.topic: Northfield Road culvert alternatives and cost
budget_items.what_was_said: The applicant's engineer said DEP's alternatives-analysis form asks for cost information even though the commission itself does not consider cost a factor in permitting. He said the wider alternatives would only increase cost with no offsetting habitat benefit.

budget_items.topic: Solar tax credit deadline (560 Mopus Road)
budget_items.what_was_said: The applicant's representative said they are trying to get the ground-mounted solar system installed and activated before the end of the year, citing the tax credit going away and winter weather, to help the homeowner.
Under old business, the chair noted the conservation budget, now called the land use budget, with no updates to report.

Mary explained the current recreational trails grant, funding engineering/permitting for three parking/access projects, closes December 31st; the Mulpus project consumed about 50% of the award, two other projects (Table Rock, Cry access road) are stalled on wetland and agency issues, and she has asked the grant administrator whether an extension is possible.

decisions.decision: DPW will handle work on abutting private property via a temporary, unrecorded grading access letter agreement with the homeowner rather than a recorded easement, for the Northfield Road culvert project.

The commission determined it cannot approve work on someone else's property without written permission from the property owner in hand, and will require that before acting on the Northfield Road culvert NOI.
Going forward, applicants' engineers should respond to DEP comment letters in writing, uploaded to the OpenGov portal, so there is a record of the response.
No replacement planting or replication is required for the 20 dead trees removed at 44 Hemlock Terrace, given the density of remaining mature trees and understory shown in Mary Wilson's site photos.
The chair/grant contact will ask the state grant administrator whether an extension can be requested on the recreational trails grant before its December 31 close.
The master plan steering committee feedback spreadsheet will be placed as its own agenda item at the next meeting so commissioners have more time to review and comment.

meetings.headline: FY25 school budget surplus of roughly $600K traced largely to a grant line double-budgeted, unspent
meetings.summary: The School Committee reviewed a reconciled FY25 budget surplus, with the business manager and superintendent explaining it stemmed mainly from a paraprofessional line double-budgeted against a grant plus general underspending on maintenance, custodial and instructional lines, none of which affected the separate cuts made for FY26. Extensive public and committee questioning pressed on accountability, Munis reporting reliability, and the need for regular budget-to-actual reporting and backup support for the business manager going forward. The committee also worked through a draft FY27 capital plan, debating how to finance a needed turf field/track replacement alongside a possible solar revenue project, and took votes on line-item transfers, a music program donation, a grant application, new legal counsel, and added secretarial hours at the high school.

meetings.headline: Committee elects new chair, narrows scope to town hall/Ritter/Brooks House, and pushes for a town-wide capital priority list

minutes.summary: A reconstituted Municipal Building Design Committee elected a chair and vice chair, then reset its charter after a prior building project failed at the ballot: the plan now focuses on renovating Ritter/town hall and rehousing PAC and ACE (in the Brooks House) rather than building new space in town hall. what_happened.line: The committee reset its charter to renovating town hall/Ritter and moving PAC and ACE out of town hall into the Brooks House, dropping the earlier new-construction plan that failed at the ballot.
Members elected Dave Blad as chair and Tony as vice chair, both by unanimous votes.
Several members pushed for a town-wide capital project priority list, citing a wide range of figures for what combined major projects could cost, before any plan goes back to voters.
The committee plans to interview town departments directly, tour other town halls, and set its next meeting for September 29.

why_it_matters: Any renovation of town hall/Ritter or relocation of PAC and ACE into the Brooks House will eventually come back to residents as a debt-financed building project.
How this project is ranked against other large capital items, such as Turkey Hill and Marshall Park, will shape how much residents are asked to approve and when.

minutes.headline: Trust Fund Commission got its first detailed investment briefing in years; no votes taken
minutes.summary: The Trust Fund Commission held an afternoon meeting mainly to question its investment manager, Bartholomew and Company, about how the town's pooled trust funds are managed, fee structure, the shift to the prudent investor rule, and expenditure oversight. what_happened.line: The Trust Fund Commission cast no votes, but got its first detailed briefing in years from investment manager Bartholomew and Company on fees, strategy and the shift to the prudent investor rule.
The commission is still waiting on the town manager to decide whether the town's workers' compensation fund would join the pooled trust investments.
The chair agreed to rewrite the commission's written policy to spell out members' right to pull funds from the pool and invest independently.
For outdated trust documents, the commission decided to pursue attorney general cy pres filings rather than probate court.
The next regular meeting was set for October 9 at 5:00 p.m.

why_it_matters: Trust funds cover things like cemetery and perpetual-care accounts, so how they're invested and who can withdraw from them affects programs that draw on that money.
Moving the workers' compensation fund into the pooled investments would change how a town liability obligation is managed and reported, pending the town manager's answer.
A rewritten withdrawal policy and a plan to publicize the funds in the special town meeting booklet could open an application process residents or boards may want to use.

meetings.headline: Commission approved shutter and rooftop cupola changes for a Main Street building; no vote yet on town green/center input
meetings.summary: The Architectural Preservation District Commission corrected the record on a previously approved determination of applicability (fixing an address from Three Main Street to One Main Street) and approved a new determination of applicability for shutters and a rooftop cupola at the same Main Street building (Bad Larry's/Hilltop Farms convenience store), owned by Lunenburg Village Realty. The bulk of the meeting was spent working through a master plan steering committee questionnaire about a proposed town green near TC Pacios and the adult activity center and a town center development plan, with members discussing gazebo relocation, population density, and conditions under which they would support demolition of nearby buildings, but no formal vote on the questionnaire answers was captured before the recording appears to end.

decisions.decision: Commission agreed to correct its August-approved determination of applicability to show the address as One Main Street rather than Three Main Street, since no Three Main Street exists in town assessors' records.
Commission agreed it would support relocating the current town green gazebo, noting it is not historic and citing traffic and parking concerns, for input to the master plan steering committee.

Commission agreed to tell the master plan steering committee it supports reuse and opposes demolition of the Brooks House, while demolition of the TC Pacios building would be acceptable in exchange for increased density in a town center redevelopment.

meetings.headline: DEP is pressing the district to force relocation of Woodlands' kayak racks out of the Zone One wellhead area
meetings.summary: The Water District Commissioners discussed a dispute with the Woodlands over kayak racks that DEP is expected to require moved out of the Zone One wellhead protection area, agreeing to wait for DEP's official letter before responding further. The superintendent reported the Rolling Acres water main replacement was nearly complete and on schedule, and the board discussed pursuing a multi-year capital plan for main replacement, next steps on PFAS testing near Keyes (requiring a future warrant article), and eventual replacement of aging excavation equipment. The meeting closed with a motion to enter executive session to discuss employee reviews.

meetings.headline: No quorum was reached; members informally discussed heat pump, solar and geothermal grant projects
meetings.summary: The Green Community Task Force never reached a quorum, so no official business or votes occurred; present members had an informal conversation about past and possible energy projects. They discussed the mini-split heat pump project at the schools (framed as both AC and heat, which unlocked grant funding), geothermal well drilling at another school, frustration over losing track of Turkey Hill's solar panel savings after the installer went out of business, predatory solar sales tactics, whether the town's ground-mount solar bylaw needs updating, and the group's ongoing push to get town departments to seek grant money before requesting town meeting funds. meetings.headline: Capital Planning re-elected its officers and began FY27 planning, tabling fiscal-policy threshold changes.
meetings.summary: The Capital Planning Committee reorganized for the year, re-electing its chair, vice chair, and clerk, then laid out its FY27 capital planning timeline: department submissions due by end of September, committee review meetings in October and November, and a final ranked list to the town manager by early December. Members reviewed a draft fiscal-policy document (proposed changes to the capital-item dollar threshold and useful-life standard), discussed grant funding uncertainty, gave initial feedback to the master plan steering committee's questionnaire, and approved prior minutes; no capital-plan figures were finalized at this meeting.

A member suggested plugging estimated placeholder numbers for known-but-undesigned future work like bridge repairs, even without a specific project identified.

budget_items.topic: Capital item dollar threshold and useful life
budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager reviewed a DLS best-practice recommendation to raise the small-capital-item dollar threshold and questioned whether minimum useful life should move from three to five years.
A member recalled the committee last raised the threshold a couple of years ago somewhat arbitrarily rather than through rigorous analysis.
A member said that aside from a federal grant for fire apparatus, departments generally have little grant funding available for routine, recurring capital needs.
A member said state grant funding is increasingly available for culverts, stormwater and hazard mitigation work, even as federal grant money for the same purposes disappears.
The town manager explained the draft fiscal policy document originated from a community-compact best-practices grant the prior town manager obtained with the state Division of Local Services.
The town manager said the town is already paying for the Clear Gov platform and wants to use it, but does not want it to become a burden on department heads.
A member cited a rough total figure discussed for a Turkey Hill renovation project, noting any significant work there would trigger major building-code thresholds.
A member noted the committee spent ARPA money last year on a consultant study comparing rebuilding versus renovating Turkey Hill, and said he disagreed with the consultants' conclusions.
The town manager said the draft fiscal policy would add a requirement that the committee make a financing recommendation in certain borrowing situations.
A member argued the capital plan should weigh projects against available funding sources, borrowing capacity and free cash, not simply present a ranked list of projects.

decisions.decision: The committee will pursue both its annual prioritized capital list for the town manager and a longer-term five-year plan with a financial-planning component this year.
Department heads' capital submissions are due before the end of September, with committee vetting to begin in October.
The committee will plan for roughly five meeting nights in October and November to review capital proposals.
Final capital-plan rankings are expected to be finalized and voted at meetings in the first or second week of December.
The committee agreed it is wise to hold additional capital planning meetings during the town's budget process, as done last year.

The committee will take as homework whether to raise the small-capital-item dollar threshold and lengthen the minimum useful-life standard, possibly carving out police cruisers, ahead of the next meeting.
The committee will not require department heads to complete Clear Gov/Collins scoring this year, leaving evaluation criteria to the committee's own discretion.
The committee agreed to consider holding an additional meeting in late September to finish the fiscal-policy discussion and answer the master plan steering committee's questions.
Members expressed general openness to moving the committee's meeting start time earlier, to accommodate town staff schedules.

meetings.headline: District disclosed a roughly $582,000 unspent FY25 school surplus that went unnoticed and unbudgeted for.
meetings.summary: The School Committee's meeting centered on a newly discovered FY25 budget surplus of roughly $582,000 (about 2% of the budget), far above the district's normal cushion, which the chair and later the business manager attributed to poor financial oversight rather than known wrongdoing. The committee approved FY25 line-item transfers and a warrant, heard the superintendent's and building principals' start-of-year reports (including the first-day fire at the middle/high school), reviewed an FY27 budget timeline, and discussed a possible best-practices/forensic audit, a stabilization fund for out-of-district special education placements, and extra Chapter 70 money for a fall town meeting warrant article; several residents used public comment to press for accountability and clearer FY25-vs-FY26 budget transparency.

minutes.summary: The Water District Commissioners reviewed the ongoing Rolling Acres water main project, discussed doing future main replacement in-house versus hiring it out and a possible multi-year warrant article for equipment and staff, and heard a clerk's report on PFAS settlement checks and legal limits on spending them. A lengthy public comment period featured a resident pressing the board to add a combined Keating-well/Lancaster treatment option to its public survey, which the board said would require a DEP-mandated pilot study and likely its own warrant article at a special meeting; no formal vote was taken on that question.

The public survey on future treatment options will stay open roughly 30 to 60 days while the district plans outreach.

why_it_matters: A pilot study and any related equipment purchase would likely require a warrant article at a special town meeting, a vote residents would be asked to take.
How PFAS settlement money can be spent is now constrained by a legal-vote requirement the board says it did not previously understand, affecting the pace of well and treatment work.
The treatment-option survey open to residents may or may not include a combined Keating-well option, pending confirmation of DEP pilot-study requirements.

meetings.headline: Sewer Commission began drafting new sewer regulations for accessory dwelling units after meeting with town counsel

meetings.headline: Commission approved a 5-year plan to hand-harvest and chemically treat invasive weeds at Lake Wham's town beach.
meetings.summary: The Conservation Commission heard several wetlands notices of intent and requests for determination, approving driveway, septic, deck, wall and tree-removal projects in buffer zones, and continuing two hearings (68A Laurel Lane for a missing NOI number, and a Tanner Cole common driveway pending peer review) to September 3rd. The most significant action was approval of a five-year order of conditions for the town's Lake Wham aquatic plant and algae management program using hand/diver-assisted harvesting and herbicides near the public beach, conditioned on an annual report. Two certificates of compliance and one tree-removal request were left unresolved pending agent follow-up or a site visit.

what_happened.line: The Commission approved a five-year order of conditions for the town's Lake Wham aquatic plant and algae management program, hand-harvesting and using herbicides near the public beach, with an annual report required.
The plan favors hand-harvesting over costlier diver-assisted suction and relies on the town website and social media rather than mailed abutter notice ahead of herbicide treatments.
Two hearings were continued to September 3: Ashley Owens's 68A Laurel Lane project, missing its NOI number, and Tanner Cole's common driveway, pending peer review.
The Commission also approved several driveway, septic, wall, deck and tree-removal projects in wetland buffer zones, and issued negative determinations for a well and a deck project.
Two certificates of compliance and one tree-removal request were left unresolved, pending agent follow-up or a site visit before the next meeting.

why_it_matters: The Lake Wham approval sets a five-year plan for herbicide use near the town beach, with notice to residents handled through the town website and social media rather than a mailed abutter list.
Wetland buffer-zone approvals for driveways, septic systems, walls and tree removal show how the Commission conditions rather than blocks routine residential projects near water.
Two properties (68A Laurel Lane, Tanner Cole's driveway) and two certificates of compliance remain undecided, affecting those owners' pending work.

meetings.headline: Commission says pooled trust funds sat effectively uninvested for two years despite a signed advisor contract
meetings.summary: The Trust Fund Commission (two members present, one vacancy) spent most of the meeting reviewing the town's contract with private trust company Bartholomew, raising concern that pooled trust funds have gone roughly two years without being actively invested despite fees being charged, and that fee/trading-volume transparency is inadequate. Members also reviewed the terms of several individual trusts (the Worthy Poor Fund, American Legion Post 283, a workers' compensation insurance fund under MGL c.40 §13A), discussed the commission's belief that its statutory advisory authority extends beyond its five named funds to other pooled trusts (e.g., cemetery, conservation), and began a read-through of a draft investment-procedure policy. The only votes taken were procedural: approving prior meeting minutes and adjourning, both said to pass unanimously.

budget_items.topic: Investment advisor and trading fees vs. net return
budget_items.what_was_said: A member said the fees charged relative to the net return the funds are getting are very disproportionate, calling it a split. He said trading fees on top of the management fee are unclear because trade volume/churn is unknown.
The chair initially read the contract's annual management fee as 20% before correcting himself, with Richard's help, to 2%; both said even 2% of the pool is a large sum for the town.
The chair read per-trade charges from the contract's Schedule A for stocks, ETFs and closed-end funds, plus additional fees if e-delivery is not used.
The chair described a handwritten 1901 declaration by a man named Nathaniel Day giving money to Lunenburg (and Shirley) for the benefit of the worthy poor.

budget_items.topic: Worthy Poor Fund and American Legion Post 283 balances
budget_items.what_was_said: Members compared recent fund balances, with some confusion between the figures for the Legion's Post 283 fund and the separate worthy-poor-type Legion fund, settling that the Lunenburg Post 283 fund and the worthy poor fund each held roughly this amount a few months earlier.

The 2013 trust declaration allows dispersements up to a set amount per year to veterans, and once the fund exceeds a threshold, up to a share of that year's interest can be dispersed to grow the fund.

The chair read the statute governing a town-established workers' compensation insurance fund, capping the annual appropriation as a fraction of equalized valuation and capping the fund itself once it reaches a stated share of that valuation.

budget_items.topic: Cemetery Commission withdrawal from the pooled trust fund
budget_items.what_was_said: Reviewing a fund report, members noted the cemetery fund had a transfer/withdrawal during the period while no other funds in the pool had any, which the chair cited as an example of spending he considers excessive.

budget_items.topic: Overall size and return of the commission's pooled funds
budget_items.what_was_said: A member noted the trust fund commission's own funds are comparatively small and asked what protects them if larger funds in the same pool incur fees from frequent withdrawals; another cited this fund total and a return rate to argue the pool is otherwise performing reasonably well net of unknown fees.

decisions.decision: The commission will continue operating with two members and a quorum while seeking a third member to fill its vacancy.
The commission will arrange a meeting with the private trust company, Bartholomew, to ask about fee levels and how many trades are executed on the pooled funds.
The chair will meet with town counsel Adam Costa around the 26th to discuss comparable towns' trust fund commission practices and next legal steps, including the cy pres doctrine question.
Rather than debate the draft investment procedure policy line by line tonight, the commission will do a read-through first and take up detailed discussion/amendments at this and a following meeting.

meetings.headline: FinCom reviewed draft town financial policies (audit, budget, capital, debt) line by line; no policy votes yet
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Finance Committee heard public and member concerns about an unexplained ~$200,000 in unspent school funds and a school athletics revolving-fund deficit, and about how the school's new business manager was hired without town finance staff involvement. Most of the meeting was spent going section-by-section through a draft town financial policies document (based on a DLS/GFOA template merged with the chair and finance director's own best-practices draft), covering audit selection, budget process, capital planning, and debt management, with the committee raising numerous edits but taking no formal vote on the policies. The committee also planned upcoming tri-board topics (health insurance analysis, culture/recreation programming) and discussed whether to hire a full-time parks and recreation director before resolving open staffing and facilities questions, then approved prior minutes and adjourned.

budget_items.what_was_said: A resident asked the committee to address a report that money was found unspent in the school budget.
A member noted the town passed an override last year and that the unspent school money is part of that override amount.
Beyond the override, the town gave the schools additional money this year toward their budget.
The school athletic revolving account went negative and the school used other unspent budget money to offset it.
A member added the figures together to argue a large sum did not go toward items presented at town meeting.
Additional Chapter 90 road funds came through this year, raising the town's allocation.
The town manager reported a net increase in state aid across various sources, with no plan yet on distribution.
A state fund is being split among 13 communities via a state agency, with rules on use still undetermined.
The town still holds a large unspent Chapter 90 reserve that could fund a big project.
Achieving a GFOA distinguished budget presentation typically requires hiring a consultant.
Draft policy language would have the town strive to appropriate a target share of the general fund budget to capital, net of debt.
Draft debt policy cites a statutory debt limit tied to the town's equalized valuation.

decisions.decision: The town manager will merge her DLS-based draft financial policies with the chair's and finance director's separate best-practices document, gather Finance Committee feedback section by section, then bring the combined document to a Finance Committee vote before sending it to the Select Board.
The committee will pause further detailed review of the capital planning and debt management policy sections until the Capital Plan Committee has weighed in, then circle back.

Detailed parks-and-recreation staffing/maintenance questions will be worked out in an offline meeting with the parks chair and facilities director rather than at the full tri-board meeting.

meetings.headline: Assessors are uncovering decades-old, undocumented property valuation discounts of roughly 10-60%.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Board of Assessors received a lengthy status report from the principal assessor covering motor vehicle excise processing in the new Munis system, chapter land rollback taxes and applications, and a systematic finding of long-undocumented functional and economic obsolescence discounts on commercial and residential properties that the board is now reviewing property by property. The board also discussed FY2026 senior exemptions and the new circuit-breaker-linked senior means-tested exemption, updated statewide chapter land value tables, approved several sets of amended executive-session minutes, voted to decline purchasing a parcel on West Townsend Road, and set a plan to respond to a town master-plan feedback survey.

budget_items.what_was_said: The principal assessor reported abutters list requests and motor vehicle excise tax abatements processed in Munis this month, awaiting payment processing by the tax collector.
Four chapter land rollback tax invoices were sent to former chapter landowners in June; one has paid, one status unknown, two have not responded.

budget_items.topic: Functional/economic obsolescence discounts on chapter land, commercial and residential properties
budget_items.what_was_said: Inspections found undocumented obsolescence discounts on many properties dating back years, averaging around 60% with a range starting near 10%; the board asked for a spreadsheet to see the scope.

budget_items.topic: Chapter land (agricultural) use-value cost table update
budget_items.what_was_said: The principal assessor updated statewide chapter land cost/value figures, moving crop/vegetable/tobacco/soil/nursery land to an 'above average' rating; the board questioned whether reclassification was justified given the size of the increase.

budget_items.topic: FY2026 senior real estate exemption COLA
budget_items.what_was_said: The cost-of-living adjustment for the FY2026 senior real estate tax exemptions was confirmed and added to the updated exemption sheet.

Residential/commercial/industrial new growth for FY2026 was estimated, with personal property and utility appraisals still pending; last year's and this year's earlier estimates were recalled for comparison.

The principal assessor explained that seniors who did not qualify for the state circuit breaker cannot qualify for the new local senior means-tested exemption, and the circuit breaker can be claimed retroactively three years by the filer but not administratively by the assessors this first year.

budget_items.topic: 41 warrant article for income limitation increase
budget_items.what_was_said: The board needs to confirm the town meeting date so a warrant article raising the income limitation for exemptions can be prepared in time.

decisions.decision: Put the property obsolescence/abatement review (with correlation to prior abatements and recommendations) on the September 3rd agenda for a possible vote.
Until told otherwise, a person receiving a veteran exemption who also becomes eligible for the new senior means-tested exemption should be allowed to receive both.
Defer deciding the frequency/timing of senior-center outreach sessions to the September 3rd meeting.
Postpone DOR's request to limit land condition factors until neighborhood value corrections are further along; add to a future goals list.
Keep the updated 'above average' chapter land agricultural values as already entered for this year and research the history of the rating in the meantime.
If called for jury duty on the day of a future meeting, the board member will try to participate by phone rather than in person.
The principal assessor will draft a proposed response to the master-plan feedback questionnaire for the board to review before September 3rd.
Cancel the September 24th meeting (a member cannot attend) and set the next September date as TBD.

meetings.headline: Committee unanimously recommends the town not exercise right of first refusal on a 222 West Towns Road parcel
meetings.summary: The Open Space Committee welcomed two new members (from the Parks Commission and Planning Board), approved minutes from a prior joint meeting, and unanimously voted to recommend the Select Board not exercise the town's right of first refusal on a 13-acre Chapter 61 parcel at 222 West Towns Road, finding it did not meet the committee's open-space criteria. The committee also noted its open space plan was extended by the state to 2029, took on a homework assignment from the town's master-plan steering committee, and rescheduled its next meeting to September 3rd.

budget_items.topic: Open space plan extension / grant eligibility
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair reported the state approved extending the open space plan from a seven-year to a 10-year plan, valid through fiscal year 2029, which lets the committee keep applying for open space grants through June 2029 without redoing a plan update next year.

budget_items.topic: Chapter 61/61A/61B tax status on 222 West Towns Road
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair explained that landowners in chapter 61 (forestry), 61A (agriculture) or 61B (conservation/recreation) get a lower tax rate, and if they sell for development they exit chapter status, pay back taxes, and the town gets a right of first refusal to match a sale price.

decisions.decision: Chris agreed to take minutes for tonight's meeting since the clerk, Eric, was absent.

The committee moved its next meeting from September 10th to September 3rd (Zoom) because the chair will be out for hip replacement surgery and the vice chair, Anna, will be in Scotland on the 10th; the following meeting reverts to the regular schedule on October 8th.
The committee decided the September 3rd meeting will remain remote on Zoom rather than in person.

Members agreed to individually review the town master-plan steering committee's spreadsheet before the September 3rd meeting, share notes informally, but not deliberate on it by email (only at a posted meeting).

meetings.headline: Committee sets fall timeline: Oct 1 committee feedback, Oct 22 public forum, plan to Nov town meeting
meetings.summary: The Master Plan Steering Committee reviewed a proposed report structure and the plan's eight community goals with its consultant, discussed how to format and prioritize roughly 100 recommendations, and spent significant time on implementation strategy, town technology/digitization needs, and getting the town's other boards to submit feedback by October 1. No funding was voted; the committee set a schedule of an October public information session, a November town-meeting presentation of the draft plan, and a subsequent Planning Board vote, and approved several sets of past meeting minutes.

budget_items.what_was_said: The consultant proposed that each master-plan recommendation note its funding sources and a rough order-of-magnitude cost (small vs. large) alongside a short/medium/long time frame. The committee discussed adding a simple cost-tier legend so readers can gauge scale.
Members discussed indexing recommendations with dollar-sign symbols to signal rough cost, giving examples of small, medium and large project sizes.
A member noted the town had applied for a competitive state IT grant due earlier in the year and hoped it would be offered again next year to fund technology upgrades.

budget_items.what_was_said: Members said two capital articles -- Marshall Park improvements and a municipal building project -- failed at town meeting this year, attributing it largely to cost concerns and competition with school budget pressures.

meetings.headline: Sewer Commission weighed letting a developer easement across town land for a new subdivision, decided nothing yet
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Sewer Commission heard a developer's request for a sewer-line easement to serve a planned common-driveway subdivision on Sunny Hill Drive, and spent much of the meeting debating the precedent such an easement could set for future development and accessory dwelling units. Members also approved the FY29 minutes and the FY2026 billing commitment, discussed a billing-system glitch, an upcoming Town Council meeting on ADU sewer bylaws, a DPW school-supply fundraiser, and got an update on the manhole repair project, without making any final decision on the easement itself.

public_comment.topic: Asked the commission's permission for a sewer line easement across his own land off Sunny Hill Drive/West Street to connect a planned four-house common-driveway subdivision to town sewer, citing a recent bylaw change allowing common driveways and a similar project he had built in Ashburnham.

budget_items.what_was_said: The quarterly bill run went out but took six days due to a software/system upgrade with the billing vendor that caused printing errors, including old 2023 bills reappearing. The issue reportedly affected other municipalities using the same vendor, not just Lunenburg.

budget_items.topic: FY2026 notice of commitment / billing amounts
budget_items.what_was_said: The commission needed to review and sign off on the FY2026 billing commitment amounts and the percentage of past-due accounts; the percent-past-due figure could not be updated until the next demand notice run. A member agreed to stop by the DPW office to sign it.

The commission recalled having discussed a possible flat-rate connection fee for accessory dwelling units of two bedrooms or fewer, with additional-bedroom scaling similar to regular connections, but noted the bylaw currently requires a separate connection to the street for every dwelling.

The commission discussed possibly spending a small amount from its budget on popcorn or cotton candy for the DPW's Touch a Truck/school-supply fundraiser, with one figure mentioned as an upper limit before a commissioner offered to donate his own cotton candy machine instead.

decisions.decision: Ed McWeeny was asked to assemble a full package/presentation, including potential problems avoided by the easement, before bringing the Sunny Hill Drive easement request to a formal hearing.
Two commission members agreed to attend the August 21 Town Council meeting on the ADU sewer bylaw question, since a quorum of the commission itself could not attend.

The commission will accept school-supply donations for the Touch a Truck event at the DPW office, and a commissioner will bring a table and a personal cotton candy machine rather than the commission purchasing supplies.
The manhole repair project is expected to be completed before the first frost, once a subcontractor is scheduled to replace framing and covers.
A formal request for the Sunny Hill Drive easement/extension will require a noticed public hearing, with at least five days' newspaper notice.

meetings.headline: Task force stalled on a stormwater utility fee because the underlying impervious-area data is a decade out of date
meetings.summary:
The Stormwater Task Force reviewed a consultant's answers to prior questions and discovered the state's impervious-area GIS data underlying its proposed fee structure has not been updated since 2016, undercounting many developed and expanded properties. The group discussed revising ERU fee tiers, weighed funding the work through a dedicated utility versus the DPW's operating budget, and decided to seek updated parcel data from the assessor's office before setting any fee, with the next meeting tentatively set for September 25th.</parameter>
</invoke>

attendees.role: presenter, Comprehensive Environmental (storm water utility fee consultant)

votes.motion: End/adjourn the meeting

budget_items.what_was_said: The task force asked why the most recent data showed 17 large-area properties subject to the fee versus 21 in earlier data; the consultant said some properties turned out not to be subject to the ERU fee.

budget_items.topic: Parcels subject to the ERU fee
budget_items.what_was_said: The consultant said about 543 parcels have been identified as subject to an ERU-based fee, excluding residential, town-owned, and no-impervious-area parcels.

budget_items.topic: Original memo property count vs. new count
budget_items.what_was_said: A member noted the original memo cited roughly 4,800 properties, which the consultant clarified excludes residential and town-owned parcels.

budget_items.topic: Proposed ERU tier and fee structure
budget_items.what_was_said: The consultant proposed expanding ERU tiers so tier one pays $60 per equivalent unit and a new top tier covers 200 or more units, to reduce the revenue gap.
One equivalent residential unit was defined as 4,200 square feet of impervious area, the basis for all tier calculations.

The DPW director's draft budget for the program, after removing Chapter 90 and one-time purchases, was cited at several figures before the group settled on roughly 873 as the revenue target for fee-setting.

budget_items.topic: Capital project money within the draft budget
budget_items.what_was_said: The draft budget included $300,000 a year for stormwater projects, though the DPW director said current annual project spending is less than $100,000 due to staff and funding limits.

budget_items.topic: Indirect costs in the utility budget
budget_items.what_was_said: The DPW director modeled about $10,000 in indirect/administrative costs into the utility budget, patterned on the sewer enterprise fund.

budget_items.topic: New staff positions funded by the utility
budget_items.what_was_said: The DPW director confirmed the plan involves three new hires, including a dedicated stormwater equipment operator and a GIS engineer, funded through the proposed utility rather than the operating budget.

The consultant suggested a cutoff (e.g. 100 square feet) below which small residential impervious areas would not be billed, which would remove about 80 properties and roughly $4,800 from the fee schedule.
A property near Lunenburg/Shirley previously listed with minimal impervious area was found to have close to 19 acres (roughly 800,000 square feet), prompting talk of adding higher fee tiers.

budget_items.topic: Correction to the large-property ERU estimate
budget_items.what_was_said: The consultant corrected her earlier figure, saying the large property is closer to 197-199 equivalent residential units, just under the proposed 200-unit top tier.

The consultant's data showed about 580 acres of right-of-way parcels, mostly one large parcel, while the DPW director's own pavement survey put town-owned roads at 238 acres, differing from an earlier-cited figure of 383 acres.
A member noted potential fines of up to $50,000 per day for MS4 noncompliance, though nobody could confirm any town had actually been fined.

budget_items.topic: Estimated ERU fee for the Walmart/Mass Ave property
budget_items.what_was_said: The consultant's spreadsheet showed the Walmart-area commercial parcel at roughly 202 equivalent residential units, which a member questioned as seeming low for the size of the property.

decisions.decision: Task force will ask the assessor's office (Linda McQuade) for a list of parcels newly built or occupied since 2016 to help cross-reference impervious-area changes.
Task force will pursue expanding ERU fee tiers beyond the current tier 10 to capture very large properties like the ~19-acre site.
Sarah Dewal (Comprehensive Environmental) will send the task force an updated parcel spreadsheet and the presentation slides by the next day.
Next meeting set for September 25th rather than the usual third Thursday, due to a member's unavailability.
Task force will try to set up a conversation with 'Jen' about the cost of hiring a dedicated consultant for the utility rollout.

Commission approved an amended order of conditions for a scaled-down warehouse project at 260 Vuola Road, conditioned on submitting grading-change documentation.

Members discussed gaps in tracking multi-year follow-up conditions on approved projects in the town's permitting software, with no fix decided.
Commission issued five certificates of compliance and approved removal of one dead tree, and resolved a wetland-boundary dispute at 390 Howard Street.

why_it_matters: This covers wetlands permitting near lakes and residential lots -- decisions that set conditions landowners must follow before building or altering land near protected areas.
Commissioners raised recurring concerns about one delineation firm's wetland-flagging accuracy, which affects how reliably nearby projects' buffer and boundary conditions are set.
A gap in tracking required follow-up inspections (like plant-survival checks) means some approved conditions may go unverified as town staff turn over.

The cable contract expires February 28, 2028; a figure was mentioned in this context but was not audible clearly.

meetings.headline: Commission will keep funding Marshall Park design but delay the next town-meeting vote about a year
meetings.summary: The Parks Commission spent most of the meeting deciding what to do with remaining ARPA and capital design money for Marshall Park, concluding it will keep funding the design but will not bring the project back to town meeting this November, instead waiting roughly a year given the town's broader financial uncertainty. It also heard a skate park funding/construction update, discussed a capital-planning wish list, and reviewed how little park user fees cover of actual maintenance and school-field rental costs compared with other towns, without changing fees.
